"CONSIDER THE. LILIES, HOW THEY GROW." Leku xii, 27. • Swevit by Soft zephyrs sweet and low, ?, 'Fair rows of wild white lilies blow - Along the dusty way, • ,Full in their loving Maker's view; • ' No blushes stain their snowy hue, For they are pure alway. , What human lineaments could brook Those shining eyes, that searching look, And not be dyed with shame I • The denizens of field and grove ' •:t Meet unabashed his look of love, Eternally the same His "friends" o'er fancied dangers fret, For simple faith reigns not as yet Within each rugged breast. . • But He, their Lord, with gentle hand Points only to that fragrant band, And lulls their fears to rest. • To-day Mong our path they gleam, They.bend to kiss the quiet stream • Or witch the wilderness; • To-morrow, swept by ruthless steel, They lie all crushed beneath our heel In shattered 10-veliness. •Born for a day, yet does their bloom OutvierheAvonderS of the loom, And mock the skill of man! Shall we be cared for less than they,. We who await an endless day, . When spent otir earthly span? This was the simple lesson, when The Lord rebuked those anxious men And bid repining cease. They see the lilies' spotless snows, And lo through every bosom Rows A stream of rerfeet eace! • • .3.raftazine. • - F. B. Dora-rm.,.

A shopkeeper having put a law case in charge of a writer, that it might be prosecuted through the various ftagm in the supreme civil court, called frequently to inquire how it was getting on. The case having at length gone before the Lords, was taken by them, ac- cording to the Scottish legal phrase, to avizandum, that is to say it was taken, Into consideration. When this stage had been reached a long delay occurred; and still, When the honest trader called to: ask about his case, he was told it was at avizandum. " Avizandum," said he at length, with an expression of great impatience, "what keeps't sae tang, at avizandum? Can ye tell me whaur this avizandum is? Is't on the •Sauchieha' road, or whaur ? tak' a noddy or the stage, and if it be —within ten miles o' gate I'll heel or I sleep." The Vorthy man would probably find in the long run that when cases have gone to avizandum they are not so easily overtaken as supposed. An amusing story is told of the late Mr. Justice Byles. The learned judge was an excellent shorthand writer, baying early in life graduated ;.s.s.:a reporter. At the Somerset Assizes on one occasion, as was customary, he read portions of the evidence to the jury, but floundered hopelessly in the middle of a sentence.., There was an '.-.awkward pause, and the jury and bar nervously awaited the result. His Lordship at last, after many efforts to decipher the missing word, dropped his dignity, and, leaning over towards the reporters „below, inquired:— " Can any of you ,gentlemen assist; me to; a word heti? I have not put in the vowels, and what I have in ray book looks as if a witness had said, 'Go and call in the baby,' but—with a puzzled look—it can't he that,the- e'ause there is no baby in the case' One of the reporters was equal to the occasion, and putting the vowel in the right place, the word "bobby" was the result, and the Judge continued his charge. Tax Morm's Nesr.—The mole is a splendid architect and sure builder. It constructs perfect subterranean galleries. The nest is a wonderful building, bearing im- mediately above it as much earth thrown up as would till a moderately-sized wheelbarrow. The soil roof of the nest is so strong that an ox may safely stand on it, in spite of its being surrounded and intersected by runs, by which the family can separately escape in case of sudden danger. In one I saw there were at least, within -a-foot from the nest, four main runs; and these main runs, again, had three immediate branch runs towards _the_uest from the wheatfield, making twelve within two feet of the neat, while there were as many escapqruns _towards the surface for hiding. A favourite place:for nests isjabout old broad hedge roots, • where the moles bare plenty of room, and where their nests are concealed by the undergrowth, which again protects their surface runs from being trampled by the hoofs of horses or cattle. --krid the moles nesting on either side of the hedge stick religiously to their own side of the field. Between the and the water there is a main run, and to an inex- perienced eye its only distinguishing feature is that it is somewhat more direct than the other runs. Butlahe mole catcher observes it in an instant, and he catches most moles there at the time whenthe moles are return- ing home from their food or water. Ikis wonderful how the moles find their long ways home,j,and it is remark- able the distance they travel; every itwenty-four : hours, in the ins and outs and confusing number of intersected runs..—James Purses, in Good Words. RICK AND POOR.—ID the essays dealing with wealth, Mr. P. G. Hamerton makes one very sensible comment. No doubt the society of: people who Lenjoya wealth and ranklis often sought from motives; that:canZonly be •called snobbish. But there is, as he points out, another side even to this. He says, in an essay headed "The Flux of Wealth'" The' cultivation of taste which re- sults from leisure, forms, in course of time, amongst rich people, a public opinion that diacipliocs every member of an- aristocratic society far more severely than the more careless opinion of the hurried classes ever discip- lines th4m. . . . Why are rich people quiet and --parer ones noisy? [He is speaking of a contrastveb- served at a French riverside inn; it might not always be 80 apparent on the Thames.] Because the refinements ,di wealthy life, its peace and tranquillity, its facilities for separation in different rooms, produce delicacy of nerve with the perception that noise is disagreeable- - and out of this delicacy, when it is. general amongst a whole ales, springs, a, stron_g Aletiarmination so to discip- liste the inenibers o 1 the cia„fhat they shall not make themselves disagreeable to the .majority. Vence lovers preference for the richer classes, of good manners have a quite apart from a love of physical luxury or a snobbish desire to be associated with people of rank." . . . . " The rich man has access to an immense range of varied sitriations, and if he has energy to profit by this facility, and put himself in those situations where he'may- learn the most, he may become far more experienced at thirty- _ fiat than a poor man at seventy. A poorenan has a taste for boating, so he builds a little boat with his own hands, and paints it green and white, with its name, the C ,ck Robin,' in yellow. . . . Sir Thomas Brassey ins exactly the same tastes; he builds the 'Sunbeam,' and whilst the 'Cock Robin' has been doing its little trips, the Sunbeam' has gone round the world. . . . If sites that you talk with the owners of the two ves- sels, you may be interested for a few minutes with the poor man's account of his doings, but his experience is sand', and soon told, while the owner of the Sunbeam' bias travelled lin the oceans and could tell you a thoy- sad things."

Cooper, in his novel Of the " Deerslayer," makes sortie sport of a parcel of red Indians speculating over a chess figure in the shape of an elephant, which they described as a beast with two tails. The incident really occurred in the case of an Irish tervant at a country house In Pennsylvania. A menagerie came along that way, aid the elephant presented himself at the gate. The mistress of the house sent theservant forward with a feed of a loaf of bread. The " help " walked once or twice the length of the animal, and returned with the loaf. "why haven't you given it to the elephant ?" "Sure," says she, "and which end shall I give it to?" ACCOMMODATING.—A travel-stained tramp called at the house of an old negro. "Have you got some wood I can chop? "Oh, yas. Dar's de pile, an' yander's de axe. Jess help yess'f." The tramp, after chopping for about a half-hour, went to the negro and said, Well, l'fin done." "Done, chopped as much as yer wants ter, s yer ?" "I've chopped enough, I think" "Uh huh, bit aoan' be no ways back'ard 'bout it. Jes he'p yess's, ab' recolleck dat when yer wants to limber up yet rinks here's de place where yeriken fin' cmiTodation." "Btit I want something to eat " That's why I chopped tie wood." Lrrrmt SITITBEAMS.—EacII. one of a thquaand acts of love costs very littli by IWlf, and yeti *hen viewed altogether, who can estimate their veld-a? What is it that secures for one the name of a kind neighbour? Not the doing of half a dozen grsat favours in as many years, but the little everyday kindnesses, neither of whieh seems of much consequence, considered in itself, bht their continued 'repetition sheds a sunlight over the while neighbourhood. It is so, -too, in the family. .The ch d- whose good offices are always ready when they ake wanted—to run downstairs„ t 9 .get chips [a. rock the cradle, or torun on arierrand, and all with, a cheerful and a pleasant temper—has a reward along with such good deeds. She can get her grandfather'S slippers, or put away his book, or gently comb his thin locks and, whether she ttlinks of it or not, these little kind= neSses that come from a loving heart are the sunbeanis thattlighten up'a dark and woeful world. Booty IN Wai.—Charles, as soon as he. had finished • conquering Lorraine, gathered his host at Besancon, and marched to Granson,.on the Neuchatel Lake. Here a garrison of 500 Swiss was betrayed to him; he haneed or gdrowned 'every man of themoncluding the monks who came as chaplains. Justly enraged, the FederatiOn gathered its whole strength,•and with 24,000 men fell upon Charles unawares and defeated him utterly. The , booty was something fabulo,us. Burgundy, taking taxes from all the rich Netherladd towns, was then the richest Power in Europe.. The spoil was valued at a quarter pf a million. You may calculate what that would be worth now. The big diamonds—one is now in the Popes tia • another was long the glory of the French rega • were among the valuables. The Duke's throne valued at 11,000 gulden,. all his plate, his silver beff- stead, his wonderfully illuminated prayer-book, were taken besides 1,090,000 gulden in his treasure chest, 10,00 d horses, and a proportionate miantity ofall kinsls of stores. No wonder the Swiss never recovered Gran- son; there were long and bitter quarrels about the divi- sion of the booty, and, the coming in of so much wealth' amongst a simple people demoralised them sadly, and led the way to their becoming the chief Mercenaries pf Europe.—Men and Mountains, by H. S. Fagan, in Gorl Words. PREVENTIVES AGAINST COLDS.—Dr. T. R. Allinson gives the following sensible directions for avoiding colds. Now that the winter is upon us they will be worth bear- ing in mind:—" To be able to stand cold well one must eat such kinds of foods as will give plenty of heat, and must also accustom the system as much as possible to cold. Heat-forming foods are rice, sago, tapioca, pota- toes, the grains of wheat oats, barley, and especially maize. Ido not recommend fat, .because it is difficult of digestion, but in moderation it is useful., Oatmeal porridge, eaten with butter and sugar, forma( a good cold-resisting breakfast: Then rice, -with peas, barley, and a little oil or fat make a good dinner; whilst for teal some brown bresrl, with butter and preserve, will do ' well. To accustom the body to cold one must not wrap up too much, but make the body adapt itself as much as possible to the cold. The human system possesses in the brain a centre fop the government of the heat of the body, by which it is always kept at one uniform height. If we heat our bodies by hot drinks, heaps of clothes, hot rooms, &c., we give this centre little to do. But if we expose the body to cold air, take our food nearly cold, and do not clothe too heavily, we keep this in good condition, and it will keep the body warm if we give it the necessary food, and is ready for sudden exposures. The body can be used to cold,by tneans of air baths, or exposing the nude body to the air. This can be done at first by taking exercise at the same time, and so no cold will be felt. In connection with heaps of clothes, I may say that I have cured two or three weak chests by making the persons throw aside their chest protectors (which are a snare) and sponge the chest daily. When cold do not rush to the lire, but take a sharp run, tam the feet, or throw the arms across the chest, making the fingers hit the' back, like cabmen do. Avoid hot fluids, as tea or soups, which give a fleeting feeling of warmth. They are very good if you want to restore a numb per- son. But if you are out much in the open air, take your food all nearly cold, the system will supply the required heat, and you will find you can stand the cold much better than if you took hot drinks." ANOMALIES IN WEIGHTS AND MEASURES.—In Carmarthen- shire the bushel of wheat is a pound heavier than in Lin- colnshire, being 631 b. in the former place, and 64 in the latter. At Aberystwith, however, before we leave the Principality, it rises to 651 b.; while on the borders, in Shrewsbury, it grows to 75, and in Monmouthshire it rises to 80. In Manchester market we have remarked two bushels in use; and when you purchase your wheat by the American and measure it by the English, your one bushel becomes a bushel and a sixth, for the one con- tained 70, the other but 601 b. An English bushel at Man- chester has a beggarly size compared with thatat Wol- verhampton, for there it is 721 b.; but we have seen already that even this huge measure is a mere pigmy to the 1681 b. of some localities, and the 4881 b. of others. There are some bushels that pounds fail altogether to measure; not from their enormous size, indeed, but from the hostility the bushel shows to any standard used to gauge its capacity. In some places it may be gauged by quarters; and with its affinity for oddity, will have them of that odd number for nuarters, five. In others it is measured by quarts and gallons; in more Still by stones. So much for the bushel; but bushels make loads and bags, and the variety, as usual, is multi- plied by a new accession of local estmates in these new denominations. In some places the bushels are five to a load, in more they are counted only three. We ha e also that odd quarter, which oddly makes five ev n fourths in the load; and there are quarts; too, as well quarters in it. In Ulverston you get 144 of these in your load; at Royston and Stowmarket they are Ito more gene- rous to the denomination, for you get 488. But we are not yet privileged to dismiss the bushel; it goes to the composition of the bag as well as it did to that of the load. Two bushels make a bag at Saltash, but they don't at Bridgnorth ; there 'tis constituted of eleven, score. The score constitutes it, too, at .Leeminster, but it is a score of twelve. Notwithstanding eleven is a favourite number with the score in the composition of the wheat bag; for we find it again at Much Wenlock and Ludlo;. But as if it could not be found a possibility that the sa e name should mean the same thing in two places in British measurement, the scores at the former places are ones pf 41b., at the latter of 10. Among the weights there is a special "weight" for wheat, and this, too, evinces the taste for variety; at Whitehaven it isl. 4 stone, while at Nottingham it is 36, and at Scarborough runs up to 40 stone. - A similar whim of change possesses the stacks, bolls, coombs, windles, and hobbets, used in the measure- ment of corn. A boll is sometimes bushels, sometimes pounds: and when it is pounds sometimes 240, semetimes 280. But 2401b5. do not always constitute a boll, for at (Beccles they would call this a coomb, and at many other places reckon it four bushels. At Wrexham they count a hobbet to be 1681 b., at Pwlhell 252. These hobbets measure wheat; but there are others for the measure- ment of oats and barley, differing from one another, and from themselves, according to the locality. We hare confined ourselves chiefly to wheat, but the variety ddes not 'confine itself to this. It asserts itself in all others just as welt—Westminster Review. •

Mill's, Neilson, and Smith, of Iladry, and sold by them to the Illawarra Company, are deserving of notice. Since last year's shearing six of these rams have been three months with the ewes, and two Of them two months, having nO special care or feed, but their chance with other sheep on the natural feed, and when shorn this year, with exactly twelve months' growth of wool, the average per sheep is only loz. less than last year. ' Average weight in 1883, 161bs. 7/ozs.; 1884, 161bs. 640 ZS. FINE FOR OVER-BRRERING I'HEASANTS.—MeSSTS. W. E. and IV. Nelson, of Liverpool, were sued at Kend*l County Court, on Thursday, for £27, damage done to thes.cropa of a farmer named William Farrer, by the over-breeding of pheasants in a coppice rented by the 4 Pheasants were conveyed to the coppice in coops, and a man who assisted hr rearing the birds said 100 phea- sant hens were laying eggs and 100 ordinary hens were bringing up the broods. .There• could nqt be, anTqueS- tion, therefore, Labout the over-breeding, and as: 100 birds had been seen running -in' Mr. Farrar's:field:When the corn was ripening, there was] no doubt as, to the damage dene. It was no more reasonable- thit'a large number , of , pheasants should be allowed to: ;teal a fafmer's corn than that the farmer should be at liberty to go into the neighbouring coppice and steal the phea- sants. In those circumstances, the judge ;awarded the farmer the damages claimed. EXEMPTIONS FROM LOCAL TAXATION.—MT. W. S. Caine, M.P., has published in the Pall Mall Gazette an article on exemptions from local taxation, in ..which he gives some striking instances of unfair exemption. Among the classes of property totally exempted, or insufficiently assessed, are unoccupied Ibuilding land in towns, man- sions and, parks, deer forests and grouse moors, ground rents and royalties. With respect to deer forests and grouse moorrs, ,Mr. Caine says that owners who shoot over them are not rated, and when they let them the rates, are insufficient. For instance, Applecress Forest, in "Rosa--shire, was let by Lord Middleton at £2,000, but was assessetLat only £6OO. The exemption of unused building plots and ground rents is a monstrous anomaly, as it encourages land-jobbing and the, leasehold system, both of which it is so desirable to put down. As to the insufficient rating of mansions and parks,that is an old grievance; only our friends in the Central Chamber have always been judiciously blind to it. .4.X OMISSION FROM THE AGRICI7LTITRAL HOLDINGS Arr. —A correspondent sends the following letter from a land valuer to show how inadequate the Agricultulral Hold- ings Act is:—" Fourteen years aga or more, Mr. ---, laid about 14 acres of land down with permanent grasses, and seven years ago he laid down about 16 more. Ile has planted some standard trees in the orchard, and wall trees in the garden. He also has made good roads to the yards and in the tick-yards, and the landlord has in- structed me, through his agent, to value these improve- ments, in order that he may fairly compensate th,e out- going.tenant for those improvements. I intimated th they would amount to £l2O or more. liotwithstandiit the ainount, the landlord will agreeably meet it., Please note the Agricultural Holdings Act, 1883, nor any other Act, does not assist the tenant in the least in this matter. It simply emanates from the high sense of honour and justice in the landlord himself. There are the claims for feeding-stuffs consumed, which the Act of 1833 gives him, 'which will amount to more than one-fourth the amount I named, which, as a matter of cotirse, the in- coming tenant must meet." silos IN THE UNITED KINGDOX—In a table appended to the agricultural returns for 1884 it appears that from re- turns up to June, 1884, there are 610 silos in England, and Wales Scotland, of-which 514 are inngland, 36 in Wales and 60 in Scotland. Norfolk has thej greatest number, 59 silos, and is followed by Yorkshire with 47, Kent, 37; Chester, 34; Lancashire, 33; :Devon, 28; Hants, 24; Gloucester, 22, with others inicourse of con- struction; Dorset, 18; Essex, Stafford, and Surrey, 16 each; Bedford and Derby, 13 each; while Scotland first appears in the numerical order with 'Argyll bracketed with Northampton as having 12 silos each. The largest number in'any Welsh county is found in Cardigan and Carmarthen, each with seven silos. In Scotland, after Argyll, follow Lanark and Renfrew with six silos each, Dumfries with five, and Edinburgh s and Inverness with four silos each. The largest silo from the returns is in the county of Argyll. The largest total capacity of silos is found in Norfolk with 142,403 cubic feet, followed by Devon with 115,710 cubic feet, and by York with 114,367 cubic feet. Argyll has a total silo capacity of 108,343 cubic feet, and Kent 101,415 cubic feet. DADDY LONG LEGS.—Both in England and Ireland corn' crops after clover ley were severely attacked by leather jackets, the grubs of the daddy long-legs. Grasp land and broken pastures suffered similarly. Miss Orraerod, guided by the large number of flies on the wing last autumn, foretold this attack as long ago as last Novem- ber. Heavy rolling was recommended so as to compress the soil, And, if possible, suffocate the leather jackets. The grubs dislike light and heat, and appear to come on the surface in largest numbers during the night. Hence, if heavy rolling were, in such cases resorted to either after sunset or before sunrise, numbers of grubs might get crushed on the ground. Besides the roller and the clod-crusher, a remedy was recommended in the form of a manure to accelerate plant growth, a mixture of 1/ cwt. guano, 2 cwt. salt, 1 cwt. kamit, and 1 cwt. super- phosphate per acre. Nitrate of soda mixed' with dis- solved bones has been found serviceable in rathiftg good grass free from attack, where the ground: had' been re- sown after attack. Where a crop has been'so injured by the grub as to render re-sowing necessary; 'such a pro- cedure would be mere waste' of money till the land had been freed from the pest, and in such cases scarifying the surface is recommended.in preference to ploughing, as' it would drag out the grubs and expose them to the insectivorous birds. Autumn treatment of land, par- tieularly of broken-up pasture or clover ley, directed to baffling the leather jacket, involves any means of dis- turbing the soil which will bring the grub to the surface., The leather jackets are very hardy, and can endure being frozen stiff or a two days' submersion under water without results. Drastic autumn dressings are also ad- vised ; heavy dressings of lime fresh from the kiln, and spread hot, gas lime at the rate of 2 cwts. per acre, 6 to 12 cwt. of salt, or an application of fresh lime and salt mixed. . STEAMING FODDER.—Taking the word " fodder " in the broadest sense, as any kind of food for graminivorous animals, we may say that it will always pay to steam or cook food for swine, and often for cows inj stables con- taining 25 head or more, while for sheep and horses it will be of doubtful expediency, and usually not advia- able under any circumstances. The cooking of food for fattening swine is so important, as a matter of economy, that it will pay, even though done with little regard to the saving of labour and fuel. On the, other hand, to cook the food for neat cattle with profit notlonly should there be animals enough to pay, but the rations should be so carefully planned that by the mingling of palatable with less relished and course food, a saving may be effected in that way. Besides, the object for which the 'cattle are kept is an important factor to be considered in the feeding. .The flow of milk is increased by steam- ing the fodder; the colour of the butter is, however, in- jured. The same ration will prove more fattening, while at the same time there will be little or no:waste, if the steaming is well managed. It is best to have the steamed ration cotnposed • of a variety of food, such as fodder, roots, hay, or oat straw, with bran and corn meal, "or cotton seed, or linseed oil cake or meal. The substitu- tion of one kind of fodder or meal for another gives tariety and relish. The' coarse fodder is cooked soft, and the flavour of the roots and of the meal pervades the mass. When a boiler of several horse power is em- ploy-ed to do other work, as pumping, threshing, sawing, grindirtg, 'cutting hay and fodder, &c., steam may be economically used for cooking fodder. Of this there can be little doubt. The steam box in which the fodder is Placed for cooking, if it be big enough, need not be filled oftener than twice a week, and if, as already intimated, 'pains are taken in the operation to save in the items of labour and fuel, steaming fodder for cattle will be found profitable. HOOSE IN CATTLE.—If the cattle have hose, it 'will account for their being out of health. Hoose usually affects calves or very young beasts, although older ones sometimes get attacked. The symptoms of hoose are a Constant hacking cough distressing to listen to, and when at this season the stockowner finds several of the herd coughing at the same time, he may look upon them with suspicion. Rapid emaciation will follow, difficulty

of breathing, and later on loss of appetite, an probably diarrhsea and death. The disease is several weeks run- ning its course, but the sooner it is treated the better when It .bas been fully identified. It is important to distinguieh this disease from other diseases of the res- piratory organs; it differs from pleuro-pneumonia (with which it might be confounded) by the absence of con- stitutiorial ~syrnptonis, by the appetite not being affected tithe ,ealier stages, and by the eharaoter of the cough, 'which, When onco heard, cannot be mistaken, the ani- mal appearing as if trying to cough something up, which in fact, he is, and above all by the ,cough affecting all or the greater part of the herd at the same time. The treatrant of bids°, husk, or hoast, as this disease is viifioualy called in different localities, consists of remov- ing the small thread-like worm parasites that are lo- cated in the windpipe and in the smaller branches of the bronchial tubes. Frau the obscure situation of the .worms it is noted hasy task to rid the Suffering patient of them without at the same time injuring the constitu- tion of the animal. The best internal medicine agreed upon by all our best authorities is oil 0i-turpentine—a medicine peculiarly destructive to worms of all kinds when it, or its vapour rather, can be brought into direct contact with them. Linseed oil 120 z., oil of turpentine 4oz. should be well mixed, and a wine glassful be admi- nistered twice a day in some warm gruel. This woi4d be a proper dose for a calfnine months old. In cases whOe the disease is obstinate,. and a large niimber of animals are suffering, inhalation is advised. This consists of making the animal breathe some poisonous as in suffi- cient quantities to kill the worms without ,injuring the calf. This is so difficult to execute as to need the assist- ance of a properly qualified veterinary surgeon. An accepted authority :thus describes the,,rnode of opera- tion :—" The mode bf administratiod is this'' Take the calves and confine them ma loose box justlarge enough to hold the. exact number -affected. Put into a basin equal parts of common salt and oxide of manganese, and over this :mixture pour li,quantity of sulphurio acid (oil of vitriol); slightlydiluted with water; stir the mixtuv well with a stack, and the chlorine gas will be immediately disengaged. The operator must leave the ' apartment the instant he has mixed the ingredients, and the door must be closed. The time during which the animak. must be suffered to inhale the gas will, of course, vary with the number of calves and size of the apartment; in general, however, two or three minutes will suffice. This inhalation may be repeated every few days until the parasites have been got rid of. After such treatment the calves having been reduced by the para- site attacks, and further, by the above treatment, are left in a very weak and emaciated state, and mild vege- table tonics should be given and their food diet should be of a generous and nutritious quality. The foU9Wing powders may be given daily :—Powdered gentian,. drachtas ; powdered ginger, 1 drachm; powdered cara- way seeds, 1 drachm. The animals should be kept entirely in yards or sheds, and root diet should be sub- stituted for grass. It-is unwise to. allow calves to run out late in the autumn, for they are very likely, to pick up the husk worms. Calves are more liable to attack on aftermaths than old pastures, and thus it is better to avoid them in depasturing calves in autumn. Even as early as September calves are better driven into an airy yard at night, and if turned to pasture during the day, when the grass is pretty dry, they will not pick up the injurious worms, for the latter pests only. creep up on to the blades of grass when it is wet; returnmg o the roots in dry weather.
THE MANAGEMEN.T OF POULTRY.
• A couple of items we have recently come across in the columns of contemporaries, are of sufficient value to warrant their inelusion ,here. The first is entitled •

- FANNERS AND FOWLN. It says ;—We are under the impression that while the labours of the fancier are all important to the farmer, and while their aims are; to a certain' extent,. identical, Yet beyond this the objects sought by each are by no means the same. The fancier introduces new breeds, encourages the improvement of all the useful vs ties by exhibitions, &c., and it is•owing to his exertions that many of the most valued birds have found their way to the farmy'ard'- In actual farm practice, 'however, it is impossible to maintain every point coming under the heading of "beauty," because constitution, prolificacy, early maturity, and size are of more importance to the poulisrly- keeper, who saes at profit. As in the human race, so it is with animals, "i.e., health and strength con- stitutewa beauty of superior value to that depending upon delineation, colour, and similar superficial charms only. In selecting breeding stock,,the -only marks that are noticed are the colours of the plumage, skin, and legs; for breeders choose- the largest, squarest-built birds. Not that symmetry or size is in -itself of such great importance, but it is in Almost every instance a sure proof of a sound constitution, whether it has been caused through careful breeding for a number of years, with hardiness at the foundation, or whether it is due to overcoming successf ullythe drawbacks of inferior parents, scanty food, or exposure. If fowls are rightly managed they are the most profitable stock on the farm ; it,Toys to Attend to them, and to' put brains into the work The pains taken will be rewarded, not only in the satisfac- tion produced by seeing things done rightly, and ad- miring fine, vigorous fowls on the premises, for they oertainly will make manifest improvement in health, and thrivs under a system of vigorous selection but it will pay M. solid cash. Brahmas- should be selected for their symmetry and squareness of build, rather than their great size; for shortness of neck, legs, and tail, and for a small, neat head, with a bright eye. In the selection of Plymouth Rocks care must be taken to get stock from a large strain; they are somewhat uneven in site, some being small and indifferent, while others are large and thrifty. With Hoodans, constitution is the principal thing; a small crest is preferable, but this matters tittle. In white Leghorns size should be looked for; the white ear lobe is of minor Importance. • . . .

As regards the point;which hold good for all varieties, they are the following :—A cock must possess in perfec- tion, as near as possible, all the qualities sought after in his breed, and he must be exempt from deformity and disease. It is much more important that the cock should be comparatively perfect than that any of the hens allowed him should be, as his blood will help in the formation of. every chicken, whereas eaph hen will assist in only a fraction of the whole. .The cock should be the very personification of activity and vigour; his comb and wattles should be a fine red; his head neat, and car- ried high; breast broad and prominent, body deep, legs medium length and set well apart, and his whole frame broad and trim. At two years of age he is in best form. Hens need not be so upright as cocks, but should be like them in build; they must lay and: sit well, be good mothers, &c. We do not favour the use of indifferent hens, neither do we expect them to possess every im- aginable point of perfection, yet a breeder must select the very best specimens he can get, and if there has to be one faulty bird in a:breeding pen, it had better be one of the hens than the cock.

When a farmer of the present 'day takes any interest in breeding big stock he looks to the future, and en- deavours to produce an animal which will:milk deep or put on flesh rapidly, and in a great :measure he achievds his object. If, however, he leaves his cattle or his sheep to mate themselves, he ;vill find out how deplorable will be the result, and yet this is identically what he is con- tinually doing with his poultry. We ;think;.we could name many little farms which have of late years lost money, and which would have shown aldifferent state of things if poultry had formed a real portion of the farm stock, bred and managed under the eye of the farmer himself, for it is altogether useless to leave them to the men, the young people in the house, or even the house- wife, if she has her share of work in the house. Eggs will pay, and thickens will pay well, but only if they are well managed and intended to pay. We cannot lay too much stress upon the fact that in the season, when poultry is dear, our farmers cannot supply them, but when they are cheap they supply them at a loss, because they have plenty; have never counted the cost, and do not consume them themselves. .In one case known to us, a body of breeders met a year or two age, and dis- cussed the season when the English market showed the highest figure; having settled when it was, they decided to produce for that particular season, and obtain the maximum price, which they have done ever since. A farmer should make a little study of poultry, ascer- tain which are the best races for eggs and chickens, and then make his selection, either keeping them pure or crossing them, and continually introducing vigorous blood, size, and constitution, with the idea of making them always better ,and more prolific than they are. There is no pure race but what can be improved, and there is no variety which for real farm work can equal a bird which an intelligent breeder can produce by crossing. The other is eminently seasonable, hinting as it does at the
ciaorcE or BREEDS.

The troubles of the poultry-keeper, it remarks, espe- cially if new In the business, begin when disease sets in. Roup, in its many varied forms, is the disease most to be dreaded. The symptoms are seldom twice alike. Those not familiar with it do not discover it until too late, when the victim is too far gone. In the seasons of sudden and severe changes of weather, there is great danger of the fowls freezing, as well as of colds. Then there is dampness and chilliness on many days, which causes colds. The fowls should be well protected by tight rooms, under a good roof, with matched siding, well battened. The fowls then fare much better in severe cold than when the temperature is higher. Some varieties or breeds have been considered tender,, because they were not understood. The Houdansare an example of this fact. They can endure almost any dry, cold weather, but are not proof against dampness, even wtih a high temperature. Indeed, no variety of land fowls can endure dampness and remain in health. I mention the Houdans, as they are often thought too delicate for common farmers' use. There is no denying the fact that the fowls of to-day. are more delicate and tender than those of a preceding generation, but admit- ting this fact, are they not double or quadruple the value, as far as profit is concerned? Localities and markets vary, and the breeds must vary accordingly in order to suit the demand of the nearest market. Early flesh-producing vareties are in demand for broilers, and these breeds are at the same time the great egg-producers. Some markets demand white-fleshed fowls and also white eggs, while another wants only the yellow-skinned carcasses and brown or coffee-coloured eggs. With a correct taste there is a difference. Yellow-skinned fowls never possess that

Mr. Bailey has been at great pains to identify and describe this interesting plant, for whose addition to the flora of South Lancathire and of Britain we are indebted to the Biological Society of Ashton and to Mr. John Whitehead. A curious feature of the plant is that the pollination is entirely effected under the water. Mr. Bailey argues that 'the presence of the plant in the canal at Reddish is; due to its fruits having been trans- poTted from Egypt with the cotton consumed in Messrs. Houldsworth's mill, the tepid character of the canal water favouring its growth. The paper is profusely illustrated and is a good eample of Mr. Bailey's careful and exhaustive way of working. It is dedicated to the late Mr. John Hardy, who, we learn, was the first presi- dent of the Leeuwenhoek Club, and who is much missed by all local naturalists. Szzos.—Mr. W. This surface will be rendered sweet and mellow, and in a more fitting condition to enter the bottom of the trench, and the roots of most crops will reach it and revel in it. The advantages of ridging are— That more of the surface of the soil is exposed to the atmosphere than in ordinary digging. Thesuestion May fairly be asked—Why not apply it to the ground about to be trenched? There is really no reason, only that it involves more labour without perhaps compensatory re- sults, as all the ridges must first be levelled before com- mencing to trench. Ground that has laid in ridges during the winter will be found in spring much drier than that which has been dug or trenched, and conse- quently more easily dealt with when it is necessary to sow seeds of various crops. In commencing to form a ridge, it is necessary to place two spadefuls of soil on one side at either end, and they will do to fill up the end of the last ridge. The operator then takes a spadeful • and turrist over to the left, and the other to the right, face to face in the vacant space in front of him, fixing them so as to stand well up. When he reaches the end ho fills up from where his next ridge is to be, by taking exactly two spadefuls. If .the cottager proceeds cau- tiously, he will be able to form his ridges tolerably straight, but if he is dubious of his ability to do so, he can stretch a line on each side, and nick the ground with the spade. ' THE FRONT GARDEN.—Dahlias may now be lifted and placed in an airy shed to dry, or, if the dad is sunny, they may remain on the surface of the so' for a few hours. If there are no names to them the colour ought to be known and written with a lead pencil on a piece of wood that has had a little white paint rubbed on with the finger: If apiece of string is attached to this it can be secured to the Dahlia root. The absence of all Marks of recognition may result at planting time in a couple of. whites or yellows, any other colour being placed side by side, instead of being separated by a colour that would create a contrast. The cooler the roots are kept the better, so long as they are beyond the reach of frost. Shduld the position assigned for them be too dry, we would place them' in boxes covered with sand or ashes to maintain them plump. Cellars are generally well adapted to preserve. Dahlia roots. If they are examined two or three times during the season, what- ever position they may be in, there will be some indica- tions of shrivelling or decaying, and steps can be taken to arrest the mischief. Another plant that should be protected in some way is Echeveria Glance, usually known by the name of House Leek, but the House Leek which may be seen growing on the roofs of old built dwelling-houses and other buildings in country places is perfectly hardy, whilst the species above, which may be seen as an edging in many front gardens, is not. It will withstand much more frost when kept dry over- head. If the plants are taken up and put in boxes and their roots surrounded with moderately-dry sell, they may be preserved in any room window whether there be fire or not. Boxes made 3 inches or 4 inches wide contain one 'row of the largest plants. Tim WINDOW.—Rooted cuttings of Pelargoniums and Geraniums of the bedding-out class are best left in their pots until spring, as they will not increase in size much during the next three months; if disturbed now, they would most likely diminish. Older plants of Pelar- goniums that were cut down and potted will need watch- ing as to greenfly, which is easily destroyed by tobacco fumes. The plants are liable to be covered with dust like others grown in the window. This is detrimental to them if allowed to remain for any length of time. Much of the dust might be moved by taking the plants outside and blowing them. If afterwards hold on their sides under a water tap they should be clean.

There are always vieak fowls to be found in every lot, and such are the first to be attacked with disease. Some varieties are perfectly hardy with the exception of lia- bility to become frost-bitten in low temperature. Other sorts cannot endure confinement and high feeding. With the right management the Asiatics are the best for the , ordinary keeper. They possess size, and will give a ' goodly number of eggs if fed aright during the winter. They require quantity rather than high quality. The new beginner is, apt to be disappointed with the breed when meeting disease, but this is wrong, for no breed is exempt. All birds should not be treated alike. The choice of breeds we have from time to time dealt with, and it cannot be too strongly insisted upon that the greatest-care is-necessary in this matter, place and markets ever having great weight in deciding the breed or breeds to be kept.

SEASONABLE HINTS. In some poultry yards the soil is heavy clay in its nature, and when this is the case water is a long time running off or sinking into the ground, so that after a shower of rain :the birds have to run about amongst pools of water. Where this is so, the best plan is to cut a few open drains in .the ground, so arranged that they, will carry off the water at Once. , If these are made about a foot wide the birds will easily jump across them, and there need be no fear of their getting into them. Any professional ditcher or good farm labourer can make them so as to be most effective, aid a pound or two spent in this way will be money well spent and prove a good outlay, for• nothing is worse for poultry than damp, in itself the cause of so many diseas,ps.
A SKILFUL SURGICAL OPERATION.

The American Ambassador at Vienna, Kr. Hasson, has lately forwarded Wilts Government an interesting account of a re- markable surgical operation lately performed by Professor Bill roth, of Vienna, which, wonderful to Sell, consisted in the remo- val of a portion of the human stomach, involving nearly one- third of the organ—and, strange to say, the patient recovered— the only successful operation of the kind ever performed. The disease for which this operation was performed was cancer of the stomach, attended with the following symptoms :—The appetite is quite-poor. There is a peculiar indescribable die- trees in the stoislach, a feeling that has been described aa a I faint' allgon e.” sensation.; a sticky slime collects about the teeth, especially In the morning, accompanied by an maples- Sant taste. "Food ' fails to satisfy this peculiar feint sensa- tion; but, on the contrary, it appears to aggravate the feeling. The eye, are sunken, tinged wit!) yellow; the hands and feet become cold and st'cky—a cold perspiration. The sufferers feel tired all the time, and sleep does not seem to give rest. At era time the patient becomes nervous and irritable, gloomy, his mind filled with evil forebodings. When rising suddenly from a recumbent position there is a dizziness, a whistling sen- sation, and he is obliged to grasp something firm to keep from I failing. The bowels costive, the skin dry and hot at times; the bl^od becoming thick and stagnant, and does not circulate / properly. After a time the patient spits up food soon after eating, sometimes ins sour and fermented condition, some- times sweetish to the taste. Often-times there is a palpitation of the heart, and the patient fears he may have heart disease. Towards the last the patient is unable to retain any food what- ever, as the ispening in the intestines becomes close, or nearly so. Although this disease is indeed alarming, sufferers with the above-named symptoms should not feel nervous, for nine hundrel and ninety-nine cases out of a thousand have no cancer, but simply dyspepsia, a disease easily removed if treated in a proper manner. FEMALE SUFFRAGE.—Mr. Woodall has put down his bill for extending the Parliamentary franchiss to women for Tuesday, the 9th of December. The Bill as reconstructed provides that " nothing in this Act contained shall enable women under coverture to be registered or to vote for all purposes of and incidental to the voting for members to serve in Parliament." In other words the Bill excludes married women from its operation. _ EXTRAORDINARY ELOPEMENT OF DEAF MUTES.— In Melbourne-street, Middlesborough, resided a middle-aged I man named Thomas Paterson, a level-hand puddler at the' works of Messrs Fox, Head, and Co., his wife Catherine, aged 42, and child, aged seven, all deaf and dumb. Ai young man named Briggs, aged 21, employed at the Lin-1 tborpe Art Pottery, lodged with them, and was also deaf 1 and dumb. The husband for some time has been in delicate health, and latterly the wife has walked out with the lodger' and shown him attentions which became the current topic amongst the neighbours. The husband on his return from ' work the other night found that the mute lovers had eloped, leaving the child behind. The woman, it is stated, had in- formed a neighbour in writing that she wanted a younger man than her husband. She had two other children, now grown up, who were also deaf and dumb. SCIENTIFIC NOTES,

Measrestuta ELEcruotheis.—Gratzers patent for obtaining magnesium by electrolysis is likely to be ex- tensively- used. At a recent sitting in Berlin of the Elec- trotechmsche Verein a ball of magnesium of superb bril- liancy, fifteen centimetres in diameter, was exhibited. It was stated that the light from magnesium possesses a greater penetrating power in fogs at sea than the electric light.

Yrttow Fxvnn.—Dr.Freire, of Rio de Janeiro, has sent to the Paris Academy of Sciences a new memoir on yellow fever, in which he reaffirms his discovery of the micro-organisms ef that malady, and adds that all the vaccination experiments made on man have proved that inoculation with an attenuated culture of the microbe confers immunity from the disease. The memoir was read by the Vice-president of the Academy, M. Henri Bouley, who stated that he was thoroughly convinced of the value of Dr. Freire's discoveries. In his latest memoir Dr. Freire states that he has ascertained that the organ- ism has an envelope which changes continually. The de- composition of this envelope produces an extremely toxical principle, which is apparently the direct cause of death. This poison is not produced by the "attenuated" cultures.

LEAVES or Titigns.—ln some recent investigations on the growth of leaves, Messrs. Zoller and Rissmuller have shown that while in early summer the leaves of 'Slants contains very considerable amounts of hydrogen, phos- phoric acid, and potash, these substances are withdrawn into the wood of the tree with the advancing season; so that before the leaves fade they have lost the larger part of what was most valuable in them, which the tree re- tains for its future use. In some of these investigations on the leaves of the beech tree it was shown that in their water-free substance the highest "per Centage amount" of nitrogen, phosphoric acid, and potash is found when they open or expand in the month of May, and this per centage quite regularly decreases till they ripen and fall, but the absolute amount of nitrogen, phosphoric acid, and potash is greatest in July, and from that time on decreases.—Journal of the Soczety of Arts. SARACENIC ART IN EGYPT.—The Athenonon mentions that among the "South Kensington Art Handbooks" now in course of preparation is one on the " Saracenic Art of Egypt," by Mr. Stanley Lane-Poole, which will treat, for the first time in English, of the Mahometan art of Cairo as illustrated in the decoration of the Mameluke and earlier mosques and monuments, and in the indus- trial arts of the engraver, p9tter, wood carver, ivory worker, armourer, and mosaic artist in the period of Saracenic efflorescence. No text-book of Saracenic or "Arab" art has hitherto been attempted in England, and this handbook will be the first essay in this direction.. It will be illustrated by numerous woodcuts of the chefs d'euinv of Saracenic art, chiefly taken from the fine ex- amples in the South Kensington Museum, and notably from the exquisite carvings and metal work of the re- cently acquired collection of M. de St. Maurice. Da. Koca's CROLERA RFSEARCHES.—Dr. Koch has re- plied to his critics respecting the "comma" bacillus, and maintains his opinion that it is the active agent of cholera. Far , from being ignorant of the existence of the similarly shaped microbe found by:Dr. Lewis in the saliva, as some of Koch's opponents have inferred, he states that he has been familiar with it fora long time past, and has cultivated both it and the cholera bacillus by means of the gelatine process, with resultegbich have convinced him that they are essentially difftinct. He denies that they appear identical even in shape or mea- stirement when examined by a competent microscopist, and maintains further that an expert experimentalist will observe differences in their modes of staining. He adds that Lewis's bacillus will not grow in a neutral or weak alkaline gelatine solution, which is specially favourable to the development of the cholera bacillus. Nothing, he says, is more easy than the distinguishing of one from the other. Dr. Koch is at present travelling in Italy, and it taking the opportunity to examine the luis- pital and sanitary arrangement A there. FRODSHAM VOLUNTEERS. PRIZE DISTRIBUTION.

The annual distribution of prizes to the members of the I Company of the C.R.V. took place at the Town Hall, Frodsharn on Saturday evening, when the chair was occu- pied by Lieut.-Col. Ashton, and there were also on the plat- form Captain Robert Ashton, Lieut. Harrison, Mr. James Reynolds, J.P., Mr. E. A. Wright, J.P., and Mr. T. H. Hit- chen. There was a moderate attendance of the general public, including several ladies. The CHAIRMAN delivered an appropriate address. Lieut. HARRISON read the list of the successful compel' tors at the prize meeting, and Mr. Jas. Reynolds courteously banded each man an order for the prize won. Captain ROBERT ASHTON announced that the number of efficients in the corps this year was 70, against 51 last year, there being only one non-efficient. Seven non-commissioned officers had gained the Government grant as extra efficient& Captain Ashton concluded by proposing a vote of thanks to Mr. Reynolds and the donors of the prizes, which was Seconded by Mr. E. A. Wright, J.P. Mr. REYNOLDS responded. Mr. WRIGHT proposed a vote of thanks to the officers, which was seconded by Mr. T. H. HITCHER, and Colonel ASHTON, in responding, said that the number of efficient members in the battalion w 8.5 800 this year, against 735 in the preceding year. There were only 12 non-efficients in tbe whole battalion.

IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
-HOUSE OF COMMONS.-SATURDAY

The House sat for a short time on Saturday to forward the financial business connected with Supply. On the committal of the income Tax Bill, Mr. 1,1131313ARD repeated his well-known views as to the unjust incidence of the in- come tax, and argued in favour of assessing it on the rate- able annual value instead of the gross value.—The CHAN- CELLOR of the EXCHEQUER, in reply, reminded Mr. Hubbard that his suggestion had been fully discussed and rejected by a large majority last April.--The Bill having passed through Committee, the House adjourned at 340. SOUSE OF LORDS.—MeNDAY, The House met at 4-5.

THE INFANTS BlM—Lord FITZGEEELD moved the second reading of the Infants Bill, the main object of which was to amend the law relating t ) the custody and guardianship of infants.—The bill was then read a second time arid referred to a select committee.

Lord GRANVILLE stated that the House would meet next day, but it would not assemble again for political purposes during the remainder of the week. Their lordships then adjozrned during rleasure. The Income lax Bill was brought up from the Commons and read a first time, and their lordships adjourned at 6.5.

THE 'COTTERSWORTH Br.TRIAL CASE. Sir WILLIAM IIARCOURT, in reply to Mr. Illingworth, said that the Clergyman who sent the dead body of ft child to the Home 'Office had offered to apologize to him,`but he felt that the offence had Rot been committed against him but against the church of which he was a rnemlcer, against public de- cency, and the arents of the child, whom he had deceived by promising to bury it. He had instructed the law officere to consider whether the Clergyman could not be prosecuted, and he intended to bring the matter under the notice of the bishop, in order that the clergyman might be removed from the charge of the parish over whet:he seemed entirely =at to preside. THE REDISTRIBUTION BILL. Mr. GLADSTONE gave, notice Of the Redistribution Bilt, but explained that he Could nut be absolutely certain when he would be in a con• dition to introduce it. He hoped that it would be circulated immediately, and that they would be able to proceed to the second reading on Thursday ie. next week.—Sir S. NORTH- COTE understood that the arritcgement was proposed partly , in view of a contemplated adjournment of the House for some days, and he offered no objection to it. THE ADJOURNMENT.—Lord Richard GROSVENOR moved the adjournment of the Housc till Monday next. Lord RANDOLPH Cuuncnert 1, asked that the House might be put in possession of the course the Government intended to take with regard to Egyptian finance.—Sir J. Emlanoor protested against the adjournment, as it would prevent a discussion on proportional representation on Friday. Mr. GLADSTONE thought the proper time for the debate was after the introduction of the Redistribution Bill. If the debate were to take place on Friday the result would be to keep the Seats Bill suspended. With respect to the state of the finances of Egypt, not a momeat would be lost in bringing the matter before Parliament. _ _

AN IRISH GRIEVANCE.--Mr. O'BRIEN said he felt bound again to call attention to the case of Joseph Poole, who was hanged for the murder of the man Kenny in Dublin, and to ask that there should be an inquiry into the circumstances. —Mr. DEASY continued the discussion, and an ineffectual attempt to count out the House was made at five minutes past eight—The SOLICITOR-GENERAL for IRELAND replied, and defended the courso taken by the Government —Sir RICHARD CROSS protested against the House ef Commons being made a court of appeal.—The House then divided on the questions that it be adjourned till Monday next :—For the adjournment 57, against 19, majority for the adf:curn- ment 38. The House adjourned at a quarter-past twelve. HOUSE CF LORDS.—TUESDAY.

The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at twenty past four o'clock. INcomit Tax Bist„,..tc.—On the motion of the Earl of KIMBERLEY, the Incetne Tax Bill was read a second time, and, the Standing Orders having been dispensed with, the Bill also went through Committee, and was read a third time and passed.—On the motion of Lord BRAMWELL, the Justices' Jurisdiction Bill and the Law of Evidence Amendment Bill were read a third time and passed. Their Lordships adjourned at twenty-five minutes to fivo till Monday.

ARRIVAL OF TROOPS AT DONGOLA -ADVANCE SOUTHWARDS.

DONGOLA, SllNDAY.—Preparations for an advance have been making fair progress since my last visit. Everything is perfectly quiet in this neighbourhood, and indeed as far as Merawi. rhe population, now that they find the expe- dition is coming in earnest, have assumed a friendly atti- tude, and it is perfectly safe for small parties, or for even individual Europeans, to travel as far as Merawi. The am- pedition is now moving forward simultaneously along the whole line, and the station left by one party in the morn- ing will be occupied by another at night. Not until Ambalm: in reached will the lead:ng boats stop, and there the whole force will gradually gather for an advance together. The sick are left behind in hospital. There are many cases of; sore feet and hands, which will take eons° time to heal. These have been caused by tramping over rough rocks, and ' by incessant work at the oars or hauling at the track ropes. The men's clothes andkoots have also suffered badly, espe- . chilly the latter; and the boots especially will scarcely hold together to Dongola if the work above proves as hard and as ! rough as that which we have hitherto encountered. Mauw of the boats have been damaged, some of them badly. The troops have taken to rowing more quickly than could have been expected, and these in the beats which have arrived here row in very fair time together. The natives are pun- zled at the fact that the a-medition continues to advance in , spite of the lowness of the river. Their owe navigable sea- son is now almost over, and they are surprised that our I boats still go up without interruption.—StaKdard. DONGOLA, MONDAY. The mounted infantry will ad- • vance to-morrow; they will go forward to a spot twenty, • miles to the south. The Guards' Camel Corps will go through here without gapping, and will join them. This is the first forward movement ,of British troops beyond Dongola. It is not, however, intended as an offensive move against the Mandi's forces. or as the commencement of a general advance, the movement having beta deter- mined upon on account of the prevalence of smallpox among s the natives here.

Pants, SIINDAY.—A telegram from Hanoi states that, in /consequence of attacks made by the Chinese upon the French gunboats Tromke and Bevolver, at Dime, on the river Claire, a column, under the command of Colonel Duchesne. attacked and completely routed the Chinese. Morin, a person who some time ago disseminated libellous statements con- cerning her. M. TEE AFRICAN CONFERENCE.

- BERLIN, SitfORDAY. - The 'Committee e the West African Conference met again to-day. Mr. Kasqon, the United States Plenipotentiary, made proposals with refer- ence to the frontiers of the Congo Basin to be fixed:by the Conference. It is generally believed that England, like Germany, France, and the United States, has agreed to re- cognise the African Association as a State. The members of the Conference dined with the Emperor to-night. The guests nwribered about O. BERLIN, MoNnay.—The Conference Committee held a sitting to-day. The discussion turned upon the western portion of•the basin, as to which no difficulty presented itself, the committee unanimously agreeing toTree Trade for that portion. Satisfaction is expressed by the represen- tatives in Berlin of English merchantile houses at the course the discussions are btizing, as it is fully believed England's trade wit: materially benefit by the establishment of the Free Trade principle. Mr. Stanley dined today with Prince Bismarck.

BERLIN' THEIRSMIY.—A plenary sitting of the Congo Conference was held to-day, under the presidency of Count Hatzfelde. The report signed by the special committee on Tuesday last, and dealing only with the delimitation of the Congo`basin, was presented for ratification, and accepted in all the essential points. Mr. Stanley will leave here on Sunday next, being under an engagement to lecture in Edinburgh early next week. It is stated that he requires from the African Association a yearly salary of £4,000.
SETTLEMENT OF THE BECHUi.NALAND DIFFICULTY.

CLPETOWN, TIMESDAY.—The Goshen freebooters have accepted the conditions of the Cape Ministers, by which Bechuanaland will be annexed to Cape Colony. They have also consented to evacuate Montsica's territory. The Transvaal Convention is to be carried out, and the rights secured underthe protectorate of the Imperial Government will be respected. AUSTRIA-HUNGARIAN ELECTIONS.

PESTH, MOUDAY.—The elections te the Hungarian Senate and Chamber of Deputies have now terminated, nearly all the results being in favour of the Government candidates. Perfect order prevailed throughout the proceedings. TURKEY.

SALONICA, SIINDAY.—A detachment n: 600 soldiers has arrived here, and been sent on to Anatolia. These men 'formed part of some troops stationed at Monastir, who mutinied at the end of last month, demanding the arrears of pay due 0 them and their discharge, as their term of service had -expired. Some cases of insubordination also occurred last week among the troops stationed at Salonica, but perfect tranquility now prevails irothe garrison.

div.p: INDIA.

MADRAS, SUNDA.Y.—A destructive cyclone has burst over part of the'Presidency. Immense damage has been done in the Vedhills, and breaches have been made in the embank- ments of the Cholavers Lakes, from which this city derives its supply of water. The supply is cut off. He (Mr. Harrison) quite agreed with Mr. Jeans that if a township had only one representative it would be wrong to deprive them of that representative, but Newton had four representetivel, so it could not be said to be unrepresented. With reference to the word " dictatorial " he might perhaps have chose a happier word, but he meant it to refer to the passage that the Board's action had been "unprecedented and quite out of place." He thought that was rather offensive and dic- tatorial, and that they might have sent in their memoriel in more respectable terms; and although, perhaps, he was not quite happy in using the word dictatorial, he thought it was not at all uncalled for. Their action was certainly not unprecedented, because the same thing had occurred before, and "quite out of place" was equally inappropriate, because it was perfectly in piece, otherwise they should have had no power to do it without the consent of the Local Government Board. They were not treating Newton any worse than Warrington, as Major Cartwright's vacancy was not yet filled, and he thought that they might very well have been spared that memorial. Mr. CALD WELL said that it appeared to him that the memorial was not of a representative charac- ter at all, and that it was only due to the 'faddy" ideas of a few of the ratepayers of Earlestown and Newton.—Mr. BLACKHORST: It Was a public meeting.—Mr. CALDWELL : It WaS a public meeting, but it was rather a stormy meeting. (Laughter.) They were always "Jim-Crowing" at their (the Board) meetings—(laughter)—and they scarcely stuck to their resolutions three minutes. It appeared to him to be ridictelous.—Mr. JEANS said he simply wished to accede to the wishes of the ratepayers of Newton and Earlestown, and he thought that it was only proper thet the representa- tion should be kept up not only in Newton bat also ire War- rington. He Was quite prepared to move a resolution that the Warrington vacancy be filled up also—The motion that the Newton vacancy be filled up was then put to the meet- ing, when nine voted in its favour wed nine against.—The CHAIRMARL 1 shall decide about my casting vote in half a moment ; I shall say fill up the vacancy. (Applause.) The Chairman then asked if they thought any steps should be taken with regard to the Warrington vacancy.—Mr. JEANS thought they should apply the same principle to Warring- ton, and he moved that the Warrington vacancy be filled DARBDSHIRE seconded the motion. He con- tended in opposition to Mr. Harrison's view that the action the Board had taken .with regard to those va- cancies was unprecedented, net merely in that Union, but also in other Unions.—Mr. HARRIsON opposed the motion proposed by Mr. Jeans, as did also Mr. CALDWELL, who said that he believed in opposing it he would be representing the opinions of 999 out of every 1,000 ratepayers. The business of the Board, he said, was now carried on just as , well es when Major Cartwright was there.—Mr. BROAD- PENT thought the two esses of Newton and Warrington did] not ran on all fours together. They had decided that a! netirGuardian shoald be eelected for Newton because the residents in that district had convened a public meeting and desired that there should be one,not that they as a Board of' Guardians wanted another member. If they had reason to believe that the people of Warrington wanted the vacancy filled up it would be eight to fill it up, but otherwise he should let the thing stand as it was. He quite agreed with Mr. Derbyshire when he said that the action of the Board was unprecedented, and the clerk would tell them that the precedent had been that when a vacancy occurred even at the time of annual elections it was filled up.—The Cheein- -I,leete said he had known many a one.—Mr. BLACKEICEST supported Mr. dune' motion.—Mr. APPLETON thought Warrington sufficiently represented already.—Mr. BLACK- ' lumen: You want to constitute the whole Board yourself. (Laughter.)—The CHAIRMAN having spoken in favour of keeping the Bowed up to its full strength, the motion that the Warrington vacancy be filled up was put to the meeting and negatived.—,The CHAIRMAN said he presumed that if the ratepayers expressed a wish for the vacancy to be filled up and didn't insult the Board by seeding an impertinent naessage—(laaghter)—it would be filled up.—Mr. BROAD- BENT : Yes, it they don't approach us in a dictatorial manner. (Laughter.)—The discussion then dropped.

,„ NORTIINVICEC WANDERERS v. WARRINGTON ASSOCIATION. —Played at Warrington on Saturday. The visitors won the toss, and chose to play with a very strong wind in their favour, which at once carried the ball into the home territory, where the visitors had repeated shots at goal, and after ten minutes' play drew first blood. Several runs were made by the home teara' but without success, and then a further point was scored by the visitors, who again shortly after from a corner put the ball behind. It was played by Walton and put out again, they claimed a goal, but the re- feree refused the claim. A claim was also made for a shot which went over the bar twine inches, and the referee, who stood close to the posts, refused that also, though their um- pire, aided by the whole of the team, protested otherwise. Fer some minutes they refused to play and threatened to leave the field, but after sundry private consultations, they signified their assent to the verdict, and soon showed their decision by one of their players deliberately charging the referee, who was kuocleed to the ground stunned. The game was stopped for a few minutes, which brought half time. Warrington now scored in about three minutes from re-start- ing. The Northwich men declared it was off-side, and un- -1 less they got the goat disallowed refusedto play any longer. The referee having decided that it was a fair goal, the game was brought to an abrupt conclusion by the visitors refusing to play. The Warrington team, having waited 20 minutes for the hail to be re-started, left the Northwich men lying about the field and in disgust. Altogether it was a most unsatisfactory game, as the strangers had Corns cleatly with the intentien of making a" win, tie, or wrangle " of it. WARRINGTON V. WERNETIL (IST TEAMS).-011 Saturday these teams met for the first time at Oldham. The vis:tors ticked off, some loose play taking place, when Warren pun- ted into touch. The home forwards being considerably 'heavier, they for a time had an advantage. Near the War- rington 25 flag the leather was held, but Werneth played on and got over the line. An appeal to the referee ruled the , ball back. The visitors then showed better form, and ; gradually gained the opposite end. A scrimmage on the line saw Barnes with the oval, and driving it across to Warren, that player drew 'first blood for Warrington. Its I value was not increased. Following the drop-out Massey I dropped into touch. Turner getting hold forced his way over the line. No goal resulted. A splendid drop at goal by Barnes was the next incident of note, and then half-time was called. Re-starting, the ball went to Walsh. who de- layed the returr, and Werneth compelled him to save. Even play then ruled, only to be succeeded by Barnes again say- ing. The next feature was a really good ran on the part of Barnes, who dodged the opposing tacks and registered the third try. The place again failed, owing to the difficult position. Warrington had much the best of the game until the call of time, when they experienced being frustrated after three splendid attempts to score. Victory thus rested r with Warrington by three tries and one minor points to three i minors. This makes the fourth consecutive win. Special mention is deserving to Barnes, Turner, Davies, Speakman, and Povev. Warrington team: T. Walsh, back; J. T. Mas- sey, T. Barnes, J. E. Warren, three-quarters; W. Speakman; and E. Gilbert, half-backs; H. Ashton (captain), F. Turner, , T. Davies, James Jolley, J. R. Calvert, J. Robinson, W. Hayes, W. Povey, and R. Littlewood, forwards. EARLESTOWN V. BOOTLE.-1 splendid game was wit- I nessed between these first-class teams at Bootle on Saturday afternoon, and the victory for Earlestown by two goals to , none was secured by some good play, and was thoroughly ; well deserved. In the Liverpool and District Cup competi- ; tion last season the Earlestown club threw out Bootle (the I previous year's winners of the cup) by four goals to none, j and last Saturday the supporters of the Liverpool club were hopeful that the latter would turn the tables on their oppo- nents. But this they were unable to accomplish, the 'Earlestonians again retiring the victors. There was a large attendance of spectators, who manifested the greatest interest in the game. Rogers started the leather for Bootle, and ; the home team quickly assumed the aggressive. The Dales- 1 tonians (who had two second men in their ranks) were I severely pressed for some minutes, and Bootle scored a corner kick. Nothing resulted from it, however, and the subsequent play in the first half was of a very fast and even character. Each goal was in tarn endangered, bat the , play of the backs and half backs for both elevens was of the I 'finest character. Jackson and Appleton were both called , upon to defend their respective goals, the former having the most shots to stop. As no point had been scored when half 1 time was called, ends were changed, and the game was re- I started amid keep excitement. Some even play ensued in the centre of the field, neither team having any advan- tage though the utmost efforts were individually put fo-th. ' After ten minutes play, however, the superior stamina of 1 the Earlestown team, which has won them many a victory, ' began to manifest itself, and the Bootle men were gradually forced to act on the defensive. From this point the E tries- , tonians had all the best of the gains, and they pressed their I opponents, who, however, defended their goal very well. A ' splendid shot by Sims scored the first goal for the visitors fifteen minutes after the change of ends, and Dagnall ' notched a second goal ten minutes later. No other point was registered, and Earlestown were thus victorious by 2 , goals to none. Teams :—Earlestown : J. Appleton, goal ; R. Green and J. Green, backs ; R. Boater, J. Duxbury, and A. Clayton, half backs ; J. Ellison and W. Murray, right wing ; A. W. Dagnall, centre ; J. Sims and J. Agden, left wing; umpire, Mr. T. Bell. Bootle : J. Jackson, goal; C. Evans and F. Woods, backs ' • D. Dixon, J. D. Murray, and J.:E. Grayson, half backs ; J. A. Eyton-Jones and J. Rogers, , left wing; A. Z. Short. centre ; H. Griffin and J. Johnson, , right wing. - 1

TECFINSCAL EDUCATIOI.7.—AUTISARS7 CONFERENCE.-Mr. W. Woodall, M.P., a member of the Royal Commission on Technical :Education, presided on Monday night over a conference of members of the Artisans' Technical Associa- tion with employers and workers in various trades, held at Anderton's Hotel, Fleet-street, London, for considering the best means of creating an interest in the minds of youths and young men in techical education through the Medium of trades unions.—The Rev. H. Solly said that now the ap• prentieeship system was, in many instances, practically dead, it was necessary, if British industries were to hold their own against foreign competition, that young men under 21 should be compulsorily required to attend classes where they could learn the technology of their trades, the employers affording facilities for this purpose. Trade unions might aid the work by insisting that those admitted to their lodges should give proof of their knowledge of the technicalities of their trade. He moved " That, in the opinion of this conference, it is desirable that the system of apprenticeship where it exists should be adapted to the modern conditions of industry, and that employers in taking apprentices and youths into their service should undertake to see that they attend technical classes a certain number of hours weekly, and, further, that previous to their be- coming journeymen their employers should invite them to pass an examination to test their efficiency."—Mr. W. 0. Peacock, secretary of the Amalgamated Society of Press- men, seconded tha motion.—ln the course of a discussion which ensued, in which representative workmen of various handicrafts took part, it appeared that it was . not the rule for trades unions to require proof of the proficiency of work- men as a condition of their admission; and that workmen were very largely ignorant of the principles which governed their respective trades.—Mr. G. N. Hooper, president of the Institute of British Carriage Manufacturers, said that in the coachbudding trade the youths engaged by certain firms were required to attend technical classes as a condition of their employment, the employers paying their fees.—Dr. Pankhurst said trades unions ought to regard themselves as the trustees of the skilled industries of the empire.—The Chairman remarked that he was bound to admit, from his experience of the work done abroad, we still stopped far short of other Countries in the matter of the facilities for acquiring technical edueation..—The resolution was unani- mously passed, and a committee was appointed with a view of securing the adoption of its recommendations.
