In submitting the minutes of the Padgate Industrial Schools Cornraittee, the CLERK read an indoor mainte- nance account for the half year ending September, 1884, with tables and appendices showing costs, list ef salaries, profits, balance stock, as follows z—Provisions consumed, £489 lie 11, rate per head Is II 034 •, necessaries, £ll4 4s 6i, rate per head, 5-32 d • clothing, £155 I.ls 104, rate per head, 7284; making £759 14s 2‘t, or a total per head of 23'114,33d. Salaries, £246 15s 64, rate per head, 11 62d ; officers' rations, £166 16s 9d, rate per head, t 844; making a total of £413 12s 34, or Is 7.2164. per head. Furniture and ' property, £56 2a 2d, rate per head, 2594; repairs. &c.. £ll5 5s rate pa; head, 5 394 ; establishment, £22 163 3d, rate per head, 1 054; making a total of £194 4s Id, or a total rate per head of 9.034. Magisterial proceedings, drugs, and burials, £7 12s 64, rate per head, 0 35d ; rates and •insurance, £l2 19s 84, rate per head,' trs6d • annual value, £1.50, one-half thereof £75, rate per head 350. d Full total (less grant £97 8s), £1,365 14s 84, or a total rate per head of 5s 3 98d. An appendix to the above report was also submitted, in which the separate sa:aries and payments to officers were set forth. The profits were given as follows : —Stock provisions at the beginning of the half year, £8 14s 14 ; at the close of earns, £lB Si 14, leaving a balance of £9 14s. Stock of necessaries atbeginning of half year. £l2, 17d &t; do. at close of half year, £l5 Ils sd; balance, £2 13s 11d. Profits from the sale of refuse, £2l 7s 111—Mr. DARBYSHIRE, in moving the minutes of the Schools Corn- I mittee, said that he thought the above report vrokild not have been submitted to that meeting as it was not yet quite complete. So for as the committee had gone into the repart they were pretty well satisfied with it. That was the first clear half year for which they had been able to work out a statement in the manner of the tables they had just been shown since they went to the schools. He hoped that next half-year the cost would be considerably less than this half-year, because there was a good deal of new Work included in the above statement which they would not be required to do again for some years. They were all aware that in some points the build- ings were left in a very incomplete and unsatisfactory man- ner, and they had consequently to repair work which ought to have lasted for years. It had either been the fault of the contractors or of the architect for not seeing that the work was properly done.—Mr. BROADSENT seconded the adoption of the committee's minutes. It had struck him, he said, ix listening to the remarks of Mr. Darbyshire, how important it was when large works had to be carried out, to employ a first.rate contractor for the purpose, and what false ecenomy it often was under such circumstances to take what appeared to be the lowest tender. (Heat, bean) How very much better it might have been in the present case if mere had been thought of the thorough efficiency of the contractors than of the fact of anyone in particular , having ()reed to do the work for the lowest price. They should probably have been very great gainers had the work been put in the hands of some first-rate Warrington or other builder. (Hear, hear.) While seconding the min- utes he wonld express a hope that the committee would net lose sight.of the suggestion with regard to the boys hav- ing woollen clothing during the cold weather. '(Hear, heart) lhacunortsr said he was rather disappointed by the report presented by the Schools Committee. He had thought they would have been in a position to tell them the total amount the schools had cost. He should also liketo know what the farm had cost them and what it had produced, so that they might know whether they were gaining or losing by it.—Kr. DARBYSRIBE explained that the report was not complete. When it was complete the committee-should be very glad to give the information asked for. He was sure there was no desire on the part of the committee or Farm Committee but to show them everything that was done in so intelligible a form that every member of the Board could understand R.—Mr. CALDWELC. thought Mr. Darbyshire's explanation was quite satisfactory, and he hoped there would' be no further discussion on the matter. The School Committee's minutes were then passed and the dis- cussion dropped.

The CLEBX said he had received a communication from the assistant overseer of Newton stating that at a meeting of the ratepayers of Newton and Earlestown, held on the 15th 'November, the following resolution was passed : " That in the opinion of this meeting the action recently taken ty the Warrington Union Board of Guardians in re- fusing to fill up the vacancy that has occurred en their Board by the death of the late Mr. Richard Walmsley is un- preceCented and quite out of place, especially considering that there are almost 18 months of the time unexpired, and also at a time when there is so much agitation by the people in faeour of larger representation.; and further, that this meeting of ratepayers is strongly la ?favour of the 'vacancy being ffiled up, and calls upon the Warrington Union Board of Guardians to take steps for that purposeforthwith"-oMr. BLAeI HURST : Have we the power to order thsovacancy to be filled up.—The Camel/kw Yes, if the Board think fit, but they have decided not to do it.—Mr. HARRISON said it appeared to him in the first place, thatthey bad no power to fill up the vacancy, because they must eo to the Local Go- vernment Board ; and, in the second place, he thought it wasoather captions on the part of those gentlemen of New- toroto send a document of that kind. It appeared to him to partake more or lese of a dictatorial character; and he did not think they ought to submit to it. He moved that they take no notice of it.—Mr. Breeonnueseere Then 't would advise the Newton people to apply to the Lock' Govern- ment Board themselves —Mr. DARBYBHIRE said he .qaite diEered from Mr. Harrison in what he said. He thought that the people who were =represented bad taken a very proper course, and he considered that Board waseloing an injustice to the Newton townchip by opposing the oopoint- meat of a guardian in the place-of-one deeeasede •-He hoped that the wish of the people, who had held a•toweis meeting, would be carried out, and if it were necessary to rescind a minute; made at a former meeting of that Board .he should be glad to ask that it be rescinded. He did not think it would be necessary, because that Board had no right to make a minute to prevent a township from being represented. Such a thing had never been done before whilst he had been a guardian except in one case when there was ohly two menthe intervening between the time the vacancy occurred and the election. But now there care eighteen months to run before the election, and he quite sympathised with the ratepayers who had sent that requisition to tne Board. He saw nothing at all wrong in what they bad done,.and there- fore he would move that steps be taken for holding an etec- tiem inVewtou to fill the vacancy caused by the death of the late Mr. Walmsley.—Mr. LACKRtRST seconded this proposals—Mr. HARRISON: You will have to give notice. —ln answer to the Rev. F. G. Roberts, the Cele= said he did not think it would be necessary for notice to be given of a resolution to rescind the previous decision of the Board because that decision was not to do something, but simply not to move at all in the matter.—Mr. JEANS said he quite agreed with the inhabitants of Newton in the view they tool: of that subject, as be thought it was quite proper that the vacancy -should be filled up. He did not mean to say that there were not sufficient guardians to conduct the business of that Union, yet at the same time, supposing Newtoa had been a township with only one guardian for a year and a half they would have been unrepresented. 'Therefore he begged to support the proposal of *Mr. Darbyshire.—Mr. Baciousenter said he entirely agreed with the view Mr. Der- byshire took of that matter. He was sorry to differ with Mr. Harrison, but he thought that hie describing of the letter from .the Newton ratepayere as 4' dictatorial " was very uncalled for on his part. He (Mr. Broadbent) thought that the general feeling of the guardians at the time the precious decision had been-come to was that they would gladly avoid any unnecessary -election and prevent any expeose,,nnd that if the ratepayers generally were satisfied things should remain as they were. The Board were not disposed to take the initiative in putting the Union to any eopense in the matter, but when they had that, as be thought, very proper representation from the rate- payers of Newton that they wished the vacancy in their district to be filled up, it seemed to him that their proper course was not to stand in the way of their wishes, but endeavour to carry them out. He should be very sorry in- deed if that Board were to set itself against the wishes of any particular township ; and he should be scry lif any proper •represeatations made to that Board were to be coneidezed dictatorial.—The CHAIRMAN men- , timed that the expenses of an election would be borne by the township in which the election took place.—Mr. Aio- ,OUTOn said it seemed very singular to him that members who were not at all-connected with Newton ehoald be so very anxious to have the vacancies filled up. He had ne obiseetion to the vacancy being filled up, but he had to the expense. This fell enirely upon Newton township, and the rest of the Union hetlnothing to do with it. They might if theyrKked take the view that Newton was not properly re- presented ; that was the most feasible view of it, else he did not see why that Booed should take each a particular interact in Newton. They were not so particular about the Warrington township, or why had they not filled up the vacancy ,caused by the death of major Cartwright.—Mr. JHANs :I propose that it be filled up.—Mr. Amer:rote thought there was quite as much need for the vacancy being filled up at Warrington as at Newton. The reason why his-friend Mr. Harrioon aid himself bad opposed filling up the vacancy was to save the township expense. That was a sufficient reason for him as overseer, knowing as he did the state cf their finances. Rut there were a lot of can- tankerous people in Earlestown, a lot of anti-vaccinationists —he dare say there were some in that room—(laughter)— and it was simply nothing at all but a whim of theirs in I order to get men in of their own sort. He did not care two- pence about an election, but he was an overseer, and was re- sponsible to a certain extent for finding money. He really could not see why the members of the Board should be so anxious to throw money away, while refraining from filling op the vacancy in their own lOWWIllip.--Mr. BROADBENT : It is only because the Newton peoplewant it.—Mr. BLACK- EIE2ST said that he had noticed that at a public meeting at Newton Mr. Appleton had opposed the proposal to fill up the vacancy. He thought it was very unbecoming conduct On the part of Mr. Appleton as the Newton people's repre- sentative to oppose their wishes in the manner he did. He hoped the Newton ratepayers would take proper notice of Mr. Appletas conauet. Why Mr. Appleton should oppose that application so strongly when he saw it was the opinion of the people of Newton he (Mr. Blackfturst) could not understand.—Mr, HARRISON zed it was

div.p: THR4COMPLAINT ABOUT THE INFIRMARY.

I With regard to the complaint made by Dr. Spinks about a man who was not a pauper, having been sent from the Infirmary to the Workhouse, the CLERK said he had writ- ten to Dr. Richmond and had received a reply. It was also explained by Mr. Harrison that when the man in question, who had a broken leg, was taken to the Infirmary he was attended to by Dr. Richmond and then handed over to the police, who had then felt it their duty to bring him to the Workhouse. Dr. Richmond was therefore not responsible for his being brought to the Workhouse, and besides he had so dressed his leg that there was no need to call upon Dr. Spinks to attend him on the same night.—A. little conversa- tion ensued, from which it appeared to be the opinion of the Board that the explanation of Dr. Richmond was Baas- factory, and the subject then dropped.

div.head: WARRINGTON HIGHWAY BOARD.
div.p: WARRINGTON HIGHWAY BOARD.

A meeting of this Board was held at the Office, Sankey- street, on Wednesday afternoon, when there were present Messrs R. Houghton (Lowton), in the chair; John Fair- dough (Burtonwood), William B. Kerfoot (Great Sankey), John Stainer (Houghton), William Royston (Poulton), J. Houghton (Woolsten), J. Grounds (Orford), J. Pennington (Hulme), J. Bridge (Celcheth), H. B. White (clerk), and Thompson (surveyor).—A letter was read from the office of the Clerk of the Peace at Preston with reference to a minute passed by the county authorities disallowing the sum of £1.36 19s charged under the head of materials, for old materials contributed by the late trustees, stating that at a meeting of the County Highway Committee a resolu- tion had been passed, saying that the committee saw no reason for re-opening the matter as the materials in question were not purchased by the Highway Board.—The Clerk said that the matter had therefore to rest there until that meeting, and it was for the Beard to say whether they would appeal by taking a special case t 3 the Court of Queen's Bench, whether they would take counsel's opinion as to their right to do so, or whether they would let the matter drop.—lt was resolved that the claim made by the Board be abandoned, on the motion of Mr. Royston, seconded by Mr. J. Houghton.—A letter was read from the solicitors to the promoters of the Ship Canal Scheme, stating that they should be glad to learn whether the Board wished the clauses affecting them to remain as before, and it was agreed that if the plans were again the same the clauses should be accepted.—This was all the business of interest.

Mr. J. Collier, the actor, told Mr. Buchanan, the author, of a childless old man, married to a young wife, who enjoys all the pride of a husband and father. Mr. Buchanan said he did not see how that could be when there were no chil- dren. " Well," said Collier, " he's so often taken for his wife's father that it's the same thing." WHAT'S Ile A NAME P—The other day a passenger from Holyhead to Dublin in one of the North Wales boats wae surprised at seeing a number of carcases of cattle on board bound for Ireland. tie inquired the reason. "Well, colonel," was the reply, "these-carcasses were American beef the day before yesterday; yesterday they were English beef; to-day they are Irish!' A French banker, who is in company with his son, re- ceives ten thousand francs from a debtor, and sets to count- ing the notes. "One, two, three, four," he says, and goes on counting up to nine, when he stops, rolls up the notes, and whispers to his son, "Never turn up the last note when you are counting money; there may be another under it." Fnau CONQUERED.—Mrs. Blank: "Do you remember, dear, that, before we were married, you always offered me your left arm ?" Mr. Blank : "Yes, I wanted to have my tight hand free. You see, I had a lover's fear that someone would try to take you away from me, and I always kept it in readiness for defence." "How sweet! But how is it that now you generally offer me your right arm ?" "Well, lam not so afraid as I was."

A well-known bishop was recently at a railway-station, and he asked a porter to look to his luggage and put it into the van. " How many articles, your lordship ?" said the man. Thirty•nine," replied the prelate, with a hum onrous twinkle, to the lady beside him. "That's too many, I'm afraid," said the man, in perfect good faith. " Oh," said the bishop," I perceive you are certainly a Dissenter." STARTED WITH A LUCKY NIIMBER.—" I hear • Gail Fatter, who left here a few months ago, is married and living in Indianopolis. Did he marry well ?" "Oh, yes, he mar- ried well. He was well when he married." "No joking. I mean did he get a good start by marrying?' "Oh yes, he got a good start—he married a widow with seven chil- dren."

Jones: "See here, Smith, I don't like to harry you away from the boys, but you are a married man and I am afraid you will have trouble if you stay with us any later. It is nearly midnight." Smith: "Oh, don't worry abut me; I'm all right." "But yen said Mrs. S. nearly took the roof off when you got home after midnight." "Yes, but there is no danger this evening." " Won't she awake?" "Oh, she will be wide-awake enough, but my eldest daughter had her beau with her this evening." " What difference Can that make?" "A very big difference. She will h.tve all the clocks in the hease two hours slow."

A WIFE CHARGED WITH MURDER.—At Hayes, Sussex, on Tuesday, an inquest was held on the body of Mr. James Gibbons, a contractor, aged 63. Deceased's wife deposed that on Saturday night she and the deceased quarrelled in the bedroom, and he flourished a revolver, upon which she went downstairs. Hearing shots, she returned and found him dead on the floor. Medical evidence disclosed four bullet wounds on the body, one of which it was held could not have been inflicted by deceased himself. The inquiry was adjourned, and the police meanwhile arrested Mrs. Gib- bons on a charge of murder. TRAGIC DEATH OF A POACHER—Late Oil Saturday night a gang of poachers, returning heavily laden with game, , rested for a short time near the landing-place of the Cale- donian Canal steamers at Inverness, with the view of ar- ranging as to the best mode of carrying their spoil into town. 1 A poacher, named Colin Campbell, had the circsse of a young deer in his possession, and had a double-barreled rifle secreted under his coat. One of the barrels was loaded, I and while Cameron was endeavouring to place the deer inn better position on his shoulders, the weapon fell to the ground and at once went off. Staggering across the road, Cameron fell, exclaiming that he was -done for. Medical aid was got, but he died in a few hours. Cameron was 30 years of age, and a native of Cullode.n. FEARFUL EPIDEMIC OUTBREAR.—An outb:eak of fatal epidemic is reported from sum remote counties of Notth- West Virgmia, adjoining Kentucky. The drought having dried up the ordinary wells, the inhabitants drank water from some mineral wells which producsd a peculiar diseae as deadly as cholera. Several entire families perished, the effects of the disease being terribly sudden. The mortality is variously estimated at from :400 to 800. Few of those attacked recovered, the proportion of fatal cases being from GO to SO per cent. The whole district is reported to be in an abject condition. The New York Traune or to-day pub- lishes intelligence from Hinton, West Virginia, stating that the reports of the fatal epidemic were not exaggerated. Ac- cording to the latest reports it is estimated that 2,000 per- sons have perished from the disease, which was, however, not of a contagious character.

I. THE LONDON MISSIONARY SOCIEAT • - • A M.EETING,AT RUNCORN. The 'annual sermons in aid of the LonaonMisslonity' Society were preahhed in Bethesda Con'gregation&-Chapel, Runcorn, on Sunday, by Mr. T. Lord, of Madagascar. There were goad congregations at each service. On Tuesday even- ing the annual missionary meeting was held.' It Was pre- ceded by a very pleasant and enjoyable teaparty of AU infor- mal and social character, several ladies of the congregation having prepareclthe tea, coffee, and other refreshments pree ,vided. Mr. Thomas Rigby, of Sutton, presided over the subsequent proceedings, and he was supported by the Rev. E. B. Rice, and Mr. T. Lord (deputation) ; the Revs. J. D. Thomas, R. Cl. Hughes, E. Williams, and W. Vause; and Mr. W. Handley and Mr. F. Cl. Warne. After devotional exercises, the Rev. J. D. Thomas read the secretary's renort which stated that the sums obtained during the past year for the society, were as follows : Widows anl orphans fund, £2; Bethesda new year's cards, £7 10e. 2d. ; class boxes, £2 4s. 10d. ; St. Luke's Sunday school collection, £1 Os. 51d. ; missionary box, Thos. Brookes Handley, £1 17s. Od. ; subscriptions : Mr. Jno. Williaise, £1 ; Mrs. Handley, V. is.; collections on previous Sunday, £4 183.2 d. ; total £2' Us. N. In a short address the Chairman referred with pleasure to the fact that so many young people were present. (Hear, hear.) He was afraid that the elder members of Christian churches were So thoroughly imbued with the duty that ' devolved 'upon them of supporting the mission deld, that they attended to it year by year as the missionary. 'meeting came round, and did not think much of stimulating ordirect, log the young to take up the same work with interest and devotion. It was just possible that they might have got into the habit, as the annual services came round, of making their contributions to the cause, and then thought that their werk connected with the mission was all acomplished. It had some-• times occurred to him that it would be better to see the Christian church giving more constant attention during the interval that elapsed between one year and another, net merely subscribing and contributing annually, but regularly throughout the year, making it a point of duty to do this, and also to evince an interest in missionary work. Theriot fore he thought the young should be early impressed with the good work, and led to give as much attention to it are they well could do. The Rev. E. B. MGT., who had spent 11 years as a missionary in South India, described the nature of the work of the missionaries there in a very interesting manner, and. referred to what had been accomplished. The Hindoos, he said, had not accepted the Christian religion as we in Eng- land accepted it,but through the teachings of the missionaries they had lost confidence in their idols and their heathen doe- trines, and they were prepared to embrace at some future period the Gospel of the Lord Jesus Christ. (Applause ) Mr. LORD spoke in an eloquent manner of the physical as- pects and the Government of the island of Madagascar. He referred to the humane and wise laws under which the Mala- gese now lived, dealing principally with the educational part of the subject. Every child eight years ot age and upwards was compelled to attead school, and there were upon tne island 1.167 schools, and the registers contained the names of 150,000 children. (Applause.) He described the wonder- ful change which had taken place in the lives and actions of the people, and in the ruling power of the country during the past twenty-five years. From a savage, idolatrous people, enveloped in mental and moral darkness, there was arising an educated and Christian nation, and the Govern- ment, which was most harsh and oppressive in all its Acts, now recognised the sacred rights of conscience and gave full religious liberty. The French Government, in its unright- eous pretensions, was not seeking to bring uader their authority a rude collection of savages that were continually at war with each other. They were attempting to stamp out the life, the energies, and the liberties of a nation which had given great promise for the future. It was a sad and terrible thing to see a great nation like France sending its hoe clads and soldiers to destroy ths liberties of a young, rising, and hopeful nation like Madagascar. The French occupation of Madagascar meant the destruction if English trade and commerce there; that British influeneeS which the people had always gratefully recognised as helpful and beneficial to them were to be abelished ; that the Blble which now lay open before many thousands of people, had to become a closed book, and that its precious and glorious truths were to be replaced by the false doctrines of the Jesuit priests, and that the Church, which in days past had brought forth its faithful martyrs, was to become the prey of the dark hearts and intrigues of the Jesuit priests, lie prayed them to ask God that such might never be the fate of the land or the people. (Applanse.)—The Rev. E. Wm- trams proposed, and the Rev. W. VAIISR seconded, a vote of thanks to the Chairman and speakers, and it was carried with acclamation.—Theladies who had prepared the refresh- ments were also cordially thanked on the motion of the Rev. J. D. Tawas, seconded by Mr. F. G. Wein:E.—Me collece tion amounted to £2 9s.

div.p: WESLEYAN I'OfiTIGN MISSIONS.
MEETING AT WARRINGTON.

Special services in aid of the Wesleyan Foreign Mission Society were held in the Bewsey-road Wesleyan Methodist Chanel, Warrington, on Sunday, when an excellent sermon was preached both morning and evening by the Rev. J. A. Macdonald of Manchester. There were comparatively large congregations, and the collections realised the sum of £9 18s.

The annual public meeting was held in the same place of worship on Monday evening, when there was a large attend- ance. Mr. John Bennett, of Bewaey Hall, presided, and he was supported by the Rev. J. A. Macdonald, of Man- chester, and the Rev. H. W. Holland, of Liverpool, who attended as a deputation from the parent society ; the Rev. James McTurk, Rev. C. Cutting, and other gentlemen. The meeting was opened with singing and prayer, after which the Rev. C. Catting was called upon to read an extract from the annual report —The Rev. C. CUTTING stated that the re-- port of the operations for the last veer was found to be one of the most encouraging and hopeful it had ever been their privile re to lay before the supporters of the society. The work of Christian missions was arduous and beset by diffi- culties, but God had been with them. The condition of Ireland, though still unsatisfactory, was much better than it was twelve months ago, and the work continued to ad- vance and flourish in France amid very peculiar difficulties. The Italian districts still prospered, and in spite of many difficulties Methodism was advancing in Germany. In Germany. In Spain and Portugal steady and persistent work was being carried on ; and each was the case in Malta. A good work was being done amongst our sai:orfe and soldiers which had not only won their gratitude but the acknowledgment of the naval and military authorities. The spiritual condition of the West Indies was never more satisfactory than now ; but in Western Africa two things had militated against success during the past year. Trade had been in a depressed state, and there bad been numere one little ware; bat still a very gracious work had been done. In continental India and Ceylon the work being car- ried on would bear fruit in the future—a reaalt they ought 'to bear in mind at home. A good educating work was go- ing on and the Lord would give a manifest success. The report was favourable in every detail, but it was true much remained to be done. Let them be thankful for what had been accomplished, for abroad as well as at home the bles- sed enirit of God was leading ransomed sinners to the feet of the Saviour. One lifetime had seen all the results in connection with Wesleyan Miseions for all bad been accomplished iu 70 years. Let them therefsre, remember that the scciety was still in the spring. time of its growth, and before it lay the summer with its clustering fruit. The willing hand and prayerful heart and a self-sacrificing spirit was more and more required, and as long as the society was overruled and directed by a divine power it would go forward with incalculable blessing to mankind. Turning to the finances be foaled that £145,000 were forwarded into the Lord's treasury last year, connected with their Foreign Missionary Society. Of that amount Liverpool district, In which Warrington was situated, con- tributed £7.600, showing a gratifying increaee on the year of 4'500. Warrington did its share in connection with that amount, but they were going to do more in the present year. That was their first missionary meeting in connection with the Bewsey-road chapel, for in previous years they were united with the remainder of the Warrington circuit The Warrineton circuit lest year contributed £240, of which £l5 were expended. The Bold-street and Beweey-road chapels together contributed £llB 2s lid. There were, many willing workers in connection with the society, era they were deserving every encouragement in their grard and blessed work. (Applause.)—The CHLIRMiN &Jesse quently addressed the meeting, remarking that he was glad to hear the report was so satisfactory. The large atten- dance at that meeting showed a hearty interest in the work of the society. He would like the gospel pushed on a little faster than it had hitherto been, and it could be done by everyone putting their shoulders to the wheel and h 1 ping forward the gospel chariot. They could do their best by prayer and other means, and they ehould have sparks of gold and sparks of silver to help the missions along. There were plenty of sinners unconverted in Warrington and other towns, but they were wish- ful to send the gospel into foreign lands • and might God mess their efforts in that direction. (Applanse.)— The Rev. J. A. Macdonald next gave an address, in the course of which he said that the age gi more societies.l onTr eh ewn ohbi mission- ary t than wau livedhm ,otnwghhisatid b c which was e en as so ccrhieeaptrirreceess tehenreit sedediddbayns not thhake tnaomgwee tnoln ef society was one whose object was to make earth like heaven and men like God, and could they conceive a so- ciety whose aim was nObler than that? Everyone connec- ted with a society like that must certainly be encoble4, as they Diertook of the society of it. The miesionary society was the embodiment of the highest principles, and was as noble as it appeared to be. Sanitary science, social science, and medical science relating to the good estate of the body of man were things to be commended, but after all there was a nobler thing than the body—there was that intellig.nt resident enshrined therein, which was vastly and infinitely nobler than the body, and the missionary society had par- ticular reverence for its good estate. The highest kind of philantrophy was therefore contemplated by the soc:ety which raised the soul from its degradation through sin to a family relationship with the King of Kings and Lord of Lords, placing them into the royal family of heaven, and making them heirs of everlasting felicity. That society was therefore worthy of the highest commendation and enthu- siastic support. Its missionaries were inspired by the love of Christ when they went into inhospitable climes, and landed on shores that were in many cases malariotts and deadly. The ferocity of cannib2is had been faced by their missionaries, anl he thought such godly men were deserv- ing of every support and assistance. A noble spirit of benevolence animated the collectors, and he earnestly ap- pealed for an increased interest in the work of tl-e society. —The Rev. H. W. Holland, of Liverpool, a'eo cave an in- teresting address on the mission cause; after which a col. lection was made in aid of the tunas of the society.

THE TREDEGAR CATASTROPHE.---ThB coroner's inquiry concerning the death of one of the fifteen men killed in the recent explosion at the Hochin Colliery, near Tredegar, was concluded on Wednesday. The jury found a verdict of I "Accidental death," there being no evidence to show how the explosion was caused. FATAL FIRE IN LONDON.—Abont midnight, on Wednes- day, a fire broke out in the house of the lodgekeeper at the Penrose-street Board School, Walworth, London, and the caretaker's wife, named Mary Ann Harroll, was so severely burned that she died shortly afterwards in the hospital. Her eldest child, seven years of age, was also injured. ALLEGED MURDER OF A HUSBAND..—.At Uxbridge, Sur- rey, on Wednesday, Elizabeth Gibbins was charged with the murder of her husband by shooting him with a revolver. Inspector Morgan, of the Criminal Investigation Depart- ment, said that the prisoner had since her arrest stated that she was in the room when the shots were fired. She was re- manded.

ITHE WIGAN FRAUDS—At Liverpool Assizes, on Tues- day, before Mr. Justice Day, William Holt, 64, bookkeeper, and John Caldwell, 46, stockbroker, were indicted for hav- ing, at Wigan, in October, 1878, feloniously stolen the several sums of £lBO, .£4O, and £220, the moneys of the Mayor, aldermen, and burgesses of the borough of Wigan. The prisoners were also indicted for having received the above sums knowing them to have been stolen. Mr. Le- resche prosecuted. He said on October 15th, 1878,a clerk of Caldwell's named Hampson heard Holt say, "1 can find no money at all except Corporation moneys," and Cald- well replied "Money I must have." Hampson then left the room and heard no more, but next evening ho was sent by Caldwell to Holt for some money, and the prisoner went to the Corporation safe, took out £lBO, and received for it an I 0 U from Hampson, who handed the money over to Caldwell. He received £4O on October 18th in the same manner, and £220 on the 30th. Speaking of the part played by Reynolds, the learneel counsel said that up to the spring. of this year he (Holt) had kept Reynolds in idleness, and had paid him more than the salary he himself received every year.—On Wednesday the charge was one of conspiracy to defraud preferred by the Wigan Corpora- tion against their late treasurer, William Holt, their pro- fessional auditor, John Caldwell, and his clerk, John Rey . noldst and was opened before Mr. Justice Day at the Liver- pool Assizes. Holt and Caldwell were convicted on the previous day of stealing large sums of money from the Corporation. So long ago as 1870 a sum of £1,359 was owing by private property owners to the Corporation, and that money Caldwell was directed to receive and pay into the bank to the private improvement account of the Corpor- ation. Soon after that bad been done the cashbook rela- ting to that account disappeared, and in some manner came into the, possession of Caldwell. In 1871 Holt was appoint- ed borough treasurer, and Caldwell, who had been acting as treasurer pro ton, became merely the professional auditor. Holt immediately after his appointment entered into exten- sive stock and share transactions, and the books of the Cor- poration were soon affected by those transactions. Cald- well lent him large sums of money to make up his bal- ances and certified that Holt' accounts were correct. When Caldwell became bankrupt in 1876, the private improve- ment account, the existence of which was said to have been forgotten by the Corporation, was drawn out of the bank in order to furnish Holt with money to repay Caldwell. Rey- nolds apparently also knew of the forgotten account, as a paper in his handwriting was found in bolt's office in August last in which he mentioned it. It is allegel that he repeatedly obtained sums of money from Holt under threat of divulging the frauds that were going on. When the case for the prosecution was concluded Caldwell stated that he knew nothing of the private improvement account until It was mentioned at the police court. The court then ad- journed until next day. On Thursday, the case was con- cluded, all the accused being found guilty. Counsel for thr the prisoners addressed the Court in mitigation of pun- ishment, and his Lordship deferred passing sentence till etzt morning.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
BATURDAY, NOVEMBER 29, 1884.

THE House of Lords has shrunk at the last moment from facing the storm which it has provoked. It is something gained that it has turned tail before entering upon another pitched battle, for, although there could be be no question as to which side would in the end be victorious, fighting takes time and time has become precious. It is worth all that Mr. GLADSTONE is likely to concede, and much more—for we do not hear that he is about to concede anything—to ensure the passing of the Franchise Bill and Redistribu- tion Bill during the present Parliament. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, who is behind the scenes, says we shall have "a Redistribution 'Bill which will be more radical and complete than any which seemed possible a few months ago." This means that the Tory party, and the Lords as a part of that party, having made up their minds to surrender, are disposed to "go the whole hog "as a means of ingra- tiating themselves with the new electors. If they cannot any longer keep Hop-GE out, they will try to make it appear that they have always been anxious for his admission. In- deed, he may count now upon being received, as MILTON has it, with Nods, and books, and wreathi'd There is nothing new in this, as there is nothing new under the sun. The Tories fought a fierce battle twenty years ago against any lowering—" degrading" they called it— of the borough Franchise; but when they found that the pressure was getting altogether beyond their power of resistance they con- ceded household suffrage—at the bidding of Mr. GLADSTONE ! Up to the present, the PRIME MINISTER has not asked them to make a sacrifice of the House of Lords; their time has not yet come, but it is rapidly approach- ing. So far as he is concerned we are ready to admit that he took the right course the other evening in voting against the motion in the House of Commons for the Reform of the House of Lords. He occupies a most peculiar position; he has lost no opportunity during the past few months of pointing out to infatuated peers that, like the possessed swine we read of, they were rushing headlong to destruction. Their only chance of safety lay in surrendering themselves to him at discretion. They have taken heed of his warning—they have surrendered, and it would be ungracious, not to say mcon- sistent, if, at the very moment that they put themselves into his hands, he were party to an assault upon them. Mr. GLAD- STONE is bound dnring the present Parlia- ment, by ties which he cannot break, to take no decisive action against the Upper Cham- ber. Great as he is as a Reformer, he is great as a Constitutionalist, and it is obvious that he does not think he would be justified in countenancing any proposed alteration of the Constitution which was not prominently be- fore the country at the last General Election. But if the PRIME MINISTER is held back by the enormous responsibilities of his position, other people, outside the Ministry, are under no such obligation; and we would

urge upon electors, and those who will shortly become electors, the duty of pressing forward with the agitation which has been so successfully begun against the House of Lords. The division on the question in the House of Commons on Friday night was, all things considered, a most encouraging one; and we believe Sir WILFRID LAWSON is quite correct in saying, " No great reform move- ment has ever had so good a division on its first introduction into the House." There is a leaven in 71 as against 145 which, if the conditions be favourable, will not take long to leaven the whole lump. And it is for the people themselves to make the conditions favourable. They have for some time been "pulling hard against the stream," and have made extraordinary headway. It will never do to take in oars and drift back to the old place. The task of reforming or abolishing the House of Lords is one of course that must be left to the next Parliament ; but meantime the question requires to be kept to the fore- front. Great changes, as Mr. W. CROSFIELD remarked in his address to the electors of Warrington, are made slowly; but they are made, and they are made as the result of incessant action. It is satisfactory to see that a resolution was passed at the meet- ing on Monday night in favour of dealing with the Peers; but something more will be required than isolated re- solutions. Earnest, resolute, and intelli- gent men in every part of the kingdom must be banded together, working on common lines and to a common end. With this object in view, there was a representative meeting in London, on Tuesday, at which body and stimulus were given to the newly- formed "People's League for the Abolition of the Hereditary Legislative Chamber." Sir WILFRID LAWSON was appointed President, and, as he is a politician of experience, tact, energy, and good humour, we do not doubt that he will lead the way to victory. The payment of one shilling per annum, and adhesion to the platform of the organisa- tion, will constitute membership ; so that the League will be brought, as it ought to be, within the reach of every working-man who is anxious to do something for his country's ' good. There are some, of course, who would prefer to talk about " reform" rather than "abolition ;" but it should be noted that the League does not pledge anyone to the prin- ciple of a single Chamber. What it aims at is the abolition of the hereditary principle in i legislation, and there are few, indeed, who call themselves Liberals who are prepared to 1 say that because the wise father may have been made a peer it is right that foolish sons shall be legislators to the third, fourth, and fourteenth generation. An agitation for re- form, to be effective, must have a principle as its basis, and, this settled, the pl-ttform should be of the kind that will be least likely to divide those who are to be called upon for its support. The " feople's League for the Abolition of the Hereditary Legislative Chamber" possesses these essential elements of success, and as such we commend it to the attention of all who are interested in putting an end to the mischievous meddling of an irresponsible House of Lords.

Li THE Conservatives of Warrington, as we f gather from a report in the columns of a con- , I temporary, have been having a "rearing dinner" in connection with their new club. The proceedings seem to have been charac- terised with" sweetness" if not with "light," for everybody was plentifully " sugared " as the toasts went round. The CHAIRMAN (Captain REYNOLDS) proposed in genial terms the health of the borough member, Mr. J. G. Mc MINNIES—a proceeding so cour- teous and considerate' seeing that Mr. McMirnirEs is a Liberal of Liberals, that we cannot help wondering how it could happen that there should have been a lack of cour- tesy to the press, in that a representative of this journal was ript invited to attend the gathering. Can it be that the " sweets " were laid on at the last moment, and that there was some fear of a possible acid element? People who would have a reputation for be- ing gracious should not be guilty of these little sins of omission. Whatever opinions we may express in our leader columns, we feel that we can lay unquestioned claim to fairness in reporting, irrespective of politics. Mr. MCMINNIES was not of course present to respcnd to the toast of his health ; he was, ; let us say—with humble deference to the , chairman of the Conservative Club—better employed in attending, to his Parliamentary duties. But how came it to happen that Sir GILBERT GREENALL was also absent? Was 1 it that he .cannot stand the night air? Or i was he, as on the week previous, " indis- posed ? " It could not be that he was averse I to the " sugaring " process, because as to that he is so well qualified to give as well , as take that he may be classed as "A 1 at ' Lloyds," and Warrington, and everywhere else. Indeed, in this respect it may be said of him, , as Shakespeare says of Cardinal Wolsey, that I he is a "man of an unbounded stomach." Mr. PORTER reminded the workmen present , that Sir GILBERT had said he would "stick to them if they would stick to him," but it does ; not look much like sticking to them when he , is absent on an occasion of this kind. Per- haps he has come to the conclusion that ' "absence makes the heart grow fonder," and ; that the less they see of him and the better they will like him. Captain REYNOLDS ought ' to have explained; he was evidently in a ; candid mood, for he is reported to have said in giving "a few facts about those who had I been instrumental in the erection of the club," that it was determined they would "have a club in Warrington that should be large and convenient enough to house all the Conservatives in the town." Happy man! We congratulate him on the result. We congratulate the Liberal party, too, for if the premises in Sankey-street are large enough to house "all the Conservatives in the , town," Sir GILBERT GREENALL may "smoke the pipe of peace" while catching stickle- backs in Walton Reservoir, for he cannot have the ghost of a chance of becoming the member for Warrington. •

LAST week we drew attention to the pro- secutions at St. Helens for selling lottery tickets. This week several other persons have been heavily fined at the same place for a similar offence. We raise no objction to the law being enforced, providing the police authorities act consistently—punishing par- sons who may offend equally with publicans. It is satisfactory to find that we are not alone in the view we take, for we learn that "the Mayor of Biimingham has resolved not to allow the use of the Town Hall for bazaars in future, unless upon the distinct understanding that no lotteries shall take place. This de- cision arises from a consultation between the magistrates and the Watch Committee on Thursday, when it was decided to prosecute the promoters of bazaar lotteries in the same way as other gamblers." This is as it should be; it is making justice a reality.

WHAT is called the glorious uncertainty o the law has, so far, been strikingly exempli- fied in the action for libel instituted by Mr. CHARLES WARREN ADAMS against the Hon. BERNARD COLERIDGE, son of Lord Chief Jus- tice COLERIDGE The proceedings arose out of a!letter written by the defendant to his sister, Miss MILDRED COLERIDGE, who is engaged to be married to the plaintiff. The letter was well calculated, supposing its contents to be true, to cause any woman to hesitate before , committing her future to such a man as Mr. ' ADAMS was said to be. But Miss COLERIDGE, from the knowledge she possessed, did not hesitate to characterise the statements re- garding Mr. ADAMS as "miserable false- hoods," and demanded from her brother the "fullest retractation," on pain of handing the letter over to Mr. ADAMS. No retractation was forthcoming, and the case was taken in court, and heard at some length on Friday and Saturday. It was practically admitted that the letter was one which, under ordinary circumstances, would be set down as libel- bus; but Mr. Justice MANISTY pointed out that it was privileged, as a communication between brother and sister. The question for the jury to decide was not whether the state- ments in the letter were true or false, but whether the defendant believed them to be true when he made them, and whether they were made without malice or improper motive. RUNCORN SONS OF TEMPERANCES. The recent concert in aid of the widows and orphans of deceased members. resulted in a profit of £l5 LIBERAL ',Reruns —ln Bethesda Lecture Hall, OR Thurs- day evening next, Mr. B B. Hackney will deliver a lecture on " Free Trade or Fair Trade" DENSE FOG AT RIINCORN.—The town was enveloped in a dense fog on Tuesday night, and traffic on the river was at a standstill. No casualties are reported. WIDNES C.E.T.S —A devotional meeting was held on Thursday evening in the National Schools, the Rev. A. P. H Wilson in the chair. Addreeses were delivered to a moderate audience by the Vicar and Mr. Foley. LECTURE ON PERSIA.—Lt the Camden Mutual Improve- ment Class, Runcorn, on Friday evening, Mr. F. G. Warne, of the judo-European Government Services, delivered a lec- ture on "An Englishman's experience in Persia" Sr. Perm's Cauncu, Wumots.—The opening services of this church were continued on Sunday. The Rev. J. Wright Williams preached morning and evening to large congrega- tions. The collections at all 'he opening services amounted to £llO. A NEW LINE OF STEAMERS FOR WIDNES —A. fleet of five steamers, which has been called the "Fell Line," will commence running direct from Widnes to London on Wed- nesday next. The vessels will convey goods from Warring- ton, St. Helens, Runcorn and other places. Mr. White is the Widnes agent. THE BANKRUPTCY OF MR. IrAPP.— The public examin- ation of John Yapp, corn miller, dm., of Halton, near Run- corn, was fixed to take place at the Warrington County Court on Thursday, but on his name being called out he failed to put in an appearance. The Judge Mr. W. Wynne Ffoulkes, adjourned the case sine die. DELAY TO MAIL BAGS AT RUNCORN AND. WIDNES.—Itt consequence of the severe frost of Tuesday morningthe mail bags were an hour and a half late at Runcorn. The driver of the mail was compelled to leave the horse and trap at Hall Wood, and walk home with the bags, so elionery were the roads. The mail cart from Warrington wee, from a similar causeon hour late in arriving at Widnes. WIDNES PARISH CHURCH IMPROVEMENT CLASS AND Gratteaspost.—At the weekly meeting of this class in the National Schools on Wednesday evening an interesting de. bate took place on 'Oliver Cromwell; is he worthy of our admiration?" Mr. S. Cook opened the discussion in the af- firmative, and Mr. J. Treacy replied in the negative. An animated discussion ensued, in which Messrs. J. F. Whittle, D. 1. Brooks, and J. W. Machin took part. Further consi- deration of the subject was adjourned to Wednesday next. The Rev. A. P. H. Wilson presided. SUDDEN DEATH AT WIDNES. —• Ann Caine,6o years of age, wife of Patrick Caine, of 26, Helena-etreet, Widne., died very suddenly on Saturday night. About five o'clock the deceased went to Ann-street West for the purpose of making a purchase, and shortly afterwards she was found lying on the ground making a gurgling noise in her mouth, and having the appearance of being in a fir. She was at once conveyed home, where she died at 6 e'clock. The deceased had recently suffered from bronchitiaand had been attended by a Liverpool physician. The coroner dee- med an inquest unnecessary. DEATH OF AN OLD B4UDGEWATER SERVANT AT Russ- anzte.—On Saturday night Mr. James Lee, of Fountain- square, Town Hill, Runcorn, died at the advanced age of 77 years. The deceased entered the service of the Bridgewater Navigation Company at the age of nine, and nearly the whole of his life was spent in that employment. He was first employed on board the passenger steamers running be- tween Runcorn and Liverpeol, and he was afterwards pro- moted to a position on the pier at the old quay, where he remainea for a period of 40 years. The deceased was one of those injured in the explosion of Mr. Buxton's steam yacht at the old quay some years ago. RECHABITISM AT WIDNES. The " Onward " Tent, No. 1,475, of the Independent Order of Rechabites, Salford Unity, held a meeting in Stalin's Temperance Hall, Simm's Cross, on Tuesday evening. This tent, which has been in existence about twelve months, has a membership of 30 per- sons, Mr. J. Reay being the secretary. There was a mode- rate attendance at the meeting, and the Rev. J. Hothersall, who presided, made a speech advocating the adoption of total abstinence principles. Brother J. Dimond, P.H.C.R , of Southport. and Brother C. Duckett, D C R, Birkenhead, also delivered addresses in which they strongly urged the claims of the Rechabite order. Recitations were given by Brother T. Reav, and Mr. J. Johnson, and the choir of the Oakland-street Gospel Temperance Mission rendered several glees. Brother J. Harper being the conductor and accompanist. The usual votes of thanks concluded the pro- eeedings. SUPPOSED DROWNING FATALITY AT RUNCORN.—Cbarles Jones, who was in charge of the chlorine stills at the Run- corn Soap and Alkali 'Company's works, when the two children were suffocated a month ago, has been missing since Tuesday evening. At that time Jones, who has been dis- charged from his employment, left home for the purpose of taking a loaf to a flat lying in the canal at the Old Quay. There was a dense fog prevailing, and Jones not returning it was surmised that he had fallen into the water and beea drowned. A watchman named Ellis states that on Tuesday night he heard shouts on the canal side, but on proceeding In the direction whence they came all was still. On Thurs- day Jones' cap and a loaf were found in the canal, and very little doubt is felt as to his fate. The canal has been dragged several times, but the body had not been recovered up to yesterday afternoon. THE CHEMICAL WASTE NuISANCE AT WIDNES.—III re- ference to the action taken by the Local Board to abate the nuisance arising from the chemical waste heaps deposited near the Central Station, Mr. Fletcher, the inspector under the Alkali Acts, writes as follows to Dr. O'Keeffe, chair- man of the Health Committee :—"The recommendations that the heaps on the south side of the railway near the Central Station should be ' walled' shall be carried out, as also that concerning the laying of blown waste.' I would, however, draw attention to one subject which has been omitted from the report, namely, the question whether the neighbourhood of the Central station, so near to the dwell- ing houses, is a suitable position for the deposit of alkali waste. This is a question with which the Government in- spector under the Alkali Acts has no power to deal, but one solely for the Local Board. It is, I fear, probable that even when the greatest care is taken in layins the waste some smell will arise from it which will be a source of annoyance to those living in the neighbourhood." TEE LATE MR. W. C. JONES.—The will, with five cod- icils, of William Charles Jones, late of Manchester, and of The Elms, near Warrington, merchant, who died on the Ist August last, was proved at Chester on the 10th instant, the value of the estate being stated at .£875,863 14s 6d. Among the bequests to public institutions are £5OO to St. Mark's Hospital, London, and £lOO each to the Asylum for Idiots, Earlswood, Redhill, Surrey; St. Anne's Society, Church Missionary Society,Church Pastoral Aid Society, Manchester Phurch Diocesan Building Society' Manchester Infirmary, Manchester City Mission, National Hospital for the Paral- ysed and Epileptic, and the Royal Hospital for Incurables at Putney. To Lucretia Elizabeth Jones, the widow, is be- queathed the sum of £1,250 for her immediate use, together with The Elms, Warrington, and the house No. 35, Adelaide Crescent, Brighton. The eldest son, William Charles Jones (one of the executors the widow being the other), and the second son, Walter john Henry Jones, receive bequests of £60,0D0, and freehold land and hereditaments respectively, while smaller legacies are left to various other members of the family. The codicils are principally concerned with directions as to the future conduct of the business at Bed. ford, and the increase of the annuity of the widow fron £5,000 to £7.000. SCARLET FEVER AT EARLESTOWN.—The governing au- thorities of the Newton township are at present engaged in putting forth every effort to suppress a serious outbreak of scarlet fever in the most populous portion of the township, namely, Earlestown. For some weeks past there have been a considerable number of cases, and hitherto the endeavours to stamp out the "unwelcome visitant" have proved on availing. The sufferers are chiefly young children, and it is believed that the majority of cases have arisen through their having been sent to school where they have mixed with other children and thus, unintentionally spread the disease. In one or two streets in the town it is stated that scarlatina is very prevalent, and there have been several deaths. The local authorities, however, are bestirring them- selves with commendable activity, and disinfectants are an- plied,and other steps taken to prevent fresh outbreaks Not only is the disease prevalent in Earlestown, bat there have been a few cases in the Wargrave district—though, happily, as yet, it cannot be looked upon as an epidemic, or of a very dangerous character. So serious, however, has the matter become that last week the School Attendance Committee of the Newton Improvement Commissioners passed a motion to the effect that the Sanitary Committee should consider the advisibility of closing the day schools while the fever eontinues at its present stage. CRUELTY TO HORSES AT WIDNES...-. Before Mr. F. H. Gossage and Mr. H. Gaskell, junior, at Widnes Petty Ses- sions on Wednesday, Mr. William Rowlands, contractor. Victoria-road, Widnes, was charged with cruelly illtreating a horse by causing it to be worked whilst in an unfit state, and Henry Bartley was summoned for so working it. In- spector Greenwell, of the R S.P.C.A., stated that on the 13th met, he saw Bartley in Ditton-road in charge of a dark brown gelding which was attached to a cart. The animal was in a very poor condition, excessively lame on the near fore leg, and when it was in a state of repose stood upon three legs. The man told witness tat he always cured the horse when it was in that condition by pouring a kettle full of water upon the sole of its foot.—Mr. Robin- son, veterinary surgeon, Warrington, said he had examined the animal. It could not put down the near fore foot with any confidence, and it was very uneasy. There was an alteration of the structure of the foot. Rowlands' who was present, said it was fit for work, and that he could make the foot all right at any time by pouring a kettle full of boiling water into the "frog."—Mr. Rowlands denied having made this statement.—Mr. F. Proctor, veterinary surgeon, Man- chester, said there was enlargement of the corona of the horse's foot. It was an aged animal, unfit for work, and bad been a considerable time.—The Bench fined Rowlands £2, and costs 14s, and diemissed the case against his man.— The officer applied that the veterinary surgeons' fees should be allowed. Mr. Rowlands smugly objected.—The magis- trates allowed each veterinary surgeon half a guinea.—Mr. Rowlands (excitedly) : Well I cannot pay it. You must send me to gaol. What area to do with the horse.—Mr. Gossage : That is nothing to do with us. You have work- ed the horse in an unfit state and you must take the conse- quences,—Peter Dennett, junior, farther, Ditton, was charged with working a horse whilst it was in an unfit state on the 13th inst. Inspector Greenwell saw the defen- dant working an old gelding attached to a cart in Anne- street. Oct its back there was an old wound the size of half a crown containing blood and matter. The animal was un- fit for work, and he ordered the defendant to take it from the shafts.—A fine of 101 and costs was imposed.
WIDNES STARR BOWKETT BUILDING SOCIETY.—An ap- pr prietion meeting was bald on Wednesday evening, when M. H. A. Warton, of Church-street, became entitled to an

1 • advance of £4OO. - ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.—There was discharged from the Whines Accident Hospital on Thursday Bernard Murray, aged 69 years, who was admitted on Tuesday, suffering from a dislocated shoulder. On Monday night he Blipped on a kerb stone near the Golden Ball, Moss Bank, and falling heavily received the injury named. ST. BEDE'S YOUNG MEN'S SOCIETY, WIDNES.—The min- strel troupe in connection with this society on Saturday evening gave an entertainment to an audience of 400 persons who had assembled in the new schools. A capital pro- , gramme of the usual minstrel character was gone through in admirable style. Mr. Caldwell accompanied on the piano. i ILLNESS OF DLL GEORGE PILKINGTON, J.P. -- Our 1 readers will hear with much regret that there is no improve- ment in the health of Mr. George Pilkington, J.P., who has bees seriously ill for some time. He was removed from his Woolton residence to Scotland some time since ; but after being there several weeks, he was, on Tuesday, with the consent of his physicians, safely conveyed to his residence at Woolton. His condition remains very critical, and is a source of grave anxiety to his relatives and friends. THEFT OF COAL AT WIDNES —Yesterday, at Widnee. Ponce Court, before Messrs Brock and 11. Gaskell. junr., Mary Walton, a married woman, was charged with having in the previous day stolen from a railway siding on the old ' marsh, Widnes. 70lbs weight of coal, the property of the London mid North-Western Railway Company. P.C. ' Murray deposed to apprehending the prisoner when in the act of carryina the coal away, and as he had been twice ; previously convicted for similar offences, she was sentenced to a month's hard labour. DISTURBING THE SALVATION ARMY AT RUNCORN.— At Rtiocorn Petty PessiOns, on Monday, Henry Moores, a young man, was brought up in custody charged with being guilty of riotous, disorderly, and indecent behaviour in the Public Hall during the celebration of divine service therein. He was further charged with assaulting P.C. Smith at the same time and place. William Greenwood, captain of the local branch of the Salvation Army, stated that the Public Hall was licensed as a place of public worship, but as he Was unable to produce the certificate the Bench adiourned the . case for a week, and admitted the prisoner to bail in hisciwn recognisances of £lO and two sureties of £5 each. ROBBING A. FELLOW SERVANT AT WIDNES.—Mary Ellen Gray, a young woman, will brought before the Widnes mag- istrates on Monday, charged a ith stealing. an ulster and a petticoat, worth 9s, the property of Jane Alice Morris. Gray and Morris were both employed as servauts at Unsworth's dining rooms in Victoria-road. On Tuesday Gray bor- rowed the ulster from Morris to go and see a relative saying , that she would return in a few minutei. She did not, how- I ever, again put in an appearance, and on Toursday infor- mation was given to the police. On the following morning P.C. Cheers apprehended the prisoner at Runcorn, when she was wearing the ulster and a petticoat belonging to the prosecutrix. Toe prisoner, who said she had no intention to steal the articles, was fined lOs and costs or seven days. Tann. nv BOYS AT WIDNES.— Before Mr. ,j. Brock and Mr. H. traskell, junior, a'. Whines Police Coati on Mon- day, James Keating and Michael O'Toole, both 14 years of age, were charged with stealing three cardigan jackets, the property of Samuel Held, Alden-road, Widnes. The jackets were missed from the shop OD the evening of the I.ltii inst., and on Sunday morning PS. Strickland apprehended Keat- ing who was wearing one of the stoles jackets. He acknow- ledged that he had stolen it from Mr. Reia's chop. The I same day the sergeant found another of the jackets in the 1 kitchen of the house where O'Toole lived. O'Toole mid he I met Keating in the street, and at his instigation they went to the shop to "sneak." As both prisoners bad been pre- yionsly charged with vaiious offences, the Bench 'sentenced them to 14 days' hard labour, lobe followed by live years mu a reformatory school. AN INCORRIGIBLE Winxes I ourn.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, William Delaney, 10 years of age, whose parents reside in arrentell-st.wer, Widnes, was charged with stealing a hen, value is Si, the property of P.C. Davie. On the 24th inst Davie, who lives in Grenfell- street, missed one of his hens, which he subsequently found in a cote in the yard attached to the house of the prisoner's parents The prisoner acknowledged stealing the hen.—Mr. G. H. Denby, clerk to the School Board, said the prisoner had given the officers of the Board a great deal of trouble. He was quickly becoming incotrigible, but his mother each time the Board had taken any action had purposely kept him away from court, because she Knew it WAS desired to send him to an industrial school as the only place where be could be reclaimed.—The prisoner was remanded for a week with a view to sending him to an industrial school on is summons by the School Board. A GIRL THIEF AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Police Court, on Thursday. Margaret Taylor, 13 years of age, was charged with stealing two aprons and four pinafores, the property of Edward Hill, of the Friendship Tavern, Fryer- street, on Tuesday. The prisoner was also charged with stealing two chemises, the property of Mary Kilcullen, of Vicar-street, on the 15th instant. Mrs. Hill missed the aprons sad pinafores from the clothes line on Tuesday afternoon. The prisoner shortly afterwards went to the shop of Mr. Craddock, pawnbroker, Church-street, and offered them in pledge, but as they were wet be suspected the prisoner, and gave her into the custody of P.C. Brees. It was then discovered that the prisoner had pledged with Messrs. Marsh and Smith, pawnbrokers, Church-street, the stolen chemises.—The gia admitted having stolen the pina- fores, but denied that she had ,taken the aprons and chemises.—As she had been previously before the Bench on a charge of larceny, she was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour. A RUNCORN FARMER FINED. Before Mr. James Rey- nolds and Captain C. W. Hazlehtirst, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, John Acton Ford, farmer, of Higher Runcorn, was summoned for being drunk whilst in charge of a horse and trap. The defendant sent a young man named Parker to represent him. Parker stated the defendant was busy at work, but the Bench informed him that if his master did not appear before the rising of the court, a warrant would be issued for his apprehension.—Subsequently defendant ap- peared and pleaded not guilty. The evidence showed that on Saturday evening, the 18th inst., Edward Harrison was crossing Church-street, when the shaft of a vehicle driven by the defendant struck him in the chest and knocked him to the ground, the wheels of the trap passing over his legs. He was injured in the hip, but was now much better. He reported the matter to Police clerk Wallace, who at once proceeded to the spot and found the defendant in so drunken a condition that be was not fit to be in charge of the ve- hicle. He allowed a boy who was in the trap to drive the defendant home. A fine of 103 and costs was imposed. s BREAKING INTO A R INCORN SUNDAY SCHOOL.—At Ran- corn Police Court, on Thursday, before Mr. James Handley and Mr. G. L. Davies, Samuel Rogerson, 16 years of age, was brought up on remand, charged with stealing 2s sd, the monies of James Kirkham and another. Mr. Kirkham, builder, Greenway-road, is one of the superintendents of St. John's Presbyterian Sunday School, and about six o'clock he saw that the building was properly secured. Next morn- ing, about half.past nine, Mrs. Richardson, wife of the care- taker, entered the schoolroom and found the library and cupboard broken open and the books and other articles in the greatest disorder. The same morning P.C. Bryan ap- prehended the prisoner at his home in John-street and found 2s 51 in his posseseion. He stated that his mother bad given him the money, but he subsequently admitted that he had effected an entrance into the school through one of the win- dows and had opened the cupboard door with a table knife (produced) and the library door with a bed key. lie had stolen the money from the cupboard.—The prisoner now pleaded guilty, and he was fined 203 or a fortnight's irn- prisonment. The fine was paid. ALLEGED INDECENT ASSAULT NEAR Moorre.—At Dares- bury Petty Sessions on Tuesday, a farm labourer named James Mullins. of Moore, was charged in custody with bay- ing, on the 6th of July, at Moore, indecently assaulted Hannah Fleetwood, daughter of William Fleetwood, a far- mer, also of Moore. The prosecutrix said that she was now living in service with Mr. Charles Dawson, of Runcorn, and was 18 years of age. On the day in question, a Sunday, she was walking on the bank of the Old Quay canal towards Warrington, shortly after five o'clock in the evening. She passed near the prisoner, who was sitting on a rail, and he got hold of her and indecently assaulted her. She broke from him and ran away.—There being no evidence to cor- roborate this statement, the charge was reduced to one of assault ; and P.C. Boyle stated that when he apprehended the prisoner on the 19th inst., and charged him with indee cent assault, the latter replied "I know all about it,. I did ' put my arm round her waist, but that was all." lode- fence, prisoner said that he had known Fleetwood since childhood, and was used to joking with her. He repeated the statement that he merely put his arm round her waist. —He was fined 20s and costs, or a month's hard. labour. --Mullins was then further charked with violently as- saulting P.C. Boyle, when the latter took him into custody at Moore on the 19th inst. From the evidence it appeared that a severe struggle took place between the officer and his prisoner, and it was with eveat difficulty that the man was taken to the nearest police station, even after assistance had been gained by Boyle. For this offence prisoner was fined lOs and costs„ or 14 days' imprisonment.

WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD, The monthly meeting was held on Thursday. Mr. T. S. Timmis presided, and there were present the Rev. Father Clarke and the Rev. Father Finegan, Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. Bradshaw, Brock, Deacon, Imison, Shaw, Davis, and G. H. Denby (clerk).—The General Purposes Committee recom- mended that the School Management Committee be au- thorised to increase tho salary of Mr. T. Appleton, caretaker of West Bank School, from 21s to 25e per week, at their discretion, the increase not to be made before the let Januarr, 1885.—The District Education Committee reported that during the month of October (five weeks) there were 175 applications for the payment of fees, and they were re- commended to be paid in 167 cases. There were 71 persons prosecuted before the magistrates for contravention of the Education Act. Convictions were obtained in 65 cases, one boy was sent to an industrial school, and rive attendance orders were granted.--The School Management Committee recommended that the resignation of Mr. R. Calland, as- sistant master in the senior boys' department of the West Bank schools be accepted; and that the tender of Messrs. 11. Evans and Co. for the supply of slack and best Orrell coal until June 30th, 18811, be accepted.—The Sites and Building Committee recommended that the plan for the in- creased infant accommodation at the Weat Bank Saools be ' approved, and that the committee be authorised to obtain tcnders for carrying out the same..--Mr. Brock explained that the Education Department had sanctioned the plans which differed very little from Cm original suggestion; and

as far as the committee could see it was the only way in which the additional accommodation for 150 infants could be obtained. The one great objection was that a portion of the playground would be occupied, but the plans were arranged that the least possible space would be taken. It would he far less costly than building a separate school outside the site of the present building.— Accounts amounting to £407 7s lid were recommended for payment by the Finance Committee, who also reported that during October there had been paid into bank £173 Is 4d, including school fees from Simm's Cross school £7B 17s 6d, Warrington-road £29 63 9d, West Bank £62 16s 10d. These minutes were all contirmed.—A letter addressed from 51, Croxteth-road, Sefton Park, Liverpool, 15th November, was read from Mr. S. K. Muspratt. It stated "I have felt for some time time there ought to be in the Board schools at Simm's Cross, Warrington-road, and West Bank, a proper place where the children can drink water, inserted in the walls. If the School Board will accept two fountains to be placed in each department of the above-named schools (6 in all), I will provide same, the only stipulation I request to make is that the Widnes Local Board provide a perpetual supply of water gratis."—lt was decided on the motion of the Chairman to accept Mr. Muspratt's generous gift, and I the Clerk was instructed to forward a copy of Mr. Mug- prates communication to the Local Board, end request them to comply with the condition mentioned.—Tbis concluded the business.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held at the offices. Bridgewater- street, on Wednesday. The RQv. Canon Barclay presided, and there were present Rev. Father Fennelly, Messrs. J. Pritchard. R.. LOA, P. Brie.coe, T. Norman, and F. Rigby (clerk)—On the proposition of Mr. Norman. seconded by Mr. Briscoe, the seal of the Board was attached to an agree- ment between the Board and tha Runcorn Property and Investment Company for the purchase of 3,712 square yards of land off Greenway•road for the site of the proposed new school, at the rare of 5s per superficial square yard. The total cost of the site is Dm. Mr. Holmes, architect, Liver- pool, had an interview with the Board, and produced plans of the school, which he explained. They were adopted.—A discussion took place on the removal of the Board's offices to Waterloo House. Mr. Norman urged that some steps ought to be at once taken for the Board taking up its occu- pation in that building,. and eventually it was decided to advertise that the offices of the Board in Bridgewater-street were to let.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The ordinary meeting was held on Tuesday, at Dutton Workhouse. Present The Rev. Canon Barclay (in the chair), the Revs. .11. W. N. Tanner, J. Lockwood ; Messrs. John Ashton, T. Norman, W. Handley, R. Ashton, Lewis, W. Fisher, Aaron, Whittaker, Weir, Darbyshire, Andrews, Mclntyre, Campkin, H. Linaker (clerk), W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk). Fitstawmg —Rev. J. Lockwood reported that the Finance Committee recommended the payment of accounts amount- ing to £lO5 5s 3d. The tr,:asaret's cash book showed a balance to the credit of the Union of £2,746 14a; and there was only five weeks of the present quarter to run.. .

THE BOARD AND THE reHESTE.II BRIDGE —Mr. Aaron moved that the clerk write to members for Mid-Cheshire And West Cheshire and *SA them why they allowed an Act of Parliament to be passed this year giving power to the county justices for Cheshire to vote money, a portion of which would come out of the pockets of the ratepayers of Mid and West Cheshire, towards freeing the Dee Bridges without hest communicating with the onntrihnti rig authori- ties of Mid and West Cheshire.".—The Clerk observed that It was usual for members of Parliament to send bills affect- ing authorities in the districts they represented, down to the Authority's.—Mr. Aaron said they placed gentlemen in Par- liament to watch their interests, but when they obtained their seats they cared for nothing.—Mr. R. Ashton had great pleasure in seconding the motion. The Clerk pointed out that within two months of the Bill being paesed the magistrates voted the money.—Mr. Derbyshire thought the clause a bit of sharp practice on the part of Chester Corporation.—The motion was carried unanimouslv.—Mr. Hmdley then submitted the following resolution, which had been submitted by the committee appointed to consider the subject :—" That the Guardians of the Runcorn Union, after considering the corespondence which has passed between the clerk of the peace and the clerk to this Board relative to the Chester Improvement Act of 1894, by clause 114 of which Act the magistrates of Cheater, Flint, and Denbigh were empowered to vote to the Chester Corporation such sum as they might think fit for the freeing of the Dee Bridge tolls, and by virtue of which the magistrates for the county of Chester in quarter sessions assembled have recently voted £l,OOO therefore oet of the county funds are of opinion that all future bills or portionteof bills empowering magistrates to vote money out of the county funds should be submitted for the consideration of all contributory authorities prior to the introduction f such bills or portions of bills to Parlia- ment ; and that copies of this resolution be sent to the Clerk I of the Peace and the members of Parliament for the county."—Mr. Mclntyre seconded the resolution, which was passed nem. cons—Mr. Handley also moved "that the clerk write to the clerk of the Chester Town Council and mac if the magistrates for the counties of Flint and Denbigh have voted any, and if so, what sum under clause 114 of the Chester Improvement Act, 1884."—Mr. Aaron seconded.— ' Carried unanimously. Puecernoes Aoateeer FIRE —The committee appointed to consider the means el extinguishing any fire that might occur at the Workhouse recommended that tenders for 100 yards of hose and couplings and three dozen leather buckets be invited from Messrs. Handley, Lea (Runcorn),and Caldwell (Warrington), and that Mr. Jones test the yield of the well. —The Rev. J. W. N. Tanner moved the recommendation, but only the first portion was passed, as it PM considered unadvisable to waste any water from the well, as there was a great scarcity in the neighbourhood at the present I time. INFORMATION, WANTED.—Mr. Aaron moved that the clerk to the Assessment Committee provide each member of the Board with a list of the assessments of all gentlemen's man- sions and parks in the Union over a hundred pounds.—Mr. Norman seconded the motion, which was carried.
