div.p: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHDRITY4

The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday, under the presidency of Mr. John Ashton. There were present the Revs. J. W. Tanner, 3. Lockwood; Messrs. Andrews, Darbvshire, Mclntyre, Aaron, R. Ashton, Lewis, H. Linaker (clerk). W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk), and Adams (Medical officer). THE POLLUTION OF THE OLD QDAY CANAL—The Deputy Clerk read &letter from the Local Government Board with reference to the pollution of the river Irwell and Old Quay Canal, stating that as there was no, definite purpose in the Authority asking for a local inquiry to be held by one of the Board's inspectors, they declined to accede to the Autho- rity's request.—The Cnairman remarked that they had shit ted the responsibility to the Local Government Board, and that was what they wanted to do.—lt was understood that the-clerk would write to the Board saying the Au- thority considered they were released from all respon.si- bilitv. .

Tart MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.—The Deputy Clerk said draft chums had been received from the Manchester Ship Canal promoters for the protection of the Authority. They were almost identical with those inserted last vear.—A com- mittee consisting of the Rev. J. Lockwood, Messrs. Ashton, Lewis, Thomas, and Aaron consider the clauses. Emporium Foa FRODMIAM.—The Chairman signed the apportionment of the cod of executing certain works of drainage for the benefit of the Frodstram township and lordship. The proportions were as follow 7.—Township, 041 5s ; lordship, £ll5 15$; total,.£4o. THE. FRODSHAM WATER.SGEIEME.—The assistant secre- tary to•the Local Government Board wrote asking for more definite information with regard to the actual yield from the wells of the proposed waterworks for Frodsbain before fur- ther considering the application of the Sinitary Authority , for sanction to borrow money for the esecution of the scheme.—Mr. Bancroft, the engineer, addressed to the clerk a letter in which he stated that it was most unfortunate that the Local Government Board had not at once sanctioned the further expenditure upon the wells dm., for now that the frost had commenced he was afraid it would mean fur. .ther unnecessary expenditure through the delay. Tin SEWERAGE DIFFICI7LTE AT WESTON.—The Deputy .Clerk read a letter from Mr. Edward G. Amin, of ,thiaMersev Salt and Brine Company, with reference to the proposed sewer through land at Weston Point leased from the Bridgewater Navigation Company. The Brine Company were willing to agree that the sewer should be laid, but they wished for an agreement with the-Authority that the sewer should be laid in the line shewn on the plan, and to the en- tice surrender ef the land of the old sewer, ,kc ,the expenses lathe agreement to be borne by the Sanitary Authority.—On the motion of Me. Aaron, seconded by Mr. R. Ashton, it was decided that the clerk acknowledge the communication say- ing that whatever agreement the company might require to protect themselves, they must pay the costs of both parties, as the Guardians did not require an agreement at all OUTBREAK. OF TYPEIOID FETER.—The Medical Officer presented a special report in which he stated that four persons had been attached with typhoid fever at Kingsley. Referring tothe source of the outbreak, the medical officer stated that one of the patients had drunk water from Kingsley Dnook previously to his illness. He therefore con- sidered it to be his duty, notwithstanding repeated !Tinsels to a similar request, to again suggest to. the Authority that the wates in Kingsley Brook be analysed. The question If its likelihood to engender typhoid fever should at :once be formally settled, in order that the inhabitants of Kingsley might receive the benefit to be derived from such know- ledge. He recommended that two of the patients should be removed to the Infectious Diseases Hospital at the Work- house.—lt was stated that there was an abundance of pare water in the township, bat a brook which ran through the place had been occasionally used.—The inspector was ordered to have the samples of the water analysed, and it ' was decided tbat the patients mentionsd by the medical officer should be brought to the hospital. A. REPORT WASTED.—The Local Government Board drew the attention of the Authority to the fact that during lthe quarter ended the 315th September last there bad been seven deaths from typhoid fever in the Runcorn registration , sub-district, and requesting that the medical officer should prepare areport on the recent prevalence of fever.—Mr. Adams said he bad prepared a rough draft of his report:: The sublept was postponed for a fortnight.

REPRESENTATION OF LIVERPOOL—The Executive Corn. tnittee of the Liverpool Liberal Association on Tuesday night discussed the question of redistribution as it might , affect Liverpool, and declared in favour of dividing the city I into six wards, giving one representative to each.

div.head: 1 OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: 1 OUR LONDON LETTER.

LONDON, THDRSDAT. It is difficult to say which is the more remarkable, the change which has suddenly overspread both political parties, Or the unemotionable manner in which the country has ac- cepted the phenomenon. It is hard now to think that only a fortnight ago Liberals and Conservatives were drawn up in battle array, and were hourly approaching a crisis in which the very Constitution was involved. Then suddenly, in the twinkling of an eye, the whole scene was changed. Arms were laid down on both sides and the hosts which on Tuesday morning were manouvring for position in a desper- ate fight, were shaking heads and exchanging congratula- tion,. In the House of Commons the new situation hat been promptly and unreservedly accepted. Out of doors, though perhaps with a little tinge of bewilderment the same condition of mind exists, and alter coming to the very brink of the precipice everybody walks quietly beck, and things go on in their old way as if there had been no autumn recess and no Midlothian campaign with their multi- tudes of angered men.

Sir W. Lawson and Mr. Labouchere are still angry. They thought they had the House of Lords almost within their grasp, and to have it suddenly snatched back is more than they can bear with equanimity. But in other quar- ters below the gangway it is now seea and f ally admitted that Mr. Gladstone, quick to see his opportunities, and skilful in availing himself of them, has really obtained more by friendly negotiation than by the completest victory on the battlefield. It is no slight thing that the country should be spared the turmoil and unwholesome excitement that would have followed upon a renewed rejection of the Franchise Bill by the House of Lords. Had Mr. Gladstone conducted the affair in other, and, at the moment, more se- ductive, ways the Franchise Bill would at this moment have been rejected by the Lords, Parliament would have been prorogued, the campaign in the country would have beers renewed, and next session there would have been another fierce tight in Parliament, with the Franchise Bill carried through the desperate resource of creation of new peers. Thereafter there would have been all the labour of passing a Redistribution Bill, heightened by bitter opposition in both Houses.

Now we shall get the Franchise Dill forthwith, and the Redistribution Bill so far settled that its passage through Parliament will be remarkably speedy. Of course, as the Redistribution Bill will be partly their own offspring, the ordinary opposition of the Conservative party will be reduced to a minimum. Where opposition will come in will be from the extreme tail of both parties and from the Irish members, who are already in a state of impotent rage at dis- covering a reconciliation between the two parties upon whose quarrels they established their power. The very least that has been gained is a whole year of legislative life and activity. But if the expectations of Mr. Chamberlain and Sir Charles Dilke are realised there is more than this gained, for we shall have a Redistribution Bill more Radical in its principles than the Radicals have dared to hope to see within the next five years. A few days hence Lord Randolph Churchill sails for India. When he comes back he will probably find the Redistribu- tion Bill through the House of Commons. It is curious to think that he should voluntarily efface himself from Im- perial politics as this particular crisis. Bat the fact is that the step is not in a full sense voluntary. Lord Randolph's state of health is not in that lively vigorous condition that might be inferred from the character of his speeches. He Is scarcely ever well, a state of things that seriously handi- caps him in the political race. Mr. Gladstone has attribu- ted a considerable proportion of his own success to his 'mag- nificent corstitution and almost unvaried good health. Lord Randolph Churchill never knows from day to day whether he will be able to get through its duties. The necessity f a prolonged holiday has been forced upon him through the past year. The prospects of a renewed fight in the recess deterred him from making arrangements for a journey. But as soon as the corning together of Lord Salisbury and Mr. Gladstone promised peace he decided on the Indian trip. At one time his intention was to go to the United States, his wife's relations having frequently urged him to visit New York. But Mr. Gorst's account of the charms of India in the winter proved irresistible, and Lord Randolph quickly determined upon a voyage thither. He has at present ar- ranged not to return till April. But I should not be sur- prised to see him back a month earlier. One thing he can- not stand on any terms is hot weather, and it is pretty warm in India in March. Lord Randolph is sure to have a warm welcome in India, and will doubtless avail himself of the opportunity of thoroughly studying Indian questions. In spite of his flighty manner and occasional recklessness in dealing with matters of fact, he has a great gift of applica- tion, and with great rapidity masters any subject, however complicated, upon which he fastens. Poor Mr. Justice Manisty is for the present moment the best abased man in England. He has contrived to give universal dissatisfaction. It is hard to say whether any one is pleased with his c,,nduct of the trial—except the plain- tiff. The best case lawyer on the common law bench is ac- cused of not knowing his business, and a strictly honest and conscientious judge of favouritism and partiality. Every- thing he did was unfortunate. Even so small a thing as declaring that members of the bar not acteally engaged in a case have no more right than ordinary spectators to the bar seats in a court of justice was unfortunate. Sound lawyers think he WAS quite right in letting the jury give their ver- dict, and for this reason : Suppose he is right in his law the verdict goes for nothing. Suppose he is wrong the amount ef damages is fixed, there is no need of all the expense, de- lay, and publicity of a second trial. The matter of every- thing the judge did was right, the manner was wrong. It certainly looked like partiality. The truth is that scarcely any judge can be impartial. He must take one side or the other, and especially where inti- macy or association of office is concerned. I question, if somebody else's sons had been before Brutus, whether he would have been in such a hurry for their decapitation. And I think that the apparent partiality of the judge swelled the damages. The general opinion is that the plain- will hold the verdict. If he is. wise he will get counsel to argue the case. He will find no difficulty in getting emi- nent barristers willing to argue a legal proposition. The damages are thought to be very smart ; but then juries take an all-round view of the case. The plaintiff will probably marry the lady—if she consents. She will come to him with no portion, and so the £3;000 will be so far an assistance. Sergeant Adams was one of the best known of the old genera. tion of lawyers, a man not merely of learning but of accom- plishments, and I am told an intimate friend of Lord Coleridge's father, who was also a common law judge. I managed to get into the court for a few moments on Sat- urday, a feat compared with which the passing of a camel through a needle's eye is scarcely worth mentioning. The place was crowded to the door, and outside was a group of briefiess barristers--cerhaps the most insolent creature in the world when it has got its wig and. gown on—all struggling for admission. On these occasions there is a. great routing out of wi.rs and gowns on the part, not only of men who, though higher, habitually sit in the courts, but of others who never held a brief in their life, and have given up all expectation of doisg so. It is quite startling to make discoveries of friends one has known for years with- out being aware of the fact that they have been called to the Bar. Adams, the plaintiff, is a man well known about London. He was for some time manager of the luckless Hour. I have seen a description of him somewhere as a fine,.band- some man. He struck me as being big and flabby, with the unwholesome general appearance ei a man who 8141 in hia clothes. Miss Coleridge is a !spectacled, not particularly attractive, lady, of the kind one is accustomed to meet at Social Science Congresses. She was exceedingly. self- possessed. and seemed on the whole to be rather enjoying the proceedings. She made her way smartly to the witness box when her name was mentioned. "I shall not require- you, thank you,' said Mr. Adams. "Oh, won't you?" she ;aid, and went off rather ..isappointed, I thought.

On Wednesday a petitien was filed' ha the Halifax Bank- ruptcy Court on behalf of Messrs Scarborough Bros., spin- ners ad manufrcturers, whose liabilities were stated at £150,000. ATTEMPT TO BLOW HP A TOWN HALL—What is sup- posed to have been an attempt to blow up the Town Hall at Royton, near Oldham, took place about six o'clock on Wed- nesday evening. It is believed that the substance used WWI gunpowder. All the windows in the basement of the hAll and a number of windows on the ground floor were blown out. No one was injured. THE BOLTON AND OLDHAM MITEDESS. DOL'ELPt EXECETION AND CONFESSIONS.—Kay Howarth and Harry Hammond Swindells were executed in Manchester, on Mon- day morning, at the County Goal, Strangeways. Howarth has been convicted of the murder, at Bolton, of Ricbd. Dug.. dale, commercial traveller ; Swindells of the murder, at Oldham, of James Wild, his wife's brother-in-law. Howarth. since his conviction, has seen attended by the Rev. James Dreaper, the prison chaplain, and Swindells by Mt. Cox, Wesleyan town missionary in Oldham. Swindells had from the first gratefully accepted the ministrations of Mr. Cox tt Howarth's demeanour had been more indifferent. On Sun- day night, Howarth went to bed about eleven o'clock and slept well. Swindells remained up until three o'clock next morning, and what sleep he had afterwards was broken. R sing at six, the men had breakfast,, and were then visited by Mr. Dreaper and Mr. Cox, who remained with them to. the end. The officials present at the execution were the, Under-Sheriff (Mr. C. Costeker),. the goveenor of the gaol (Major Preston), Dr. Braddon ancl Dr Paten (the gaol sur- geon and his assistant), and the chief warder. As the Inn walked to the scaffold the burial service was read by Mr. Dreaper. Swindells made the responses in a firm voice. Howarth sobbed a good deaL On the scaffold Swindells I said, thank Thee ; Thou art my Saviour,' and " Lore, receive my soul." Howarth said, "0 Lord, help jet each case death seemed to be instantaneous. The drop was eight feet. Berry, of Bradford, was the executioner. Both men had confessed their guilt. When visited on Sunday night by the governor, Howarth denied the murder, but said "he would not die with a lie in his mouth." On Mon- day morning he handed to Mr. Dreaper a confession in writing that he hod murdered and robbed Dugdale. Swine dells told the governor that he did not go to the house 'An which the crime was committed with intent to murder. To Mr. Cox, however, he admitted on Monday morning that he went to the house "with intent to kill." An inquest on tbs bodies was held by Mr. F. Price, district coroner, in the reading room of the gaol. The jury returned the usual for. mal verdict.

THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL SCHEME. KEELING AT WARRINGTON.

On Saturday afternoon a public meeting was held in the Public Hall, Warrington, in support of the Mayor's resolu- tion to all the Ship Canal Scheme and for the purpose of concerting measures to ensure success at the poll, and also te protest against the demand of the poll. There was a large attendance, amongst those preeent on the platform be- ing Aldermen Burgess and Kean, Councillors Dr. Mackie and John Pierpoint, and Messrs. George Woods, H. Whitham, P. Caldwell, Thos. Tunstall, John Hampson, W. Stirrup. J. Lawrence (Manchester), J. C. Fielding (Manchester), E. Woods, Richard Siddall, Win. Pucill, Wm. Perry, Henry Roberte, William Crosskill, J. Kilduff, and J. L. Tunstall and Wm. Roberts (hon. secretaries.) Alderman Burgess was voted to the chair on the proposition of Dr. Mackie, seconded by Mr. P. Caldwell, and the notice convening the meeting was then read by Mr. William Roberts. The CRAIRMAN said he was very glad indeed that the promoters of the Ship Canal scheme had convened a meet- ing of workingmen that afternoon for the purpose of secur- ing, as far as was practicable through their instrumentality, that success on the poll which was requisite to enable the Council of that borough to pass a resolution whereby an amount of money equal to a rate of 2d. in the £ should be given to the promoters of the scheme in getting the Bill through Parliament. (Applause.) He thought, judging from the nature of the meeting convened by the Mayor and held in that hall a short time ago—so large and so unani- mous a meeting as it WAS—Warrington ought not to have been pat to the expense of a poll on that occasion. (Ap- plause.) He thought it was somewhat too bad that War- rington could not give its money without being taxed by some handful of people—for it would be found it was only a mere handful of people—who by their action had caused an expenditure of perhaps not less than £7OO, which was money absolutely wasted. (Hear, hear.) So far as Warring- ton WAS concerned, if the Bill became an Act, and the shares were subscribed for, the Corporation could have the money repaid if they thought proper to ask for it; or, on the other hand, if they elected to become shareholders and owners of a portion of the property the money they were now paving could remain as capital fund in the con- cern. (Applause.) Mr. J. LAWRENCE, of Manchester, said the Act under which it was proposed thst the Warrington Corporation should subscribe the money WAS known as the Municipal Borough Funds Act. 1872. The sole condition in that Act was that when, in the judgment of a governing body of any district, it was expedient for such governing body to promote or oppose any local or personal bill—that was a bill like the Ship Canal as contra-distinguished from the Bankruptcy or other Acts—they might do so, and subscribe for such purpose out of the borough fund, borough rate, or other the public funds under their control. The interests of the ratepayers were fully and amply protected by the Borough Funds Act. It was held as a sound proposition in law as well as in common sense that the power to promote any bill by a governing body obviously included the power to join in promoting. The larger power included the lesser, and he did not think when the question was decided that it would be found that the law officers of the Crown differed from that opinion. In connection with this power to pro- mote hills, what did the Corporation get for it? A quali- fication was added in the Act that it must be for the benefit of the ratepayers. So far as the Town Council had vet given any informal opinion, the Ship Canal, in their judg- ment, was a project which would ultimately be for the benefit of the ratepayers of Warrington. (Applause.) The Corpora- tion by becoming joint promoters would acquire precisely similar rights as the Manchester and Salford Corporations, as defined in the agreement between the promoters and these municipalities, providing amongst other things that the Cor- porations sheuld have a share of the control of both the Act of Parliament and of the plans. Now, that was a most important point for the ratepayers of Warrington to con- sider. The Corporation by giving this £l.OOO would be able to sit at the Canal Board to say how far the bill should go and how far it should be altered or improved for the benefit of the ratepayers of Warrington. (Applause.) The duties of the Corporation of the future were likely to be of a much larger character than they had been in the past—(hear, bear)—but he would give them a few instances of what had been done, and for that purpose would take their nearest neighbour, Liverpool. Liverpool found the capital for the construction of the docks of the city. and. in the earlier stages, they applied for and obtained the cost of getting every Act of Parliament necessary to enable them to execute works such as docks. Therefore, the principle of municipal identification both with dock construction and, in the earlier parts, the getting of Acts of Parliament to construct docks was shown to have existed in the case of Liverpool. They had got the mos of the river Weaver, their next nearest neighbour. The magistrates of Cheshire, as they knew, paid the costs of getting an Act of Parliament to con- etitate a trust. In the city of Chester they had lately sub- scribed the sum of £15,000 towards a fund of about £36,000 which was being raised for the purpose of extinguishing the tells which were charged upon vehicles crossing the bridges in Chester over the river Dee. The Duke of West- minster had given £lO,OOO, the magistrates had given £l,OOO, and private persons had given other sums down to five pounds, but the principle was there that the Corporation out of the rates of the city of Chester had given a sum of £15,000 for the purpose of easing the burdens on locomo- tion. What was it the Corporation of Warrington was do- ing? Giving £l,OOO toe fund to get an Act for a canal which would help to reduce the burdens on the transit of merchandise and goods. (Applause.) The river Tees was almost analogous to their own river, because it had an estuary at its month ten miles long and three miles broad, and they had always quoted the case in Parliament, because it was physically almost analogous to the Mersey. That river had been improved through the action originally of the boroughs of Stockton-on-Tees and Middlesborough, and it was now managed by a trust. The original Acts were obtained by the municipalities, and Middlesborough, not many years age a small place without trade, was now dis- tinguished for its vast iron trade. He might mention other instances, such as Sunderland, Dublin, Belfast, Dundee, and London, but he would close by referring to the application to Parliament of the Corporation of Southanspton to enable them to contribute to the capital or the docks owned by the Southampton Dock Company. They would see that the principle of identification with works of that character was fully establisbed, and he thought it could not be said that there was no precedent for what vas attempted to be done by the Corporation of Warrington. (Loud cheers.) Mr. GROWER WOODS then addressed the meeting and pro- posed the following resolution:—" That the ratepayers of Warrington in this meeting assembled, heartily approving of the resolution come to at the town's meeting held on the 23rd October last in favour of a contribution out of the Borough rate tre the cost of the promotion of the Man- chester Ship Canal Scheme of a sum not exceeding twopence in the pound upon the rateable value of the borough for one year, do heartily pledge themselves to vote at the forthcoming poll iii favour of the said resolution, and to use every possible legitimate effort to carry the matter to a triumphant issue." (Cheers.) He said he considered it was a great hardship on the ratepayers of the town that they should have been put to the expense of a poll by merely a handful of men. As those present knew' there had been false prophets in every age and country. The great George Stephenson knew a great deal about them. M. de Lesseps, who carried through to a successful issue the Suez Canal, also knew something of false prophets. He (the speaker) did not take Mr. Dodds as an authority, but he did take Sir William Forwood as an authority, although he worked heart and soul in opposition to the Canal and attained his object. What did that gentleman say to the Mersey Dock and Harbour Board a few weeks before the Bill was thrown out? He would try and remember his words. They were something to this effect:—" Gentlemen, don't you think for a moment that the money to construct the Manchester Ship Canal will not be raised. I tell you that it will, therefore it behove us to use every effort in our power to throw out the Bill," and they did so. They were successful. They threw out the Bill, but it was a satisfaction to know for two days before it was thrown out he gave this pledge, viz, that if the Manchester Provisional Committee would construct the Canal in the way already drawn out, and which would now be carried out, that Liverpool would withdraw their opposition. (Applause.) It was said that they were estab- lishing a bad precedent in Warrington; but they contended that it was no precedent at all, and Mr. Lawrence had given instances of this. They were simply following examples which had been set by other towns. Instead of making use of vague arguments about the canal, let their opponents prove that trade would not come into the town. Let them prove farther that land and property would not be enhanced in value. On the other hand, would there not be a greater demand for their labour? And a better demand simply meant better wages. (Cheers.) If the Bill was obtained if they wanted their money back they could have it, if not it could remain till they were part owners in the Canal. (Cheers.) Mr. HENRY WHITRAIII said he had much pleasure in ' seconding the resolution. He did so as a workingman, and be looked upon the question from a workingman's point of view. Whatever workings there might be behind the action of Messrs. Davies and Sleekly they were not aware of them, but they were certainly justified in saying there was a secret history to be written of their manceuvres during the last few years, and when it came to be written he thought their character would be none the better for it, but that tbe town would give great praise to several gentlemen who had upheld the scheme from the first, and who he was glad to RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS, say were on the platform that afternoon. WARRINGTON BOROUGH COURT. SATURDAY.—Before Aldermen Burgess and Chandler. THREATENING LANGUAGE—Frederick Norman, labourer, Dakin's.court, was bound over to keep the peace for six months in £5, and one surety of £5, or in default one month's imprisonment, for using threatening language to- wards his wife on the 21st inst. Mosner.—Before the Mayor (Al&rman Harrison), in the

. - and Mr. John Fairclough. DrtuNamewass.—The following cases were heard :—Mary Cowen, dismissed on promising to sign the pledge; Samuel Davies, fined 5s including costs; Thomas Burke fined in the costs; Winifred Flanigan, fined 53 and costs; Geo. Lynch, drunk whilst in charge of a horse and trap, fined 10a and costs. SLEEPING Ocr.—John Bibby, Wm. Stokes, Margaret Fleming, Winifred Noon, Mary Shields, and Julia Ann Shields were brought up In custody on a charge of being found sleeping in an unoccupied house in Dial Court, at 3-30 the same morning.—Julia Ann Shields, who had gone in search of her sister to induce her to go home, was dis- charged, and the other prisoners, who said that they were drunk when they went to the house in question, were each sent to prison for a month. Bairn/ca.—John Cane, a middle-aged man, was sent to gaol for seven days for begging in the streets. CHIMNEYS ON FIRE. John Fleming was fined 5s for allowing his chimney to be OH file on the Bth met; and Joseph Bitchall was fined 3s 6.1, and Peter Finlay is for similar offences. Scmoor, ATTENDANCE CASES. -- The following people were summoned at the instance of Mr. Riley, school at- tendance officer, for neglecting to send their children to school, viz. :—john Fleming. John Taylor, Patrick Leon- ard, James Ratcliffe, Ann Costello, and Ann Floyd, fined Sc each ; James Roony (two children), fined 10s, and Thomas Urrnson (two children), case adjourned. DISTTIRBING THE PEACE.—James Boardman, alias For- rest, and George Frangleton, young men, were ordered to be bound over to keep the peace, themselves in £lO each, and two sureties in £5 each, for disturbing the peace by fighting in Sianenny-fields.—Patrick Dolan, charged with fighting in Buttermarket-street, was discharged on a promise not to offend again. OVERCROWDING CASES.—Thomas Waldron. occupier of a registered lodging -house, was summoned for allowing a greater number of people to sleep there than the house was registered for, on the 6:h inst. The registered num- ber was five, and seven people were found sleeping in the house. A man, who gave his name as " Rhoda " Kelly, was charged with keeping lodgers in an unregistered house. A fine of 103 and costs was imposed in each case. _ _ _ .

TIIESDAY.—Before hir. C. Broadbent. SLEEPING OuT.—A youth named Thomas Ward was charged with sleeping out on the previous night in Rose- yard, not having any visible means of subsistence.—After being cautioned, he was handed over to his parents. DEUNICENNESS.—John Garvin was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-street.—Dis- charged. WEDNESDAP.—BefOre Mr. .John Fairclough and Alderman

Chandley. Srzatirro BOOTS.—John Ashworth, factory hand, last from Oldham, was sent to prison for a month for stealing a pair of boots, value 9s 6d, the property of Charles Lan- den, 4, Lime-street. SLEEPING OUT.—Jane Flynn. and Esther Ann Harrison, young girls, were sentenced to a month's imprisonment each for sleeping in an uninhabited house in Rose-yard the same morning. Flynn was stated to have served 17 terms of imprisonment, varying from 14 days to 12 months. Har- rison had also been previously before the Bench. TEURSDAY.—The business is reported elsewhere. FalDAY.—Before the Mayor, Alderman Harrison (in the chair), and Captain Reynolds. Arr OrTcasr.—George Gerard was charged with being a rope and vagabond, and with sleeping eat. He had been sixteen times before the magistrates and was now sent to prison for three months' hard labour, the Chief•constable remarking that he (prisoner) never worked unless when in gaol. P.C. Corbett apprehended the prisoner. ALLEGED ASSAULT. Peter Tickle failed to answer a summons charging hiln with assaulting his wife Mary Ellen Tickle. A warrant for his apprehension was granted.

PaMAY.—Before Mr. W. Blinkhorn and Mr. C. J. Bishop. I DAIINKENNESS.—A fine of 5s andbosts was imposed upon each of the fellovring persons for being drunk :—J. Marsden, Parr; T. Morris, Windle; W. Lyon and W. Jones, Eccleeton. James Whitehead, Suttsn ; Joseph Cheetham, Samuel Gresty, Peter Webb, Parr; Martin Hickey, Peter Garrity, Eccleston ; and Edward Molyneux, Sutton; were each Stied 7s and 6d and costs for a like offence; and the following persons were fined 108 and costs each :—James Hayes, John Kean, Parr; William Forrest, Thomas Finsley, Windle ; Martin Hogan, Eccleston ; and James Scalley, E^.cleston. MISCELLANEOUS.—Bridget Rock was fined 5s and costs far using obscene language in Victoria-street on the 15th lust; and Mary Lawrenson was fined 2s 6d and costs for using profane language in Parr-street.—John Johnson was summoned for having the chimney of his dwelling-house at Parr on fire, and was fined Is and costs.--Mary Molloy was bound over tc keep the peace for three months, having been summoned for committing a breach of the peace on the 15th inst. HAWKING WITHOUT A LtcaNsE.—Williani Austin, a young man, was charged with hawkinz without a license at Eccles- ton and was fined 25 6,1 and costs.
YONDAY.—Before Mews. J. C. Gamble, W. W. Pilkington,

and C. J. Bishop. DRIINICENNESS.—The following persons were fined n and costs each for being drunk and diserderly at the place men- tioned :—Sarah McLoughlin, Market-place; John Doyle, Ecclestonestreet ; Samuel Ander3on, Windle; Jas. Donoughe, Liverpool-street ; Ann Pingerley, Windle ; James Butler, Church-street; Wm. Tanker, Church-street ; Mary Walsh, Liverpool-road ; Ann Monaghan, Higher Parr-street; and Thomas Holmes, Short-street, Eccleston. A Yournyur. LAW BREARER.—Aaron Grestv, a lad, was summoned for hawking chalk and stones at Eccleaton, on Saturday last, without a license.—The defendant stated that he had been sent oat by his father, wi,o held a license for hawking.—The Bench remarked that the fact of the father holding a license did not entitle the defendant to sell as wall. The defendant was cautioned against repeating the offence, and the summons was dismissed. BREACHES OF THE PEACE.—Mary Jane Hunter was sum. moned for committing a breach of the peace by striking a woman, whose name was unknown, at Windle, on the 17th inst.—The defendant, who alleged that she only acted in self-defence, was bound over to keep the peace for three months.--Samuel Davies and Thomas Hall. young men, pleaded guilty to a breach of the peace by fighting in Hard- shaw fields on the 22nd October.—The defendants were each bound over in one surety Of £5 to keep the peace for three months. DISORDERLY Benavrora.— Elizabeth Thompson and John Pring were together charged with an act of indecency committed in a passage off Corporation-street.—The Bench impo-ed a fine of 103 and costs, or 14 days, on each prisoner.

DRUNKENNESS.—John Allen, for being drunk and disor- derly at Appleton on the 15th inst., was fined 5s and costs. —Henry Starkey and Edward Atherton were each Cued dci and costs for being drunk on the highway at Dares- bury on the 10th inst. RETUSING TO Worrrall was charged with being drunk and disorderly on the 14th of November at Appleton, and with refusing to quit the licensed premises of William Lang Greaves, at Stretton, on the same day. He refused to leave the house when requested by the landlord, and a pOlieeman had to be sent for to eject him. He was fined 103 and costs for each offence, or a month' in default. UNJUST SCALES.— James Speed was fined 103 and costs for rising a pair of unjust coal scales, fifteen ounces against the purchaser, at Preston Brook.

wanted their Corporation to place themselves so that they should benefit in the same way as their kingdom had bene- fited by the great Suez Canal scheme. They must persuade their friends and neighbours to vote for it, and by that means they would not only be doing good to themselves but to their children and their children's children. (Cheers.) Councillor MACY'S supported the resolution. He pressed Mr. Adamson to come to the meeting if it were possible, but he gave him prettystrong reasons for his absence and be had followed them up by a letter which he read to them. Mr. Whitham had made a reference to the bills put out about the rates of some gentlemen who were en the plat- form at the last meeting; but they ignored the fact that there were at least 7,000 ratepayers represented there that night who came willingly, not to tax the few rich men who stayed away, but themselves. (Cheers) A sneer had been made at those on the platform, and he had been amused at the fact that all the statements that went out about rate- paying were more or less got up by Some half dozen men who claimed the same places, and said that they represen- ted £5,000 of rates. The men before him—and he would net use any language that was not literally correct—repre- sented at least £140,000, and after tbe sneer that was madeat him personally he would throw it back in their faces and tell them that they might have at least allowed Mr. Woods, himself, and others whose names he could mention, a simi- lar connection with the places in which they were interested, and not merely their humble homes. In 1722 Warrington stood on an equality with Manchester and Liverpool as to population. The three places conjoined to form a waterway between Manchester and Liverpool, but Warrington had some traitors in the camp even 160 years ago. They were men who were, to say the least, not up to the wants of the times. Liverpool became a great seaport. Manchester be- came a great emporium for national manufactures, while Warrington remained a poor and comparatively small place even to a very late date. They had another opportunity of raising Warrington to the position it ought to have oc- cupied contemporaneously with Liverpool and Manchester.. And he hoped that the decision not of that night—for that would be all right—but next week would be of such a nature that when it was known at the Home Office that the poll at Warrington had resulted heat least nine out of every ten voting in favour of the Ship Canal, that it would be seen at once that there was not a doubt in the matter. Let them record their votes next week in earnest, let them bring their friends and neighbours to the poll, and let them determine that the men who stayed away from it from bad motives should ten marked men in the future with regard to the interests of Warrington. (Cheers.) Mr. FIELDING, at Manchester, said as long as they had to pay the cost of the poll, let them take care to make it a triumphant success. Lt them record their votes in such numbers as to warrant the Committee in saying that it was universally the feeling of Lancashire that the Bill should be passed. He did not regard this as a private undertaking. and be sympathised with the efforts of municipalities to support it. This great movement should never decend into the hands of a private company. He had from the first ad- vocated a public trust. It was cheap carriage. They would naturally expect that a man putting machinery in a workshop would put in the best to be had. That was a common expectation. It was as vital to the interests of trade that they should have the beet methods of transit as that they should have the beat methods of production. It was as economically sound that all the outside communication should be perfect, as well as our inside, and every country was moving in the direction of trying to make itself a bet- ter and a cheaper producer. If they were to compete suc- cessfully it was either to be by the best appliances or by ex- traordinary cheap labour. Then there was the cotton trade. Every ounce of the raw material had to be imported into the country to be manufactured ; it was not like the coal trade. Those countrres that had the growth of cotton in their own contiaes stood in the first instance a better chance of competition, because they had not the transit of the raw material to cantend with. (Cheers) If they could not grow their own material on their own soil, let them get it las cheap as possible, and with as few taxes upon it as pos- sible, and with as few people living upon it as possible. He wanted the meeting that afternoon to understand that in Manchester they had had no poll, and yet by a side wind their opponents were trying to make it appear as if there was a strong feeling against the Bill. The dose was being repeated in Salford. Although there was no demand for a Mill there, there was a petition being got up to make the Home Office or the Board of Trade, or the Commissioners of Works, feel that there was a strong objection to the Bill. Warrington was, therefore, the only town that had the op- portunity of a full and a fair expression of opinion on the subject; and he rejoiced with them that they had—and be hoped that they would make it so —an opportunity of making it so uninietakeable that it would be a valuable fac- tor and argument when they went to the committee show- ing the state of public opinion of this big town on the ques- tion. (Cheers.) They had already deposited once more the sum of £2Bs,ooo—(cheers)—as a guarantee they would go on with the work if they obtained the Bill. Notwithstand- ing the great railway traffic they saw, and all the great sta- tions in Manchester that had become absolute mazes and puzzles ; that the traffic was doubling every ten years, and that the railway companies insisted upon taking passengers and the luggage traffic on the same lines! The railway com- panies would have to lay out four times the capital that was required for the making of the Ship Canal in the next 20 years unless the canal was made' and the latter was the truest means of providing for the growth of this great country, a, well as adding to the industry of the country, the cheapest and best means of extending trade. (Cheers.) Mr. W. STIRRUP supported the resolution. Reference had been made, he said, to the raining of £l,OOO towards the promotion of the canal, but he would have them give £50,000 if necessary to have the canal come to Warrington, as it would be such a grand thing for them. (Applause.) Mr. JOHN FIERPOINT said they were all aware that if the Canal Bill passed, from the information they had received from Mr. Fielding, there was a positive certainty that the work of making the canal would be carried out. (Applause.) And if it were carried out it must necessarily bring a great share of work to Warrington. He not only referred to the question of the labour which would be acquired to construct the docks, which would cover 20 acres of land in Arpley. He only regarded that as a fleabite with regard to what would follow. By the construction of the docks in Arpley one side would be available for Cheshire and the other for Lancashire, so that in a few years to corns the docks would be considerably more central than they could imagine at the present time. They could not have docks in their midst, as they knew, without warehouses and buildings of all descriptions being erected, and the erection of ware- houses meant the transit of goods to be stored, then to be manufactured, and when this took place it would be a great inducement for additional manufacturers to come to War- rington and find additional employment for the working classes. (Cheers.) Mr. H. ROBERTS then gave some explanations with re• ference to the poll. There were about 7,500 persons en- titled to vote at this election. It was desirable that 6,000 or 7,000 should record their opinions one way or the other. It would be of little value to the promoters of this magnifi- cent scheme if out of that large number of people only 2,000 or 3,000 thought it worth their while to record their votes. (Applause.) The resolution was then put to the meeting and carried with only one dissentient. Alderman Burgess having left the chair, which was taken by Councillor John Pierpoint, Alderman KEAN proposed a vote of thanks to Alderman Burgess for his services.—Mr. SAMUEL BARLOW seconded the resolution. Mr. LAWRENCE next made some remarks about a pam- phlet issued on the Ship Canal. The vote of thanks to Alderman Burgess was then put and carried, and the proceedings terminated.
GENERAL 'NEWS.

The Rev. John Dupuis, Vice-Provost of Eton College, died on Saturday. The Very Rev. Hy. Law, Dean of Gloucester, died on Tuesday morning. It is proposed to open subscriptions for a "Fawcett Memo- rial Fund," to be devoted to the higher education of the blind. The sum of £2,500 has been assessed by the committee of arbitration to the sufferers by the mill chimney disaster at Bradford two years ego. Mr. Samuel Morley, M.P., has consented to become Pre- sident o! the English Congregational Chapel Building So- ciety, in succession of the late Mr. Robt. S. Hudson, of Ches- ter. Mr. Morley has at carioas times contributed £3,557 to the society's funds. At the Central Criminal Court, London, on Monday, be- fore Mr. Justice Stephen, Charles Thomas, Thomas William Nash, and Edward Gunnell were indicted for forging the will of Mr. James Whalley. Henry Whalley Priestman, the testator's eon, was examined, and the court adjourned. On Thursday a witness deposed to the prisoner Nash hav- ing stated that the affair was a swindle. The trial appears likely to last corns days. GAMEKEEPERS CHARGED WITH MURDER.— Five game- keepers were remanded at Driffield On Monday on a charge of murdering a poacher named Fenby, who died from the effects of a bullet wound received in a poaching affray near Driffield on October 15 last. The prisoners were admitted to bail. HUNTING IN IRELAND, except in a few places, is being proceeded with without molestation. The local papers report excellent runs of the local packs in Limerick, Gal- way, and elsewhere. In North Kilkenny, where Viscount Clifden has given an impetus to the sport by paying off a large debt, the hounds hunt regularly. THE CHURCHILL-0 ORST BREACH HEALED —The quarrel between Lord Randolph Churchill and Mr. Crorst, writes a London correspondent, has been made up. Mr. Gorst on Monday night resumed his place beside Lord Randolph, and be has evidently forgiven his chief for the whipping he received a few nights ago. The " chief "is about to sail for , India. NARROW ESCAPE OF A ROCHDALE FAMILY.—EarIy On Saturday the residence of Captain Frank Schofield, Roch- dale, was almost destroyed by fire. The family and servants had a narrow escape. Captain Schofield was burned a little in gallant efforts to save his wife and children, and was at , one time almost suffocated. The other half of the villa was damaged by fire and water. Linn BY A " SOCIETY " PAPER.—Counsel for the de- fendant in the case ef Mrs. Blood against the proprietor I of Modern Society, for libel, in which £l,OOO damages , were awarded on Saturday, applied on Monday to Mr. 1 Justice Denman to stay execution on account of excessive damages. The just,ce replied that he thought them too . small. It was a case for very substantial damages. The libel stated that Mrs. Blood had been divorced—a state- ment of which slight inquiry would have shown the utter falsity. . _ .

MAYORS AND WORKINGMEN. The example of the ex- Mayor of Liverpool is being copied and improved upon by his successor in the mayoral chair (Alderman Ratcliffe), who will shortly hold a reception of working-men in St. George's Hall, for which 4,000 invitations are to be issued. Each invitation ticket includes the wife, daughter, son, or near friend of the artisan, as the case may be. Refresh- ments will be served, and short science lectures given, and an old English ballad concert is being arranged. Scien- tific and other objects of interest will be on view. THE PRIMROSE LHAGUE.—The ruling Council of the Primrose League have received the formal approval of Lord Salisbury and Sir Stafford Northcote to their organisation. Lord Salisbury gave his blessing in a somewhat cold-hearted way. He confessed that he did not know much about the character of the League, but he trusted that it might be found useful in assisting the Conservative party at elec- tions. Sir S. Northcote was more cordial, but, like his brother leader, did not waste many words on the Leaguers, who comprise the Earl of Limerick, Sir. H. Wolff, Sir Algernon Borthwich, and Mr. Marriott. FOREIGN COPPER AT A Hisave Dtsconar.—The quantity of French copper in circulation in England has seriously affected the income of the London Hospital Saturday fund. In the collection of this year the copper contributions amounted to more than £l,OOO. If this had been all in English pence and halfpence it would have been all right, 1 as a few weeks would have cleared the amount off in wages. But the French and Italian coins formed so large a propor- tion that the £I,OOO could only be exchanged into available money at a discount of from 20 te 25 per cent. THE KILLING OF A RACEHORSE.—Acting under a warrant district inspector Tyacke and a posse of police searched the house, at Distowel, of Michael Malony, and discovered a coat and trousers with what are believed to be bloodstains upon them. Maloney was placed under arrest and was charged with having caused the death of The Rover, at Inchyngallnah, Woodford, the property of Charles Henry James and Lucius Henry Deering, the official assignees of the Court of Bankruptcy, and Michael Ryan, the creditors' assignee in the matter of David Shine, a bankrupt in the town. The accused was formally charged with the offence at the petty sessions on Saturday, and remanded. THE ABOLITION OF THE HOUSE OF Loans—On Tues- day night Sir Wilfrid Lawson presided at a meeting in London consisting of representatives of Radical clubs and associations, at which it was resolved to establish a people's league, having for its object the abolition of the hereditary legislative chamber. It was arranged to hold meetings in various places in due course, at which lectures and addresses will be delivered by membe,e and agents of the league, and to circulate suitable literature, setting forth the object of the movement. Sir Wilfrid Lawson was elected first president, and among the vice - presidents are Messrs. Storey, Labouchere, and Bradlaugh, who were present. THE SKYE Crtorrens.—H.M.S. Assistance left Deinve- gan on Saturday, and arrived at Portree at 4-20 p.m., and the chartered steamer Lochiel, which conveys the county I authorities and the police arrived shortly afterwards. in the morning a small number of police were stationed at Deinvegan, and 25 marines were landed and quartered in the hotel. There was no demonstration on the part of the crofters, and the landing there, as well as in the other places, was effected without any resistance. The gunboat Forester is at Deinvegan' and the Banterer at 131 g. The marines left at Staffin and at Uig still remain there. The procurator fiscal of Skye has finished his inquiry at Dig, and will shortly report to the Lord Advocate. THE TORQUAY MURDER.—A statement has been made by Kate Farmer, the young woman to whom the prisoner was engaged to be married. She says that at six o'clock on the morning of the murder the prisoner came to her hoses and roused her, and as bhe was at ber bedroom window he stood on the footpath and told her that a fire had broken out at The Glen, and that Miss Keyse had been burnt to death. He added that he had cut his arm in breaking the glass of the dining-room window, but he did not state that the de- ceased lady's throat was cut. He made the observation that "they would all be marched off to the police-station." This was before anything had been said to him inculpating him in the affair. He had been in Kate Farmer's company the night before up to 10-30, when he went direct home to The Glen.

THE POST OFFICE AND TELETSONES.—The new form of license for telephone companies is for 31 years from the Ist January, 1881, and the following are the principal points on which concessions have been made :—The license contains no limit of area nor restriction as to running bunk wires from town to town. Call offices may now be opened whereby members of the public can communicate with subscribers. The claims of the Post Office to provide in the license for the supply of telephones to the Department by companies, and the proposal that companies should pay a royalty to Government npon private wires erected and maintained by it have been given up. By a separate agreement tele- phone exchanges may be connected with the Post Office, and subscribers may send and receive telegrams by tele- phone.

THE COLERIDGE LIBEL CASE.—The action for libel brought by Mr. Charles Warren Adams against the Hon. Bernard Coleridge came on again for bearing on Saturday. before Mr. Justice Manisty. The plaintiff having gone into the witness box and called evidence, the Attorney-General submitted that there was no case to go to the jury, and that there ought to be a non-suit. The Judge, however, thought it safer and better to take the opinion of the jury, reversing the right to decide the case as he thought proper in point of law. The Attorney-General, in reply, contended that the law was that a brother writing to his sister on the subject of her marriage, in relation to that marriage which was to result in her happiness or misery, was protected by virtue of the duty which was cast upon him, and that there was no occasion for him to enter into a personal controversy with the person against whom he was warning her, provided that he wrote4he letter in honest faith and for a good purpose, and not with the object of gratifying any malicious feel- ings. The Judge held that the letter of Mr. Coleridge, addressed to his sister, was a communication—that was to say, the occasion and the circumstances under which it was written protected the defendant from any action, unless it could be shown that he was actuated by malice in fact. Tne jury, after a deliberation of three-quarters of an hour, returned a verdict for the plaintiff, assessing the damages at £3,000. Mr. Adams applied for judgment in accordance with the finding. The Attorney-General asked for his lord- ship's ruling upon the question whether there was any evi- dence upon which such a verdict could be founded. Mr. Justice Manisty said there was not, and gave judgment for the defendant, with costs.—Mr. Justice Manisty, on taking his seat on Monday, said—" In the case of 'Adams v. Cole- ridge,' tried before me on Saturday, no application was made by the plaintiff for a stay of execution, but I have no doubt the case will be taken by the Court of Appeal. With- out any such application, I think it right to make an order —perhaps it may not be necessary—that execution be stayed till the case is disposed of in a Court of Appeal. As I have mentioned the case, I will take the opportunity of saving that there seems to be a very general misunderstand- ing as to the course I took on Saturday. It seems to be thought an unusual thing, and, I may say, in some quarters an improper course; but it is a course which I have taken before, and which I shall certainly take again under similar circumstances. And the reason why I did so is because it is, in my opinion, in the interest of both parties to bring litigation to as speedy an end as possible. It is especially in the interest of the plaintiff, but it is in the interest of both parties, and it was for this reason that I did it. And if I was wrong, the Court of Appeal will say 80. And if they should think that the verdict was right, the course taken may avoid exposing the plaintiff to the cost of the delay, and also all risk of a second trial. In this case what I look to is the due administration of the law and the further- ance of justice, and if possible, to render litigation as little 'costly and as short as it conveniently can be consistent with justice."

THE SHIP CANAL AND THE FUTURE OF WARRINGTON. BY " ARCMS." That the future of Warrington will be very vitally influenced by the Ship Canal is a proposition which will, I think, be disputed by nobody. Yet, although on the one hand we have predictions of boundless benefits to be derived and on the other undue depre- ciation, there have been wonderfully few attempts free of bias or prejudice to forecast what are likely to be the real effects of the canal on Warrington. It will, therefore, perhaps not be out of place to attempt to do so in as impartial a manner as possible. Speaking generally, I think the influences of the canal on Warrington may be classed under the two heads, national and local. Under the former head will come those influences, which what is really an enterprise of national importance must have on the whole country, Warrington of course included; while under the latter head will come the special influences by which the canal, owing to its proximity, must affect Warrington. Now with regard to the national influences of the canal, it is hard to see how they can be otherwise than beneficial. It will be a great labour- saving contrivance, by which the labour of one man will be rendered as effective as that of two or even more is at present. It will facilitate exchange, and thus bring foreign commodities to English doors at a re- duced cost. As the Saez Canal may be said to have benefited the whole world, so may it be said of this canal that it will benefit the whole of Great Britain. If it cheapens the carriage of cotton, it is not only the Manchester manufacturer who will reap the reward but also the user of cotton cloth in the remotest corner of the kingdom; and if it reduces the price of imported food its good effect will be felt in every cot- tage in the land. Warrington will of course share in these benefits along with other towns, but over and above this it will locally be affected in a way which no other town will be. On the national issues it has seemed to me that a decisive verdict in favour of the canal must be given ; now the question arises what will bp its local influences? It is confidently assumed by the advo- cates ef the canal scheme that, locally speaking, the canal will bring nothing but blessings, and it may at once be granted that on the face of it they are not without very good grounds for this assumption. The canal is to be a great artificial waterway, and of course it is known by everybody that nothing con- duces more to the growth and prosperity of a commu- nity than an easy access to a river or other means of cheap water-carriage. This canal, we are told, is to be a great and commodious waterway for Warring- ton ; therefore what more obvious or justifiable con- clusion than that it will benefit Warrington in the same way that other waterways have benefited other towns? New industries will spring up and old industries will revive and be ex- tended ; population will increase and bring with it a consequent increase of business to tradesmen, and enhancement of the value of residen- tial property. In fact, we are promised that the construction of the canal is likely to make all the difference between a busy and prosperous town and a town in which trade, if not positively declining, is dull and stagnant. Now I am quite willing to admit that the canal will be quite sufficient to work even as great a change as is claimed by its most ardent advocate, but there are a couple of considerations which cannot but give one pause to ask whether after all Warrington will be the place which will reap these advantages. These considerations are in the first place that the canal will never come within the boundary of the borough ; and in the second place, that it will be out off from almost the whole of the town by a river the whole traffic over which is confined to one nen ow bridge, and still further by a railway, which is another formidable impediment in the way of traffic. In the face of these considerations we cannot but ask where will this increase of population which is likely to take place settle, and where will these additional manufactories and industries be established? Within the borough? After the canal is made a very small increase indeed can be accommodated at the Cheshire side of the river, and is it likely that the promoters of new industries will come to the north side of the river, and thus neutralise to a great extent the ad- vantage of the canal? Therefore if not within the borough where are the great benefits to Warrington to be derived from the canal? May it not be urged that if the increase of population and of manufac- tures which is to spring from the canal is located out- side the borough boundaries a positive harm will be done to the town? If this extraneous community assumes large proportions as it is more than possible it may do, is there not a danger that, as it were, the centre of gravity may shift from Market-gate to somewhere in the neighbourhood of Stockton Heath, or even of Walton? And again, it is quite conceiv- able that works which are at present on the north aide of the river may be removed to the south side, in order that the facilities offered by the canal may be more fully enjoyed. Such ideas as these may seem. somewhat fanciful, yet if we try to anticipate what will be the changes wrought by the canal, they are almost forced upon us. We may put it in this way: Population and industries are expected to spring up because of the superior facilities offered by the canal. Where will this increase of population and industry settle? Will it settle where the facilities offered by the canal are largely neutralised by the river and other impediments? or will it settle where full and unrestrained access can be had to the canal? Surely it may, without any hesitation, be concluded that it will settle where access to the canal is free and unrestrained, and that will, to a very large extent, be outside the boundaries within which the Corpora- tion of Warrington can levy rates and tolls. It may thus be seen, while 'admitting to the full the most sanguine expectations of the most zealous advocate of the Canal, that it may not be such an unmixed bless- ing to Warrington after all. More than that, it is far from impossible that it may be a positive draw- back. By raising up a new centre of industry on the very borders of the town it may diminish both its present population, and consequently that custom upon which tradesmen depend, and thus like a para- site feed upon the body which perhaps had a share in calling it into existence. No one who has considered the flux and shifting of population within the last fifty years, by which many ancient towns have be- come comparatfiely deserted and poverty stricken will contend that such changes as I have alluded to may not follow upon the carrying out of so gigantic an undertaking as the Ship Canal. It may be urged that it makes no difference whether this increase of business, this renewal of industrial activity which is anticipated from the canal takes place on the Lancashire side of the river or along the banks of the canal. All that is wanted is that it should take place. 8o far as the main body of the working classes and those who have no irremovable connection with Warrington, either as to propsrty or business, are concerned, it will probably make little difference. To them it will only mean a short removal, a trivial affair when made for the purpose of obtaining good employment. But what about the preperty owners and those whose whole pecuniary interests are vested in Warrington, and what, in a word, about that entity of brick and mortar we call Warrington P Will it not be in danger of degenerating, as so many other ancient towns have done, into the "Old Town, ' interesting, no doubt, because it is old and because of the traditions of the past, but showing all the signs of age and decay ' • while dose by will be the upstart offspring of modern enterprise, full of business and ac- tivity, and with a promising future before it. In making these observations I have, as will be seen, taken for granted the predictions of the promoters of the canal, not only as to the construction of the canal, but also as to the great changes in population and industry that are to spring from it. I have tried to forecast what will be the real effect of those changes, should they take place, with the result of finding that from a purely local standpoint they may by no means be so beneficial as may be expected. But, while wishing that the canal project may be carried to a practical issue, let us hope that it will not be quite so success- ful and fraught with so many changes as I have as- sumed it will be; and that, though ocean-going steamers may pass up to Manchester, those manu- facturers in Warrington who are dependent upon the railways, and will continue largely to be so depen- dent, will not find that they are so completely beaten in the market by competitors who take full advan- tage of the canal that they will also have to remove their works clone to its banks.

It is reported that whilst Mr. Gladstone will not under- take to do anything actively to further the interests of .Mr. Woodall's bill for the political enfranchisement of women, he will, in case of a division, not vote against it. THE MIGNONETTE SUBVIVORS.—In the Court of Queen's Bench, on Tuesday, Baron Huddleston, on the application of the Attorney-General, arranged that Exeter Assizes should be adjourned until December 4th, to give farther consideration of the special verdict in the Mignonette can- nibal ase.

THE COMPROMISE NEGOTIATIONS.—Lord Salisbury and Sir Stafford Nerthcote proceeded to the Premier's official residence on Wednesday afternoon for further conference with Mr. Gladstone, I,oord Hartington, and Sir Charles Duke on the redistribution scheme. A final agreement with regard to the redistribution scheme has not yet been arrived at, and a further conference will be held. On Thursday the negotiations were brought to a close. It is understood that several important points are left open for discussion in Par- liament, though the leaders of the Government and the Op- position are said to be in substantial accord as to the basis of the Redistribution Bill. The Boundary Commission is expected to begin its work early in the new year.

div.head: HAYDOCK.
div.p: HAYDOCK.

HAYDOCIC LOCAL BOARD.—The monthly meeting of the Haydock Local Board was to have been. held on Monday afternoon, but owing to the absence of a quorum of mem- bers the meeting could not be held. There were present Messrs. William Balharry and William Alker, along with the clerk (Mr. Thos. Turnbull), and it was decided to hold the meeting on the following Friday afternoon. PROPOSED NEW WESLEYAN METHODIST SCHOOLS; The Wesleyan Methodists ,Jf Haydock have been greatly caippled of late years in their Sunday school work by the want of more commodious and serviceable school premises. A meeting to consider the subject was held in the chapel on Thursday evening, which was preceded by an excellent tea served in the schoolroom. A eoodly number of persons partook of the good things provided, the tables being pre- sided over by Mrs. John Jackson, Mrs. Henry Twist, Miss Stockley, Miss Picton, Miss Fairhurst, Miss Johnson, Mrs. Hunt, and Mrs. Raxendale. At the meeting in the chapel, the chair was occupied by the Rev J. Shipbam (superinten- dent minister of the circuit), who was supported by the Rev. G. Smith (St. Helens), Rev. J. M. Fairbourne (Earles- town), Dr. McNicoll (St. Helens), Messrs. T. P. Hewitt (St. Helens), John Jackson, Jacob Billinge, Stockley, Taylor, ckc. The Chairman said they were met to discuss the ex- pediencv or necessity of increasing in one way or another their Sundae' school accommodatlon. There were only two ways in which it could be d ,ne, namely, either enlarge their present school or build a new one altogether. He thought he was quite safe in saying that the general feeling was in favour of a new school, which would mean an expenditure of £l,OOO at leaet.— Mr. Jacob Billing° (one of the Sunday school superintendents) stated that they had at present in the bank £lO5, and the promised subscriptions, which were to be paid within two I years, male a total of £225. It did not need any argu- ments from him to convince them of the necessity for better school accommodation. Five years ago they felt it, when they suffered from overcrowding in the schoolroom. As a superintendent, he would say that if they were to hold their own, and if Methodism in Haydock was to prosper, they must have better accommodation in their Sunday School, and unless they had it their church would go lower than than what it was at present.—ln reply to the Rev. J. M. Fairbourne, Mr. Stockley stated that the subscriptions were promised on condition that they went towards a new school. —The Chairman said he hoped the friends at Haydock who had promised subscriptions would not withdraw it their own individual wishes were not exactly carried out. Addresses were afterwards given by other gentlemen ; the meeting concluding with a vote of thanks to the chair- man.

SUPPOSED MURDEIt IN WESTMORLAND.—At Kirkby Stephen, in Westmorland, on Thursday morning, a young woman named Scott was discovered lying dead on thehearth in her house. There were indications of a straggle having taken place. Some months ago the deceased had some money left her by an uncle, a rich farmer. It is expected that the postmortem examination will throw same light on the mysterious affair.
