BLACKBERRY.—NO shopkeeper should be without W. P. Hartley's Blackberry with Apple Jelly. May be had whole- sale from E. H. Monks, 78, Sclaoles, Wigan. In 31bs., 21bs., and 11b. jars —Advt. THE VACANCY ON THE BOARD OF GUARDIANS. It will be seen from our report of the meeting of the Warring- ton Board of Guardians, held on Wednesday, that a long discussion took place with reference to the Newton vacancy on the Board, and that the Guardians reversed their former decision that no election should be held. ENTERTAINMENT. -- A public entertainment under the auspices of the Hope of Earlestown lodge of Good Tern- plats, was held in the lodgeroom, Bridge-street, on Satur- day evening when the chair was occupied by Brother John Taylor, W.C.T., and there was a good attendance. A pro- gramme of songs, recitations, and readings was gone through. _

GOOD TEMPLARS' MEETING. A meeting of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Templars was held in the lodgeroom, Bridge-street, on Monday evening. There was a large attendance, and Brother John Taylor, W.C.T., presided. The programme for the evening was headed "Night of harmony," and in accordance therewith a selec- tion of songs and melodies were sung by the members. THE CONSERVATIVE CLUB Drscussiorc—The adjour- ned meeting of the discussion class in connection with the Conservative Club, Earle-street, Earlestown, was held on Wednesday evening, when Mr. William Maudesley presi- ded. There was again a very good attendance. The sub- ject of the debate for the third time in succession was "Fair Trade versus Free Trade," and a lively debate took place. The general opinion seemed to be that it was very neces- sary a special commission should be appointed to inquire into the subject and report thereon. THE BILLIARD HAND/OAP AT THE CONSERVATIVE CLUB.—The final rounds of the billiard handicap among the members of the Conservative Club, Earle-street, Earles- town, have this week occasioned a keen interest. The principa; prize was value 30s, the second prize 15s, and two other prizes of 5s each. Forty-eight members entered their names as competitors' and having been duly handicapped, began the contest a fortnight ago. Since then handicap games have been played each night, the result being that at the commencement of the present week there were only twelve players left in the competition, to take part in the third round. The subsequent games have been played as under : T. Owen (25 start) beat T. Adams (25) by 12; C. Singleton (25) beat S. Leather (25) by 17; P. Bent (10 behind scratch) beat J. Howe (50 start) by 5; W. Maudesley (40) beat J. Wrigley (33) by 15; W. Moss (201 beat J. Williams (40) by 40; and J. Whalley (15) beat J. Gibson (50) by 22. lii the fourth round C. Singleton beat T. Owen by 11; P. Bent beat W. Maudesley by 36; and W. Moss beat J. Whalley. In the semi-final Bent beat Singleton by 17, while Moss had a walk over. In the final tie, which was played on Thursday evening, P. Bent (10 behind scratch) and W. Moss (20 start) were pitted against each other. Towards the close Moss bad all the best of the I play and won the first prize, amid considerable applause, by 27 points. Bent therefore got the second prize. T. Owen, W. Maudesley. and J. Whalley afterwards played oil for the remaining two prizes of 5s each. SAD DEATH OF A MARRIED WOMAN—The death of Mary Ann Shaw, 35 years of age, wife of Henry Shaw, a I labourer, employed at the Viaduct Works, and residing at 153, Regent-street, Earlestown, on Tuesday forenoon, was attended by circumstances of a peculiarly sad character. It seems that on the sth instant the deceased was confined of a daughter, and during her illness she was attended by several neighbours. Mrs. Shaw, however, did not satisfactorily progress towards recovery, and accordingly Dr. Handyside, of Earlestown, was called in. That gentleman duly attended and prescribed a certain treatment, but subsequent visits afterwards revealed the fact that the doctor's instruc- tions were not being. carried out, and he thereupon . .

informed the woman's husband that he could not again attend his wife under the circumstances. He then stopped visiting the house, but as the woman was evidently growing worse, he was again sent for a few days later. Dr. Handyside, however, carried out his intention not to visit the house again, and he declined to go. On the _

lowing day (Tuesday) the poor woman exp-ired before any further medical assistance had been secured. The circum- stances of the death were investigated by Mr. W. T. Hus- band. deputy coroner, who held an inquest on the body at the Oddfellosys' Arms, Lzgh-street. Earlestown, on Thurs- day afternoon. Evidence in accordance with the foregoing facts was given by Martha Sanders, Alice Houghton and Lilly Holman. It was added that on Mon- day last when Dr. Handyside refused to attend, Dr. Watkins of Newton, was sent for, but that gentleman could not attend until the following day, when the poor woman had expired. Dr. Handyside stated that he had attended the deceased, but on Thursday last week he found that his prescriptions were not being carried out, and he informed thorn he would give up visiting the house and they had better get another doctor.—The Deputy Coroner, in summing up, remarked that he could not see there was any blame attached to any one. They certainly could not blame the doctor, for he could always please himself whether he visited any particu- lar house. He was not compelled to accept anybody as a patient.—The jury returned a verdict of "Death from natural causes." NIEWTON CONGIIEGLTIONAL SCHOOLS: ENTERTAIN-

MENT.—In aid of the fund to clear off the debt on the new organ at the Congregational Church, Crow-lane, Newton, an entertainment of a very successful character was held in the school-room on Monday evening. There was a large attendance, and the chair was occupied by Mr. B. B. Glover. In opening the meeting the chairman said he would like to state their position with respect to the new organ. They would all know that Messrs. Thorold and Smith were the

contractors, and as far as the instrument was concerned it had given every satisfaction. It was erected at a cost of £754. It was a very easy matter to give an order for an organ and get the contract fulfilled, but they found the most difficult part was raising the money to pay the account with. The amount raised by the members of the congrega- tion was £609, church collections £23, Mr. Pyne's recital £l6, entertainment by the Band of Hope last year £5, from friends outside the congregation £lO, Mr. Darman's recital £7, making up to the present time £670 towards the item of £754, leaving a sum of £B4 to be raised. Towards the liquidation of this debt that entertainment was being held. Besides that, the committee had made arrangements for another recital next month and one in February ; and It was by those means they expected to meet the whole or a large portion of the debt. Miss Berry then commenced the entertainment with a a nice pianoforte solo, after which Mr. T. Merry recited "The Spanish Champion." Miss Glover (in the absence of Miss Owen) sang "Angels ever bright and fair," and in response to the appeal for a recall she hewed her acknow- ledgements. "Darby Doyle's Swim to Quebec," an amusing reading, was given by Mr. W. Gilbey, who was enthusias- tically applauded, The Scottish air, "''he Campbells are Coming," was executed as a pianoforte duet by Miss Berry and Miss Pope; after which Mr. T. Pilling sang a comic selection entitled "Could you lend my mother a sauce- pan?" and Miss Thomas gave a recitation "Mischief Makers." After a short interval, Mr. Hayes excellently gave "Blue Bells of Scotland" on the pianoforte, which was suc- ceeded by a song effectively rendered by Miss Glover. Mr. Horridge recited " Heaw to cure a brutal husband," and Mr. Gilbey sang " The Masher and the Monkey." Mr. &They's efforts elicited prolonged applause, and on being recalled he sang "The Grocer's Boy." This, too, was warmly ap- preciated, and then Mr. Gilbey again sang "The Spelling Bee." A pianoforte solo by Miss Berry was well executed, and Mr. T. Pilling was applauded for his song "The Wolf." A pianoforte solo, consisting of selections from Scottish melodies, by Mr. Reyes, was succeeded by a humourous sketch entitled "Wanted a Confidential Clerk," in which Messrs. R. Berridge, T. Merry, J. Bothwell, J. Merry, T. Fazackerley, and R. Owen took part. This brought the programme to a close, and the Chairman then thanked those present for their attendance, and those who so kindly gave their services in the entertainment.

div.head: MISSIONARY MEETING.
div.p: MISSIONARY MEETING.

On Thursday evening, the annual missionary meeting in connection with the Baptist Chapel, Earlestown, was held in the chapel. The chair was occupied by the Rev. Hugh Stowell Brown, of Liverpool,who was supported by the Rev. W. C. Tayler and Mr. Richards. of Liverpool. A hymn baying been sung and a prayer offered up, the Rev. W. C. Tayler said that no doubt the congregation were asking what had become of the other gentleman who was to come from Liverpool. As far as Mr. Jones was concerned, he wrote that there were so many names on the placard that the speakers would be tumbling over one another, and there- fore be thought it was far better that he should remain be- hind in Liverpool. There was not such a large attendance at that meeting as he (Mr. Tayler) had anticipated, but that of course was not the blame of those who were present, and it need not make that meeting less interesting. Mr. Brown, who as they knew was a host in himself, had promised to give them a sketch of the history of the Baptist Missionary Society. (Ap- plause.)—The Rev. H. S. Brown then gave an interesting address on the history of missionary work. Ile referred to the establishment in 1701 in connection with the Church of England, of the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel in Foreign Parts. That society, he said, was the eldest English institution for missionary purposes. It was for a long time subsidised by the State, and it was an attempt at carrying out the State Church principles and arrangements in other parts of the world. It was not, however, in the first instance what they would call a mission of a general character seeking the evangelisation of all men. At that time England had become a great planter of colonies, and this society was to furnish their own people and those con- nected with them with the means of grace and with the ordinances of religion. The society had now, however, gone far beyond the original and somewhat limited idea of mission work, and is active in very many parts of the world in its own way. The speaker having stated he believed that the Bap- tist Missionary Society, although not the oldest society, was the oldest which had for its object the conversion of the heathen, went on to give an interesting account of the origin of the society, and the work which it had accomplished in various parts of the world. In conclusion he expressed the hope that measures would be taken for the institution of a systematic auxiliary work in support of foreign missions in connection with the Earlestown chapel. Those in Liverpool were rather proud of that Earlestown chapel and of its con- gregation, and their satisfaction would be completed if they found that systematic missionary work was going on there. (Loud applause.)—Mr. Taylor said that that last hint ought to be deeply impressed upon their memories. They must see what they could do to complete the satisfaction of their Liverpool friends.—An earnest address in support of missionary work was next given by Mr. Richards, after which the meeting was brought to a close.

div.head: BIRMINGITAIII BISCUIT FACTORY
div.p: A BIRMINGITAIII BISCUIT FACTORY

[BY A 'mum] Hitherto the town of Birmingham has been so thoroughly identified with hardware and nothing else, that a Birming• ham biscuit comes upon us with a sense of novelty, a sort of paradoxical lucus a RCM lucendi, in fact. We go for akes to Banbury and Dundee, as naturally as we go to Richmond to eat Maids of Honour, Chelsea for buns, the Isle of Wight for dough nuts, and Gravesend for shrimps; all these places, and many others, have been associated with good things in the way of eating, from the time when the memory of man goeth not to the contrary. And now, thanks to the Warwickshire Company, Birmingham will ere lung be as famous for biscuits as it is for jewellery. Having been in Birmingham recently, I took the oppor- tunity of going over the factory and watching the process of biscuit makinv from beginning to end. Now there are biscuits and biscuits, varying from the old familiar Captain and Abernethy, to the soft toothsome delicacies, which have as many varied ingredients as a wed- ding-cake itself, whilst some varieties are "iced " in a similar manner. Between these extremes there are an in- definite variety of intermediates. The Warwickshire Com- pany manufacture over sixty kinds of stock biscuits, but of course their capacity for adding other special varieties is unlimited. The resources of the Biscuit Baker are un- limited and, like a poet, he is born not made, though he wants many years to mature that knowledge which can Only be obtained by experience, and besides the development of that intuitive knowledge which all great poets, chefs, and musicians possess. For instance, an expert knows the peculiarities of every variety of flour and its peculiar fitness or unfitness for particular kinds of cakes, biscuits, or pastry ; whilst the properties and qualities of the flour differ as much as do the countries where it was grown. Flour is, however, only one of the ingredients of the many biscuits which the Warwickshire Company manufacture, besides an infinite variety of other good things; eggs, with their orange yolks, waiting to be transformed by the whisking machine into a light homogeneous mass, fresh butter, lard of snowy whiteness, sugar ditto, currants, raisins, delicate flavouring essences, candied peel, syrups, and, in short, all sorts of nice I things.

Next comes the mixing department. The first thing that strikes a visitor here is the elaborate care taken to secure cleanliness and the success attained. Here the dough has its first exLstence, and the initial combination and partial kneading of its ingredients are managed by a form of ap- paratus termed a "mixer." This consists mainly of a large hopper of galvanised iron, which rises a short distance above the floor, and the bottom of which is closed at the floor- level by a hinged plate of iron, which opens downward into the room beneath. Whilst this plate is closed, the flour, water, milk, salt, sugar, spices, and the needful ingredieats requisite for the special kind of dough to be prepared, are placed in a big hopper, all having been first carefully weighed or measured in due proportions. In this receptacle the materials are partially mixed and incorporated, and when brought to a sufficient degree of amalgamation the iron trap-door falls, and the great mass of dough drops from the "mixer" on to an iron table in the floor below, whence it is removed en masse to the "break." This machine consists essential of a large iron receptacle containing several spindles, which are driven by steam, and whose shafts have a seiies of knife-edged arms projecting at right angles. Shut up in this prison, the dough is seized by the sharp protu- berances. whirle I round and round between the spindles, slashed into slices by the many knives, and recombined again and again by the whirling motion until, after it has undergone this ordeal for about twenty minute', the now homogeneous mass is turned out from this power- ful machine upon an iron slab to undergo the next operation. The succeeding apparatus consists principally of a pair of polished steel rollers, which can be set to different guages or widths apart, and have a smooth iron slab working between them, which, were it not forth. delicate cleanliness characterising every part, bears some slight resemblance to the " rolling machine " of the book- binder or copper-plate printer. Here the dough is rolled out into a perfectly smooth and level stratum, rattier thick at first as it rests on the slab. But the guage is set closer, the action of the rollers reversed, and the dough in its passage back is brought to a thinner sheet. Again and again the beautifully smooth surface passes backwards and forwards under the heavy cylinder, at each journey gaining in com- pactness and uniformity of texture. Then it is cat into sheets, which are consigned to a similar but more advanced machine. Here again the sheet of dough is passed and re- passed between glossy steel cylinders, whose guage is constante ly being decreased until at length the dough becomes a masS so concrete and uniform in texture, colour, and perfect dis- tribution of the different ingredients that no product of mere handiwork could equal it. The sheet of dough now looks something like a beautiful piece of cream-coloured felt, but with a surface far more level, and the illusion that it must almost be some textile fabric of the loom or felting- machine is increased by the facility with which it can be lapped together and doubled over. From this machine the sheets of paste are borne one by one by an endless cloth "feed " to the " docking " appara- tus, where they are passed over a metal cylinder, which presses the dough against an iron platten or box placed above the roller, and bearing the shapes or cutters which stamp out the biscuit from the sheet of paste. These steel patterns are specially cut, and cost in design, work, and tempering, a considerable sum each. These cutters are made in the form of big hollow punches, their sharpened edges being adapted to cut out the dough to the necessary form, while inside they are provided with arrapgements ac- cording to the biscuit to be made. Thus fer a " Brighton" a plain circular cutter only is required. For a " Captain's biscuit" a larger one, provided inside with sundry stiff wires, which " dock " or make the boles in it needed te allow the heat ti pass through when the biscuit is in the oven. Again, if the biscuit is to bear any inscription, or a zoologieal, alphabetical, or other Kindergarten pattern, metal type of less height than the edges of the cutter itself is arranged therein, Whatever the kind of biscuit upon which the machine is engaged, a number are stamped out together, the" scrap" or remnants of the sheet of dough from which they are punched is laid aside, and again welded up by the action of the heavy rollers. Very interesting is the process of baking. In the main it is automatic, and goes on, in consequence, with that clockwork regularity and aplomb to which manual effort is unequal. This application of machinery to the baker's oven is a recent feature of the biscuit manufacturer's att. The self-acting" breaking rollers" for preparing the paste, and the "dockers" for stamping out the biscuits, were in use, for instance, in the Government factories for making Navy biscuits, while yet each six-Sided cake of dough had to be thrown by hand on the baker's "peel," or flat shovel, as it lay at the mouth of the oven, and the thee of exposure to the heat was left to the discretion of the workman, who was simply guided by that result of long experience, yclept the "rule of thumb." Par parenthese, that act of throwing the unbaked ship's biscuits upon the peel at the rate of about sixty per minute during a working day, was a feat of manual dexterity and endurance remarkable to witness. Infinitely more surprising and interesting are the "chain ovens," in which the greater portion of the crisp products of modern biscuit makers are baked. Stand at one ex- tremity of the hot chamber, forty feet in length, and you see the employes bring a large tray of sheet iron, upon which are ranged in orderly rank and file a battalion of macaroons or a brigade of spice nuts, and set it down at the . entrance of the oven. No sooner is the fragrant freight thus deposited, than it begins a steady but inevitable march to its "baptism of fire," and is presently lost to view.

div.head: Let us walk to the other end of the chain oven. We shall
div.p: Let us walk to the other end of the chain oven. We shall

not have long to wait. With the same deliberate majesty with which our battalion marched to the ordeal they emerge • therefrom, not, indeed, bronzed veterans of the vieux 27101 a. lache order, but with a delicate brown tinting their chubby cheeks, which indicate they are in truth done to "a turn." The actual means by which the unbroken train of large trays, filled with biscuits of various descriptions, is moved at a uniform rate of progression through the oven is, an apparatus of chains, arranged longitudinally in the large heated chamber and passing over horizontal drums at each end, by which rotation a regular progressive movement through the oven is given to the chains and the trays of biscuits placed upon them. The heat of the ovens is under perfect control, and the temperature indicated by a pyro- meter. For some classes of goods, howerer—as Arrowroot biscuits, for example—the "plate oven" is used. In this the biscuits are placed upon iron plates, and exposed to an equable temperature for a certain period. The foregoing is a general description of the manner in which biscuits are made and baked; the details vary, of course, with eaoh of the 60 odd varieties which the firm make. The machinery used in the dough mixing is the most powerful and perfect that can be made. The strain is very heavy, and, in dough mixing, very erratic. All the stamps, Presses, dies, cutters, and rollers are manufactured and fixed .)3r Messrs J. and J. Vicars, of Liverpool, who are pre- eminent in that particular class of machinery. The normal tarn out of these machines is 108,000 biscuits per hour, and working almost 24 hours per diem, they are not equal to the requirements of the Company's customers, and extra machinery is about to be laid down. One cannot fail to be struck with the thorough cleanli- ness which is apparent in every part of the factory. In the course of my career I have bad to make many sanitary in- nections,and I can answer for the perfect manner in which the drains are trapped, the efficient ventilation of the ailcling, bakehouse and ovens; the lavatories, w c.'s, and ill necessary offices are away from the food portion of the ;actory, and all those drains are distinct from the main building. The servants, men, women, and children, are compelled to don a neat, clean, white uniform on entering the works, and these uniforms are provided by the firm, as well as the washing and other laundry work. It must not be forgottten that the secretary and manager of the company, to whom I was indebted for a carte blanche in visiting the works is Mr. Frank Richards, who has so far . developed the business that the company have had to extend their operations from the Midland Counties to London, au the fame and demand for their goods is already well-known throughout the United Kingdon. A FOOL AND HIS MONEY.—The Edinburgh police have arregted two men on a charge of defrauding an elderly man of upwards of £3O on the racecourse at Musselburgh. The prisoners first induced their victim to bet iupon cards, and when they had relieved him of all the money he had in his possession they lent him £5, which they immediately after- wards won from him. Then they persuaded him to go home and fetch £l3O which he had saved, telling him that they could secure him a large fortune. The simple-minded one followed their instructions, and was then allowed to win £3O, when, becoming elated, he entrusted the whole of the £l6O to the prisoners to put on the next race. The men disappeared, and the prosecutor has not recovered any of his money. GALLANT CONDUCT OF YOUNG WOMEN—At the Central Criminal Court, London, on Saturday, James Ivey, 61, was indicted for stealing two purses, containing £7 19s. in gold arid silver, the property of a gentleman named Bayn. The prosecutor was a journalist. On the 10th instant, Lord Mayor's day. he was in Cheapside. He had in his purse in one pocket £7 19s, and in ahother pocket an empty purse. Suddenly he discovered that be had been robbed of both' purses, and at the same moment the prisoner, who had been standing close to him, ran away. A cry of "Stop thief" was raised, and the prisoner was pursued. Two young women named Rhoda and Kate Morris, sisters, who belonged to the theatrical profession, were standing near Queen- street. As the prisoner ran by they courageously seized him by the arm, and, notwithstanding his struggles, they held him, and succeeded in tak7ng from each of bis hands a purse. The money was thus recovered, but one of the 'young women during the struggle was robbed of a locket and some other articles of jewellery. The Common Ser- jeant sentenced the prisoner to 15 months' hard labour, and, after observing upon the gallant conduct of the young women who had succeeded in arresting the prisoner, said that as one of them had sustained some loss, he should mark his sense of appreciation of their conduct by ordering the older sister, Kate, a reward of £2, and Rhoda £l. There was some applause in court at this announcement. CONVERSATIONAL ENGLISH.—What interesting and impor- tant informatios often passes as word currency, and converse upon topics in which no great differences of opinion are likely to arise. Precise rules cannot be established to trace the origi- nal causes cf a prevalent idea or the various reasons why we are content to sink our prejudices when approaching what, nolens miens, has become the vogue. Amongst the many we are content to take one illustration of the rapidity with which the public appreciate being well served. The Bradford Manu- facturing Company, having made a new departure, resolved to deal only with consumers direct, as previously the public generally had little option but to pay the regulation high prices, which it is reasonable to suppose must be put upon dress goods which pass through the hands of merchants and shopkeepers before reaching the final purchaser. The Company had a keen eye to the requirements of the public, and had evi- dently carefully weighed the matter and the soundness of the principle of direct trading. Few cared to interest them- selves in the matter when the first offers were made through ,the Press to the public, but those that did avail themselves were not slow to make their friends duly acquainted with the advantages of buying direct; and so, almost imperceptibly, the system has gained ground until thousands of ladies now pur- chase direct from the looms of the Bradford Manufacturing Company, at Bradford, Yorkshire. Sir,—A representbdion hying been made to some of the members of the Town Council to the effect that those vot- ing at the forthcoming meeting in favour of the proposed rate in aid of the promotion of the bill will render themselves personally liable for the amount subscribed, I may be permitted to say that lam legally advised, and have also the authority of the promo- ters for stating, that there is not a vestige of truth in the rumour. The assertion emanates from the opponents of the undertaking, and is merely intended to deter tile mem- bers from giving it their support.—Yours faithfully, J. L. TUNSTALL. 45, Sankey-street, Warrington, November 25th, 1334. THE MAYOR'S DINNER AND THE TOAST LIST. Sir,—lf your correspondent, "W. Males," had read my letter carefully, he would have seen that I nowhere " charged" or even suggested "partiality" "on the part of the Mayor in religions matters." Therefore his ostentatious championship of his Worship is unnecessary, and smacks very strongly of the spirit of "toadyism." Permit use to say to Alderman Harrison that his explana- tion in reference to the " invitations " entirely dissipates my suspicions upon that score, and I regret that, under al wrong impression, I came to corrclusiens which were not j warranted. I must, however, again assert that the omission of the "member's health" was unjustifiable, and the letter! of the Mayor in no way improves the situation. His Wor- j ship kecie be was doing a " risky " thing in attempting to! &conduct the after-dinner proceedings without a properly- considered and carefully-arranged programme, and therefore the responsibility fell all the greater upon his shoulders. I maintain most strongly that it was the honourable duty of the Mayor, and no other person, to see that the toast in question was duly submitted, and as that was not done no- body but his Worship is to blame. I am afraid my sus- picion is correct, viz., that the omission was no "oversight," but a pre-arranged affair, and done simply to save the tender feelings of Sir Gilbert Greenall.—Yours, Ac, A DISGUSTED LIBERAL.

RUNCORN PARISH CHURCH. Sir,—l leave my friend who signs himself "A Church- man " to draw his own conclusions with regard to my not answering his letter under three weeks. It was not so much the character of the sermons (which my friend alluded to in his letter, that called forth my observations in your issue of the 15th instant, but his becoming rather too personal. He says I complain of his being personal, and that I forget that preachers are open to criticism. Well, if the words " criticism" and " personality." spring from the same de- rivation, that perhaps accounts for his mentioning the minister's name, but I was always under the impression that people could criticise without becoming personal. My friend alleges he agrees with me that people should go to church to hear the word of God, to confess their sins, and to give thanks for the mercies vouchsafed to them; yet these are tae very things he appears to have neglected. If a person goes to church to "criticise," anybody with common sense can understand their not being able to glean anything in- telligible from the sermons. I wonder how my friend would feel, and whether he would render them more explicit if he were placed in the same position. He might give one as he thought suitable to his own taste, and yet meet with the disapprobation of his audience. My friend subsequently states that good sermons from our resident curates are a thing of the past. Assuming this to be correct, has it never struck him forcibly that due rever- ence to the Church and her ministers is fast becoming a thing of the past on the part of many Church-goers. The good old times are apparently beyond recovery, not with the clergy only but with the laity. Scepticism appears to have outstripped the bounds of faith,and disturbed the unanimity which should prevail. I thank my friend very much for the information con- tained in the last paragraph of his letter. He seems to be pretty well posted up with regard to the doings of Libera- tion Societies, but he has obviously overlooked the fact that he is doing his fair share towards disestablishing the Church by "sowing dissension," by "exposing ministers," and by drawing public attention through your columns to the "scanty congregations."—Thanking you for the space you have already afforded me, I remain, yours truly, November 251 h, 1884. STONJAHEG.

div.head: FAIR TRADE.
div.p: FAIR TRADE.

_ Sir,—lt seems to me that one of the most important duties that a Liberal politician can possibly render to his party is that of constantly keeping before the public the main facts that so largely conduce towards the happiness of the people at the present time. There cannot be a doubt in the minds of those who look around them that trade is bad, that never, at any time, was there so much capital depending upon trade prosperity for that remunerative interest so necessary to a brisk trade. On all sides manufacturers are complaining that they scarcely get change for a shilling with such orders as they may get. Mills are running short time; in some branches business is altogether stopped. Drowning men catch at straws. And with the knowledge that this is so, some of our would-be statesmen come boldly forward and urge that the only remedy for our agricultural and trade depression is what they are pleased to call Fair Trade. Lord Dun- raven in the House of Lords, and Mr. Mclver in the Com- mons, propose that we at once adopt some system that would be successful in protecting certain vested interests in this country. In 1869, Reciprocity was born, had a lively exis- tence for a year or two, and then faded away before a period of good trade. Towards 1879 the babe was again brought to the front, but it required a new name, one more taking with the public, a name that would make it acceptable to every man; therefore it was christened Fair Trade. Who could object to receive with open arms such an interesting bantling? No one with a shadow of patriotism in them, sty the various wet nurses of this abortion, can for a moment refuse to welcome Fair Trade. If you ask what it all means you are met with a long string of generalities. Some would tax imported grain, so that the farmers might be benefitted ; of course, not the landlords. Some would tax sugar, so that the various interests in that direction should be benefitted. Manufactured articles of all descriptions should most cer- tainly be taxed, and then we should immediately see all our mills running full time, wages would go up, and once more we should live in peace and plenty. Look at France, Re- publican France ; this poor misguided country, I should think, is following out to tbe full what our Tory Fair Traders wish us to do, and with what result? Our daily papers tell us of miserab'e bread riots, people starving be- cause selfish t!ass interests refuse to allow cheap flour to come within the reach of the people. The French are large manufacturers of sugar. To enable the beet root growers and the sugar manufacturers to prosper, the Government. in its wisdom, taxes the whole nation so that it may pay a subsidy to the sugar interest. It follows that sugar manu- facturers send their sugar over here for less than it costs them to make it, so that really with each pound of sugar an English working-man receives into his house a French work- man has been taxed so that he may have it cheap. The rime vicious want of principle runs through the whole of the Fair Trade programme. Could we nail these Neo- ProtectiOnists down to asy one trade or business it would be an easy matter to show how full of fallacies their scheme is.

Take the wire trade, with which we in Warrington are more familiar. No doubt an immense amount in weight and value is imported into England yearly. Could she get hold of the whole of this trade it would then be scarcely second to any other business—one firm alone, the Telegraph Con- struction Company, importing near £16,000 of wire per month from Germany. from tffe thickest down to the very smallest sizes; several London firms also importing thousands of pounds worth of wire per month; Warrington and Bir- mingham between them importing not less than 100 tons of small wire every week. Those acquainted with the trade may easily make the calculation how much more capital and how many more hands would be required, had we a monopoly of the trade. Well, suppose we were to place a tax upon all this wire, what would be the conseqwence? Fair Traders must not forget one thing, the tax would have to be prohibitive, that is, it would have to be sufficiently high to cover all cost here, and thus make it impossible for the Germans to sell wire in England. Would the cables be made on the Thames it we adopted the tariff system? Nc, the Construction Company would have to remove to Germany, where cheap wire could be obtained. All the thousand and one small trades in London consuming wire would suddenly die out, and the manufacturers would follow the cheap wire, Working-men may think that if we stopped wire from being imported the orders would come to our mills. This is a mis- take; we manufacture largely for exportation, and those having orders to give out send them to those who manufac- ture cheapest. The English manufacturer would be the dearest, consequently he would miss the orders. Take another instance ; a large amount of wire netting is done in England, chiefly out of German wire. If we stopped the wire from coming by means of Fair Trade notions, it wsuld end in driving wire weaving out of the country. Now, sir, having given these very conclusive reasons against prohibitive taxation, I may be excused for saying that lam sure working-men will make a great mistake if they give the least support to those political charlatans who advocate Fair Trade. Not a responsible statesman sup- ports the movement. Lord Salisbury has all the facts within his reach, and he is in a position to form a judgment upon them. To ask for an inquiry is nothing more than an at- tempt to make Political capital out of our depreued trade. The Conservative party are playing with Protecti,m as they have hitherto Played with Redistribution; they know well that the distress teas keen.in the United States, France, and Germany. Look at the silk weavers of Lyons; they are oillya.ckbwurhny, eiet worse off than our own of icclesfield. The cotton opera.. of Lowell are worse off thanant thoseian Inquiry. a Stockport. It is said all they w is only five years ago that a Royal Commission was ap. pointed to inquire into the state of agriculture. It sat for two years, and cost the country fliers than £4OOOO, and what is the result ? If we look to the Conservative organs we find quite a different tale. It is only a few months since representatives of all the leading Tory papers in the kingdom were invited to London to partake of hospitality of responsible Tory leaders. We may be quite sure that the party left no question likely to do them good undiscnssed, and we may see in this that responsible journals and repon- sible leaders are of opinion that Protection is dead and buried. The Saturday Review thinks the party may flirt a little with the question if it is likely to catch a vote or two, but on no account must it be given out that the Tories are prepared to adopt the views of such men as Lowther or Chaplin. Sir G. Sitwell, at Scarborough, is ccquetting with Fair Trade. Ile has the help of Earl Percy, and it is thus, the Review, speaks of Protection :—" That section of the Coneervatives, which proposes a return to Protection under

the name of Fair Trade threatens serious injury to the party. A seat may, indeed, be won here and there by advo- cacy of immediate relief to interests which are unfortunately depressed. It well becomes respectable Conservatives to consider whether they may not endanger vital interests by associating themselves with an untenable cause." If our Conservative friends are in earnest in wishing to bring about a better state of things, let them join the various movements now afoot to make the land what it should be, and what it must be before long, the producer of food for the people, and not as it is in too many cases, merely a means of self-gratification to rich men. America sends las bread. Soon India will compete with her, and we shall have cheaper bread still. Then at onca set about arrang- ing to grow beef if you can't grow corn. Do something that is real; instead of importing as we do eggs, butter, fowls, and a thousand other eatables, grow them. Even for a rabbit, a shilling and tourteenpence is now asked. Why, they could be put is the maket for eightpence a piece if the right parties cared to set about it. Working-men are not to be hoodwisked with this Fair Trade movement, but should the Tories manage to get in power, should they ever dare to resort to Protection, its ill effects would so soon show themselves that they could not fer a moment depend upon Protection to keep them in office. CLIFFORD DIX.

div.head: MR. PETTY'S CONCERT.
div.p: MR. PETTY'S CONCERT.

On Monday evening Mr. Charles Petty, of Liver- pool, gave a popular concert in the Public Hall which was not, we regret to say, so well attended as might have been expected considering the excellent repute Mr. Petty enjoys in connection with the enter- tainments given at Christmas along with what are known as the Old Men's Dinner and Aged Women's Tea Party. Unfortunately for him there were several events of a public character the same evening. The night was raw and cold, and had its effect alike on artistes and assembly until Mr. W. H. Jude, of Liverpool, stormed the place by a grand rendering of Russell's descriptive song "The Ship on Fire." He apologised for a slight he-Arseness which was per- ceptible ; but, the audience insisting cn a re-call, he charmed everybody by a finished rendering of "The old Arm Chair." His other contributions were a harmonium solo—" Fantasia on Irish and Scotch airs," in which he made the instrument do wonders in the way of exhibiting life and expression, after which he sang Moore's "Snowy-breasted Pearl ;" and, being again enthusiastically encored, he snd• denly "passed from grave to gay by singing "Jolly Uncle Jack" in a most rollicking style. Mr. Jude quite captivated his hearers, this being the first time he has sung in Warrington. He accom- panies himself; and it is amongst his chief merits as a vocalist that he lets his audience hear every word. Mr. Petty, as a singer of humorous songs, is neces- sarily careful in this respect, but as to the other vocalists they were in what is the fashion now-a•days in leaving listeners to make out as best they could the purport of their songs. Mr. Petty was deservedly encored in "Down went the Captain," and next sung "Sarah's Young Man." In the second part he gave "When George the Third was King" with striking effect, substitu- ting "Oh, my story's true" on being recalled. Madame Eborall made no special impression with VVelling's "Golden Love ;" but was heard to better advantage in the " Miserere Scene" from "11 Trovatore" which Mr. George Cropper sang with her in good style. She was well received, too, in "The Miller and the Maid;" and both she and Miss Richardson sang charmingly in the duet, "The Swallow." The latter first presented herself in "La Serenata," which was given with violoncello obligato by Mr. H. Bond, and subsequently she sang "When the tide comes in" with considerable taste and feel- ing. Miss L. Horton sang "The Children's Home," and "Tit for Tat." Securing a recall for the latter, she next gave "Somebody," which was prettily rendered. Mr. Cropper's songs were "To-day and To-morrow" a new and most expressive song com- posed by Mr. Bond, and "My own, my guiding star," by Macfarren. He has a really good voice , which is well under control; but from his lacking in clearness of enunciation the meaning of his songs is r obscured. Mr. Anthony Book sang Mr. Jude's fine song " Deep in the Mine" effectively, except as to : the low notes. He was more at home with "My Home is on the Sea," which was heartily applauded. ' Mr. A. Hollis acted as accompanist, and the concert was brought to a close with the National Anthem.

div.head: CADISHEAD.
div.p: CADISHEAD.

Roan ACCIDENT.—Oa Monday a lorry heavily laden with fustian cloth on its way to Manchester was upset between Cadishead and friam station owing to the darkness of the night and the density of the fog. The horse was seriously injured and the waggon damaged. fhe Cadishead Tonic Sol-fa class held its annual concert in the Wealeyan Day School, Cadishead. There was a very full attendance. The class upon the whole acquitted itself well under the leadership of its teacher, Mr. W, L. Brown. There were numerous encores. The programme included besides glees, part songs, and anthems ;---*olo and chorus, "German watchman's song," Mr. G. Ashton; solo and chorus," No tears in heaven," Miss M. Taylor ; solo and chorus, " The vintager's evening hymn," Miss M. Hesford, Miss Owen, Mr. W. Davenport, and Mr. Heaton. Several part songs, &c., were effectively rendered by friends from Regent-road Choral Society.

div.head: INTERESTING PRESENTATIONS.
div.p: INTERESTING PRESENTATIONS.

On Tuesday evening an interesting gathering took place at the Coach and Horses Inn, Cadishead, when two presen- tations were made to Mr. Giles Owen, a member of the Navigation Lodge (Cadishead) of the Independent Order of Oddfellows' Manchester Unity •, one, a handsomely framed painting of Mr. Owen, presented by his fellow-members, and the other an illuminated address, also handsomely mounted, presented by a number of the members of ths Warrington district. Amoagst those present at the meeting were Bros. P.P.G.M. Webster, P.P.G.M. Knowles, P.P.G.M. Perry, P.P.G.M. Taylor, P.P.G.M. Whitham, P.G. Brook, and P.G. Norbury (secretary of the Warriagton Presentation Com- mittee), all of Warrington ; P.G. Giles Owen, P.G. Holmes, Dr. Hill, P.G. Shaw, P.G. William Owen, and a large num- ber of the members of the local lodge. Bro. Holmes was elected to the chair, and Bro. Perry to the vice-chair.— Before proceeding with the business, the Chairman an- nounced that several letters from gentlemen who were unable to attend had been received, including one from Bro. J. Hampson (CS.), who expressed his entire concurrence with the object of the meeting.—Dr. Hill, in making he presentation of the portrait on behalf of the Cadishead mem- bers, said that it was meant as a small token of the respect and affection that was due to dlr. Giles Owen. (Hear, hear.) Making a presentation to him had long been contemplated, and when the one they were now met to make was first mooted it met with universal favour, for they were all anxious that some recognition of his valuable services ren- dered to the lodge for a great number of years should be accorded to Mr. Owen. He presented Mr. Owen with the portrait with the fervent wish that the recipient might be long spared to enjoy the esteem and confidence of all who knav him. (Cheers.)— Brother Shaw said that Brother Owen had been to that lodge what the mainspring was to a watch. He had set the machinery going, and had always been at hand ready to direct it when required. Mr. Owen was not only respected in Cadishead, but throughout the Warrington district.— Brother W. Owen believed that it had always been thedesire of the recipient of the present to promote the prosperity of the lodge, and conduce to the comfort and happiness of the members generally by his timely advice and sound example. (Hear, hear.)—The Nice-chairman endorsed with pleasure all that had been said of Mr. Owen, and called upon the past officers of the district present to fulfill their part in the proceedings.—Brother Knowles then rose to make the pre- sentation of the address. .When they heard of the action of the Navigation Lodge they were delighted and felt inclined to join in the work. (Hear, hear.)—Brother Norbury made known to them the action of the Cadishead members, a pre- sentation committee was formed, wherever the project was mentioned it was heartily joined in, and the outcome was the procuring of the address which they were about to pre- sent to Mr. Owen.—The address having been read by Brother Norbury, the presentation was made by Brother Knowles.—Brother Webster said that for the long period he had known Mr. Owen he had always bad great respect for him. Mr. Owen was only receiving a moiety of what he deserved, and they hoped that he would live for many years to do good by his example, which proved an incentive to do their duty to all who came in contact with him.—Brother Taylor wished to bear testimony to the love and esteem with which Mr. Owen was regarded by the members of the War- rington branch, and he felt it a pleasure and a privilege to do so. He looked upon Mr. Owen as one of the band of pioneers who, without any hope of the monetary reward that sweetens labour, had worked hard in their interests, and the result was, that their Order had attained a higher standard of excellence. Mr. Owen's example as a neighbour, brother and friend, was well worthy of imitation.—Brother Whit- ham also expressed his pleasure in participating in paying respect to one who bad always proved so faithful to his duty. Mr. Owen was well respected in Cadishead— (hear, hear)—indeed, he might almost be called the patriarch of the village—and he was looked up to by all as one to whom they could go for counsel in trouble or advice as to what coarse they should take in life. Having spoken of the ex- cellent work done by Mr. Owen and urged the members to work in the interests of the Order, Mr. Whitham remarked that it was his heartiest wish, along with the wishes of all the brethren in the room that Mr. Owen might live long and, as they said in the lodge, die a good odd-fellow. (asi- plause.)—The Vice-chaiiman made a few well-chosen re- marks, after which Brother Owen, who had been kept as long as possible in ignorance of the intentions of his friends, briefly returned his thanks.—The remainder of the evening was spent in a convivial manner, and the visitors were enter- tained to an excellent supper.—The portrait was painted by Mr. wiljis, 111anchester, and the address was executed by Mr. Brooks, Warrington, and framed by Brother Norbury. It was a somewhat lengthy one, and expressed the desire of the past officers and members of. the Warrington district to present to Brother Owen a token of their esteem. It also spoke of the good offices which Mr. Owen had performed, and expressed the trust that his good example would long be tollowed by the younger brethren.

div.head: EXAMINER, TURDAY, NOVEMBER 29, 1884. LATEST NEWS.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, TURDAY, NOVEMBER 29, 1884. LATEST NEWS.

LIBERAL MEETING AT WARRINGTON. SPEECH OF MR. W. CROSFIELD, J.P. A meeting of the Liberals of North-East Ward was held, in Brick-street school-room, on Monday evening, for the transaction of annual business and to hear an address by Mr. William Crosfield, J P., the Liberal candidate for the borough. Councillor Platt presided, and there were also Present Alderman Burgess, Councillors Barker, Broadbent, and Fleming, and Messrs. F Roberts, H.Whitham, Bates, W. Stirrup, W. Roberts, and H. Roberts (secretary of the War- rington Liberal Association). The Chairman having briefly spoken of the annual busi- ness to be transacted, and referred in feeling terms to the loss sustained by the death of the late Mr. Gilooley, the meeting proceeded to re-elect the Ward Committee. The list of names of the committee was read over, and the various gentlemen were re-appointed on the motion of the Chairman, seconded by Councillor Barker. It was resolved, on the motion of Mr. Stirrup, that Messrs. Platt, Armitage, and Barker be re-electel Ward chairmen for the ensuing year; and Messrs. William Wright, W. C. Baines, T. P. Winskill, and W. Furness were re-appointed Ward secre- taries on the motion of Mr. H. Whitham. Various gentle- men were also appointed to represent North-East Ward on the Executive and General Council of the Association. The routine business being concluded, the Chairman intro- duced Mr. W. CEOSFIELD, J.P., who was enthusistically cheered on rising to address the meeting. He said: Before proceed- ing to address you I should wish to add a few words to the feeling words which have already fallen from your chair- man, and add my testimony of respect to the memory of your old friend, and my valued friend—l feel at liberty to call him so—Mr. Gilooley. He was one of the few who came to see me in Liverpool before I made my appearance among you, and I felt that so long as he had strength to work we had in Mr. Gilooley a very warm and useful friend of the Liberal cause. (Hear, hear.) I regret with you that he has so soon gone from among us, but I hope the spirit that inspired him remains with very many who are left be- hind. (Cheers.) Shortly after forming Mr. Gilooley's acquaintance in Liverpool, I attended, as many of you know, a meeting of your General Council, whose business Mr. R3berts has just alluded to, being that of the selection of a Liberal candidate. I was honoured by that selection, and I felt that in that meeting I had the very great advan- tage of the Liberal organisation as it exists M Warrington. (Rear, hear.) On that occasion I said a few words express- ing my confidence in what is called the caucus organisation, and to-night as we are met—this is the first of your district meetings to elect the new organisation for the coming year and one which will certainly to me have vastly more importkoce even than the one whose duties expire to-night —I should like to say a few words about this organisation. The Liberal party has very largely adopted the system which has been laid before you to-night. That organisation has been very successful. The Liberal party has gained very much by the enthusiasm with which it was taken up, and therein I think very largely consists the animus which is shown against the organisation by those who have suf- fered from the increased energy of the Liberal party during the last four years. They have nick-named it the caucus. That implies, I believe, in its origin, something of the "hole and corner" character, but I confidently appeal to this meeting to say whether there is the slightest pretence or shadow of "hole and corner" business in the business which we have been transacting to-night. I understand that this neighbourhood has been informed by public advertise- ment that you were going to meet here to-night to appoint the chairmen, secretaries, on the general committee, and the various representatives who will transact the liberal business —the business of the Liberal party—in Warring- ton during the coming. twelve months. I am not yet. I hope to be bye-and-bye, sufficiently familiar with your faces, your names, and your characters to tell whether we are favoured to-night with the presence of any Conservatives. but, if there are Conserva- tives amongst us I venture to assert that if there were two Conservatives here, one of whom wished to elect his friend on the organisation in order to see how the machine worked —(laughter)—that he has had perfect liberty to have pro- posed his friend's name, and if that name was accepted by you. his friend could, as a matter of course, attend all the meetings of the organisation, and he would see what tricks we were up to, and could, if he chose, expose our doings to the public. But we are not afraid of this. We have no- thing to be ashamed of. (Cheers.) Our political duties may be performed in the face of day, and what we do is what we want others to do, and the more Conservatives who come in to help us the better pleased we shall be. (Cheers.) I have said that I have hitherto reaped the advantage of this organisation, for in being honoured by the choice of your General Council, I had the feeling that I was assured- ly supported by nine-tenths, at any rate, of the Liberals of this borough of Warrington, and in accenting the nomina- tion you were kind enough to offer me I felt that, though there was certainly the risk of opposition, it would be only the opposition of those who are diametecally opposed to us In politics, and that so far as any of the various phases of Liberalism are concerned I had the support and the sym- pathy of everyone of them. (Cheers.) There I have had the advantage. Now, there are other advantages connected with this organisation, and I would just mention one of them. The General Council of this Association concen- trates the Liberal feeling of this borough into a focus. (Rear, hear.) And when special events arise, as they fre- quently do, any sudden emergency when it is desirable for the body of the Liberal party to speak out in its various districts, it is an easy matter to call together the Two Hun- dred. and that Two Hundred speaks the voice of the en- tire Liberal party here ; and when I will not say irstruc- tion, but when advice needs to be given to your representa- tive in Parliament—that advice given to your representa- tive is a very powerful incentive—the Two Hundred being called together can very readily declare what their opinion is on the immediate crisis, and that of course goes to streng- then the vote of your representative in Parliament. He then not merely gives his single voice—for votes are weighed as well as counted—but carries with him the warm feeling, hot as it comes from the oven, of the party which he represents, which is of very much greater value than his own mere vote, derived by him at an election which has taken place perhaps some years before the time in which he brings his vote into question. These are the advantagee. The benefit to you in choosing your repressntative ; the benefit your representative secures in feeling that he may at any time appeal to you for your opinion upon any sub- ject upon which he wants guidance. (Cheers.) The ques- tion, no doubt, to which all your minds are turned to-night is the immediate political situation in which we find our- selves. (Cheers.) I have had a good deal of time, and I have taken a good deal of that time to endeavour to arrive at exactly where we are. Ido not know whether you have had as much time, or have devoted that time in the same way, but I can readily believe that a good maay of you are in something like the atmosphere we have outside, and are in a fog. (Cheers.) I can readily believe that some of you may be disappointed at the position in which we stand to-night. Well, in the first place, let me say that Ido not think we know very much about it. I think that the essence of what is called com- promise is that it is done in private—that in order to come to anything like a satisfactory conclusion it must be done absolutely in the secrecy of the half dozen who represent the two parties, and that until the thing is absolutely ac- complished it is not desirable that we should know it. We, no doubt, feel some disappointment that after all the skir- mishing which we in the country have been practicising during the last four months that we are not quite as far for- ward as we think we-have a right to be; disappointed, per- haps, that Mr. Gladstone has again shown us the one weak point of his character, the tendency which he has to give quarter to the enemy in the moment of victory. We should, no doubt, have liked that he should have pursued his vic- tory to the bitter end. (Cheers.) But we cannot, perhaps, wonder that Mr. Gladstone, arrived at the age he has, should feel some reluctance to go into a still bigger fight than that which he has passed with such an enormous call upon his mental and physical strength. The way in which he has worked during the last six months has been a marvel to men twenty years his junior, and we should be, perhaps, un- reasonable if we asked him to continue this strife for a pro- longed period, and it would undoubtedly be for a prolonged period if he carried out the fight to the end which von and I wish to see him accomplish before he dies. (Applause.) In England we move slawly. We have been very many years in reaching what we have now come to. I dare say Mr. Stirrup could tell me how long it is since he and his friends began to agitate for equal electoral districts. At any rate, it is so long since that Mr. Stirrup would have been astonished if he could even have contemplated that on Saturday last there was a united committee of the leaders of the Liberal and Conservative parties sitting in the head- quarters of the Government considering the question of equal electoral districts, and that I believe they were doing on Saturday afternoon. Though things come slowly they come surely. Ido not know that we are going to get equal electoral districts, but we are going to make a very long stride towards that end. (Applause.) It is somewhat dis- appointing to us who have been booted and spurred for the battle, and who have been standing by watching, thinking the victory would come immediately, to have the order given to unsaddle and go back to our quarters, hut we must be satisfied to take that °Her, and as loyal soldiers to stand by and wait until we are called upon to come up again and fight, and when that call comes we shall he ready. (Cheers.) Let us consider what the conference has brought about so far as we are informed of it. I believe that we have gained the Franchise Bill. (Cheers.) I believe that if things had gone as they were going a month age, that we shoeld have run a very severe risk of losing that bill, or, at any rate, of getting it pushed forward so far into next year that we should have lost a great deal of the advantage that it will give us. I believe that the result of the conference will be that before Christmas the Franchise Bill will be law, and I ask you to realise what that means. The House of Lords, the Conservative party, our opponents, may stand in the way, if they will, but to move them out of the way we shall have the two millions of the newly enfranchised electors of England. (Cheers.) Realise that one fact and ' then who imagines that they will stand in the way for , any length of time P Ido not believe they will, and that I think lathe one thing that we have gained. There are certainly, as far as we can tell, an abundance of " ifs " in the contract, and I think we shall not many of us be much surprised if the final question is not arrived at, but this is one thing that I have just spoken of, I believe we have gained the Franchise Bill. If the Franchise Bill had not been gained in this autumn session I believe we might have gone on into next year, and a very large part of the year would have been passed in talking about it. And it would not have been at all snlikely that the year 1886 would have to be employed in the Redistribution Bill, which we shall now. I believe, be able to consider when Parliament meets again. (Rear, bear.) 1 have spoken of the slowness with

which measures are carried. You will remember that dur- ing this year of 1884, although there was little or no radical change to be made in the Franchise Bill, it was one of the last days of June, when that Bill was finally carried through the House of Commons, although it had only undergone one very minute change. If there was such a serious opposition to such a bill, how much longer it would have taken to pass a bill like that, and bow easy it would have been for those who really had any object to serve to throw the thing out from one year to another, and indefinitely carry it on for a leng period. Now, by this conference the power to reject the Franchise Bill is certainly curbed. Next year we begin with a Redistribution Bill. We hear of big maps being carried into Downing-street, and we suppose that some of the details are already being considered by Lord Salisbury and Sir Stafford Nor:hcote on the one side and the three members of the Government who are connected with us on the other. And if the conference comes to a vote, the Liberal party will have secured the preponderating vote of the two We are told that an extension of the boundaries will have to be considered. That is not a business which can be carried through in a few days, and that involve:, the sending down of commissioners to each borough, sitting there and receiving evidence pro and con on all sides, and I knew from my Liverpool experience that the proposal to extend the boundary there often leads to a very serious and big fight. We tried to do it. The Corporation of Liverpool tried to do it some few years ago and they were beaten by the Local Board of an outlying district in the contest before the House of Commons, and this may very possibly be going on all over the country before various commissioners and will be a long business. Notwithstanding all this, I hope that before June of 1885 we shall see the Redistribution Bill well forward, so that others in the position of Mr. Roberts will understand exactly what work they will have to do, what their boundaries are, what voters they will have to put on the list, and that then those voters will be ready by June, 1886 to give good, strong, and sound Liberal votes to carry an increased number of Liberals into Parliament. (Prolonged applause.) Councillor BROADBENT proposed the first resolution "That we, the Liberals of North-East Ward, heartily aD- proving of the candidature of William Crosfield, Esq., J.P., pledge ourselves to use every possible lawful effort to secure his triumphant election at the next Parliao,entary contest." He said that they had welcomed Mr. Crosfield to Warring- ton before, and the more they saw of him the more they liked him. That night they gave him an especial welcome from the North-East Ward, and he ventured to think that when the time of election came no ward would give him more hearty support. Mr. Crosfield was a thorough-going Liberal, but he had also that judicious moderation which characterised a true statetman. With regard to the present state of political affair he thought that Mr. Gladstone knew what he was about, and that the result of the compromise would be that the country would get what he wanted it to get, and what the country wanted. (Applause.) Councillor BA.HKER seconded the resolution. Mr. Cros- field was, he said, a gentleman who had the well-being and welfare of the people at heart, and his business abilities and the fact that he was a good Radical at heart, were recom- mendations that he was the most likely person that they could have to represent them In the House of Commons. In sending Mr. Crosfield to Parliament they would send one who would to the best of his ability carry out those maxims and characteristics that were the watchwords of the Liberal party—peace, retrenchment, and reform. (Ap- plause.) Mr. J. BATES supported the resolution, and said that he considered Mr. Crosfield a• most suitable caldidate. He was sere all good Liberals would work heart and soul to aid Mr. Crosfield's return. Mr. WRIGHT and Councillor FLEMING spoke in effective terms on the recolution, which was unanimously carried. Mr. WM. STIRRUP proposed "That 'this meeting is of opinion that the House of Lords as at present constituted is a great obstruction to necessary and progressive legislation, and demands such a reform of the constitution of the Upper Chamber as will bring it into harmony with the spirit of the times." Mr. H. WHITHAM seconded the resolution, and in a refer- ence to local affairs condemned the proposal to appoint an assistant clerk to the Board of Guardians without the va- cancy, if such a vacancy existed, being placed before the public for competition. He seconded the resolution, but should have been better pleased if it had expressed a desire to end, and not to mend the House of Lords. The resolution was carried with applause, and the proceedings termivated with a vote of thanks to the chair- man.
Tne Mayor of Salisbury presided over a town's meeting on Wednesday, at which it was resolved to erect a memorial to the late Postmaster-General.
A man, named Wm. Moore, employed at Messrs Bolckow, Vaughan, and Co's., Middleshro', was on Tuesday instanta- neously killed by touching electric lightning wires.

A violent snowstorm occarred in North Staffordshire and .East Cheshire yesterday morning. Several violent shocks of earthquake were felt at Geneva shortly after 11 o'clock on Thursday night. The death is announced from Vienna of Fanny Elsaler, who a generation ago delighted London theatre-goers by her dancinr:. She was born in 1810.

The colliers who have resumed work at Barrow collieries, Barnsley, were attacked last evening by a large mob, and some of them were rather seriously injured. At Cardiff, on Friday morning, Mrs. Thomas, daughter of Alderman Bevan, colliery proprietor, Neatb, was burnt to death in her bedroom. The cause of the fire is unknown. It is now stated that the Redistribution Bill will be in- troduced in the House of Commons on Monday, and Mr. Gladstone will ask the House to take the second reading on Thursday next. The Central News is authorised to state that a meeting of the members of the Conservative party in both Houses of Parliament will be held at the Carlton Club at noon on Tuesday next.

On Friday, in Dublin, a special meeting ef the united Synods of Dublin, Glendalough, and Kildare was held for the purpose of receiving the resignation of his Grace the Archbishop of Dublin (Dr. Trench). The inquest on the body of Miss Keyse was resumed at St. Mary's Church, Babbicombe, on Friday. There was a large crowd al,out the precincts of the ball, but Lee, the accused, was not brought up, the trial being again ad- journed. THEFT OF AMINIINITION.—Sergeant-Malor Hefferman, 3rd Durham Rifle Volunteers, was remanded at Sunderland, on Friday, on a charge of stealing a large quantity of am- munition from the volunteer armoury. It was stated 13,000 rounds of cartridges are missing. THE FIRE ON AN ALLAN STEAMER—The fire which broke out on board the Allan Line steamer Caspian, on a voyage from Quebec, on Monday, was effectually subdued on Fri- day morning at Liverpool. It was confined to the compart- ment where it originated—among some cotton. The Marquis of Lorna contributes to The Nineteenth an- fury an article on the Highland land agitation. His lord- ship is of opinion that the principal suggestions of the Royal Commission are impracticable, and that the chief grievances of the crofters are the result of unwise subdivision of the land.
COUNTY DOWN ELECTION.—The counting of the votes -

cast in the contest for Coanty Down was commenced at Dow-ipatrick, on Thursday morning. The result of the poll was declared on Friday noon as follows :—Ker (Con- servative), 4,357; Crawford (Liberal), 3,9P8; Conservative majwity, 389. The seat was previously held by a Conser- vative.

div.head: COLLISION AT SEA.-GREAT LOSS OF LIFE.
div.p: COLLISION AT SEA.-GREAT LOSS OF LIFE.

The screw steamer Durango, belonging to Newport. Mon- mouthshire, foundered on Thursday morning, after being in collision with the barque Lake Bruce, of Liverpool. The whole of her crew of twenty men, together with the cap- tain's wife and child, and the chief engineer's wife being drowned. The Durango left Dunkirk for Genoa on Wednes- day with a cargo of rails, and was to have called at Dart- mouth for coals. A later telegram from Dunkirk states that Jackson, the second mate, was injured in the collision, but managed to climb aboard the Lake Bruce. He died, however, shortly after arriving in Dunkirk. THE WIGAN FRAUDS: THE SENTENCES.

At the Liverpool Assizes, on Friday, Mr. Justice Day passed sentence on William Holt (64), book-keeper, for stealing £700„ the moneys of the Wigan Corporation in October, 1878; on John Caldwell (46), stockbroker, for receiving the money knowing it to have been stolen; and on John Reynolds (53), clerk, of conspiring with the other prisoners to defraud the Wigan Corporation. Holt was sen- tenced to 18 months' imprisonment with hard labour; Caldwell to seven years' penal servitude ; and Reynolds to 12 months' hard labour. Sentence on Holt and Caldwell for conspiracy to defraud was not passed by his Lordship. A MANSION IN IRELAND BLOWN UP WITH DYNAMITE.

A portion of Edinburgh House, the residence of Mr. Samuel M. Hussey, at Tralee, has been blown up with dynamite, the windows and part of the wall at the east eml being destroyed. All the family were at home at the time of the outrage, as well as a protecting force of police, but no one was injured. No arrests have yet been made. Two protection huts are placed near the dwelling. During the land agitation Mr. Hussey's life was threatened. A green- house fifty yards off was completely wrecked. The damage is estimated at £3,000.

div.head: RUNCORN VOLUNTEER CONCERT.
div.p: RUNCORN VOLUNTEER CONCERT.

DISTRIBUTION OF PRIZES. Tne annual concert and distribution of prizes in connec- tion with the F' and G companies of the 2nd Cheshire Rifle Volunteers took place on Thursday evening in the Runcorn Public Hall. Considering the boisterous state of the weather, there was a large audience. The concert opened with a performance by the band, who played with their usual ability under the the leadership of Mr. Ainsworth. Captain Jolnfra sang Watson's song "Anchored," and then Miss Wolstenholme, who possesses a sweet and highly-trained voice, received a well merited encore for her interpretation of " The Merchant of 'Cheapside." Later on she sang in a charming manner the old favourite, "Robin Adair." Miss Jessie Breakenridge gave Behrend's "Daddy" with much pathos and power, and she was heartily recalled. She also sang the ballad "The Bailiffs Daughter" with equal suc- cess. Miss Hankinson has established her reputVion in Runcorn as a skilful instrumentalist, and her brilliant per- fornaance of two pianoforte solos, gained her the enthusias- tic plaudits of the audience. She was once recalled. Mr. Roderick Raynor. junior, played the solos " R6verie " and "A Summer's Evening" on the violincello in excellent and enjoyable style. Captain Hazlehuret sang with grelt power and expression Molloy' s song, "The Postillion." and he was enthusiastically encored. Pinsuiis " Outpost" was given by Lieutenant Joule, who was rcarcely up to his usual form, and Sullivan's beutiful song "Once Again " was sung in a highly pleasing manner by Lieutenant Timmins. Mr. R. W. Pierpoint ob- tained a deserved encore for his tkilful perform- ance of the cornet solo "Hurricane Polka." The humourons element in the concert was supplied by Mr. Josef 'Cantor, who rendered several buffo songs in his usual. vivacious style, and he was again and again encored. The - concert concluded with the Hallelujah Chorus by the band. During an interval in the programme Mrs. John Ashton presented the prizes tra those who had been successful in the annual shooting competitions, &c. The chair was taken by the Rev. W. presto's, the officers on the platform being -The Rev. Jno. Lockwood, acting chaplain ; Lieut.-Col. Ashton, Captain Hazlehurst, Captain Jolliffe, Captlin Fluitt (Chester), Major Skidmore (Hartford), Captain Kerr, adjutant (Chester) ; Lieutenants Timmins, Joule, and Rhodes.-In a short addresi, the Chairman mentioned that he was educated for the army, and a commission was pro- mised to him by the Duke of Cambridge, but his tastes changed, and he could not say he regretted it. He referred to the rise and progress of the volunteer movement, and, speaking of the Runcorn force, said on the 9th December it would be 25 years old. It muster at first was 60 members; in 1872 it had but 34 in all ranks ; but now it had 180, of which' 170 were efficienrs, and secured the corps the grant of 30s. per man per annum. They had bes,des nine gallant officers and ten sergeants who, having obtained certificates of proficiency, secured the corps 50s per man. (Applause.) During the year 43 recruits had joined. Mr. Ashton then distributed the prizes, a complete list of which is appended. The bandsmen had prepared a surprise for their worthy conductor, Mr. James Ainsworth, in the shape of a handsome silver-mounted ebony baton, which Captain Hazlehurst at their request ' presente I to him on their behalf, as a token of their cordial appreciation of his untiring energy and ze.3l on behalf of the bend. It was also presentel as a token of their grati- tude for the many services he had willingly performed, not only for the band, but for the cause of music generally. (Applause.)-Mr. Ainsworth briefly expresse 1 his thanks. -A cordial vote of thanks was accorded to Mrs. Ashton, on the proposition of Captain Hazlehurst, seconded by the Rev. J. Lockwood, and Lieut.-Colonel Ashton suitably replied.- A vote of thanks was also passed to the chairman.
