WARRINGTON. MISCELLANEOUS CONCERT AT ORFORD.—Last evening week a miscellaneous concert was given by the members of the Orford Church choir, in aid of the funds of the cricket club connected with Orford school. The concert took place in the school-room, and was well attended, the proceeds amounting to about £5. A vote of thanks was accorded to the vocalists at the close.

WESLEYAN FOREIGN MISSIONS.—On Sunday two sermons were preached at the Penketh Wesleyan Chapel, morning and evening, by the Rev. J. Howell Jones; in the morning from let Corinthians, 3rd chap. 22nd and 23rd verses; and at night from the 99th Psalm, Bth verse. There was a good congregation at each service, and collections were made morning and evening in aid of the Wesleyan Foreign Missions.

COCKHEDGE MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.—An enter- I tainment in connection with the above society took place on Monday evening before a large audience. The programme, which was a very fair one, consisted of songs, duets, read- ings, recitations, and a comic dialogue entitled, Weetin its yed or th' Post Choilt," which provoked loud laughter and applause. The Rev. W. R. Parry occupied the chair. The meeting was brought to a close by singing the Doxology. SUDDEN DEATH.—On Tuesday evening a mars named William Burton (62), a carter, residing at 27, Pierpoint- street, died suddenly under the following circumstances. Deceased, who had been suffering for about four years with bronchitis, was left in his house by a man named John Worthing, and on the return of the latter about an hour afterwards he found the dead body of Burton lying upon the floor. F has not been thought necessary to hold an inquest.

VIOLENT ASSAULT ON A POLICEMAN.—At the Warring- ton Borough Police Court, on Monday, a youth named Jas. Clare (22) was sentenced to six months' hard labour for committing a violent assault on P.C. Baxendale, of the borough police, on Saturday night. Prisoner, with six or seven other young fellows, was loitering in Bridge-street, and the constable had occasion to speak to him. Prisoner then became violent, and knocked Baxendale's helmet off. On taking him into custody Baxendale was mercilessly kicked by prisoner and his companions, and was so much injured that he had to be carried home. In passing sen- tence, the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) said that kicking was becoming almost as violent in Warrington as it was in Wigan and some ether places, and they were determined to relieve the town of the odium of such ungovernable people, and to deal with such cases in a very exemplary manner. BURNT TO DEATH WHILE Dianteg.—On Tuesday Mr. T. Husband, deputy-coroner, held an inquest at the White Hart Inn, Sankey-street, touching the death of John Law- less, a file-cutter, aged thirty years. who resided at Silver- street and who died at the Infirmary on Sunday, having been admitted to that institution on the 16th instant suffer- ing from severe burns. On the night of Saturday, the 15th instant, the deceased went home the worse for drink, and took a seat on a chair placed near to the fire. His wife left him there and went to bed, and subsequently cries were heard proceeding from the house. Edwin Grounds and Ann Mahone, who live in the same street, burst open the door and found the deceased almost enveloped in flames, his clothes being on fire. The flames were at once extinguished, but not before his hands, back, and legs had been severely burned. He was taken to the Infirmary, where his injuries were attended to. No evidence was forthcoming to indicate how the poor fellow's clothes caught fire, and the jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death." Gorski To BE A SOLDIER.—EarIy on Sunday morning a youth who gave his name as William Connor, the son of a Wigan collier, and his age as 16 years, was observed near the cemetery by a constable under circumstances that led to his detention at the police station. He was attired in a shirt, a pair of trousers, and military boots, and on being questioned he gave the constable to understand that he was a soldier, and, in consequence of what he said, he was charged at the Borough Court, on Monday morning, with being a deserter from H.M. South Staffordshire Regiment, stationed at Salford. He informed the magistrates that he left home with the intention of becoming a soldier, but that on trying to enlist he was not accepted. Soon afterwards he met a soldier, who offered to let him (prisoner) try on his regimentals "to see how he looked." Prisoner took his coat and vest off, and, the soldier securing them, to use the words of the prisoner, said "It was all rest, and took his hook." The magistrates inclined to the belief that the boy had been duped, and not only dismissed him but decided to pay his fare back to Wigan. REARING SUPPER.—We understand that the workmen who have been engaged in the erection of the new Conserva- tive Club were entertained to supper in the Assembly-room OR Saturday evening by the builder (Mr. William Porter) and the directors. Captain Reynolds occupied the chair, and various toasts were proposed and responded to.—ln pro- posing the health of the borough member, Captain Reynolds said it would not be right if they met on an oc- casion like the present and neglected to propose the health of the geatleman who was the member for Warrington, Mr. McMinnies. (Hear, hear.) Although there was no man in Warrington more opposed to him in politics, still he thought they ought to show respect to the one returned as the mem- ber for the borough, because he had been elected by the majority of the people. He considered that Mr. McMinnies was a most :genial gentleman, and as a friend he did not know anyone he estimated more. (Hear, hear.) Mr. McNiinnies had found it necessary to retire soon from Par- liament. but he hoped that a long life of happiness and use- fulness would still be left to him. (Applause.) THEFT BY A SOLDIER.—John McGann, a private in the 82nd Regiment, stationed at Orford, was charged at the Borough Court, on Monday, with stealing a clock and a chemise, value 55.. from the dwelling-house of Mary Ford, Rose-yard. On Saturday evening both parties were in the Rose Inn and some unimportant conversation ensued between them, after which the prisoner left the house. On going to her home a short time afterwards the prosecutrix discovered that the articles in question had been stolen, and gave information to the police. " The pawnbrokers in the town were apprised of the robbery, and prisoner, who was in uniform, was given into custody on going to the shop of Mr. Greaves, in Church-street, and endeavouring to pawn a clock and chemise. The articles were identified by Mrs Ford as being her property. In defence the prisoner, who was stated to have been of previous good character, said that he was intimate with the prosecutrix, and she °fared to lend him the articles in question to pledge on condition that he should redeetn them. This, however, was denied, and the Bench fined McGann 20s and costs, or one month's hard labour. CONCERT.—On Tuesday evening an excellent concert was given in the Sunday school of the Bank Quay Working- men's Mission, in aid of the school fund. There was a fair attendance, the chair being occupied by Mr. F. Monks, jun. The first part of the programme consisted of a pianoforte duet by Misses Sykes; a song, "Charity," by Miss Woods; a comic song, "The world turned upside down," by Mr. Meteor; song, " Jessie's dream," by Miss Mills; song, "Gipsy Jane," Miss F. Sykes; comic song, Mr. Mercer ; song, "The wolf," Mr. N. Cook. Several of these pieces were very successfully rendered. Mr. Mercer was the first to be encored for his comic song, in which there were several amusing local allusions. Miss F. Sykes won a warm recall by her pretty rendering of a pretty song ;and Mr. Cook was alao deservedly encored. The second part of the pro- gramme consisted of a pianoforte duet by Misses Sykes; song, "Beautiful dreamer," Miss Wood; song, "Down in the deep," Mr. Cook, duet, "All's well," Messrs. Cook and Littlewood ; song, "Pilgrim of love," Mr. Littlewood; comic song, "Tidings of comfort and joy," Mr. Mercer; song, "Death of Nelson," Mr. C. Littlewood; comic song, "Very unpleasant." Mr. Joseph Mercer. This part of the pro- gramme was also commendably gone through, Messrs. Cook and Littlewood, as well as Mr. Mercer, being recalled. The evening's proceedings were brought to a close by a vote of thanks to the chairman and those who had contributed songs, , propcsed by Mr. Dale, seconded by Mr. Long, and supported by Mr. W. Ford. WARRINGTON CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY LECTURE. —On Monday evening the Rev. J. Freeston, of Stalybridge, gave a lecture in the Co-operative Hall. Sankey-street, under the auspices of the Warrington Equitable Industrial Co-opera- tive Society, entitled "Eclipses of the sun and moon." There was a good attendance. The chair was occupied by the Bev. R. Filcher, 8.A., who, prior to introducing the lecturer' said that he could not help thinking what a stride the world had made since the time when the Chinese used to beat tom-toms when an eclipse took place in order to frighten away the great dragon who, they said, was eating up the moon. Now thousands of people watched it in this and other countries with delight.—The Lecturer explained, in easily understood terms, partial and total eclipses of the moon, and spoke in an interesting manner on the subject of tides. It seemed, he said, simple enough that in that particular part of the globe over which the influence of the moon extended the waters should be drawn together; but how was it that on the opposite side of the earth the same phenomenon was to be seen at the same time? That was explained by asserting that while the waters on that side ef the globe under the immediate influence of the sun or moon were attracted from the earth, and the gathering up of the waters on the other side was caused by the same body attracting the earth from the waters, but with that theory he was not himself perfectly satisfied. He conc'uded by reminding his hearers of the confidence and veneration which should be inspired in the Creator by an examination of the beautiful in Nature. The lecture was listened to with great attention, and a vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Free- ston at the close, on the motion of Mr. Birchen, seconded by Mr. Jeffries. A similar compliment was paid to the char- man.

The scarcity of water at Rotherham is such that the Cor- poration have limited the supply to one hour per day. The results announced on Wednesday of the municipal elections throughout Ireland show that the Nationalists have gained a number of seats.

THE Anon RIOTS.—At the Birmingham Police Court, on Wednesday, the hearing of the summonses arising out of the recent Aston disturbance was resumed before the Sti- pendiary. The Conservative party summoned Larry Macke Edward Reed, and Charles Smith for libels, which were alleged to be contained in certain declarations made by then, and quoted in the House of Commons by Mr. Chamberlain. Mr. Jarvis was summoned by the Liberals for misdemeanour in regard to declarations which he had made. Exceptional interest was manifested in the proceedings in consequence of Mr. Chamberlain being subpcened as a witness. In reply to questions put by counsel, Mr. Chamberlain spoke to bay- ing received what purported to be the affidavit of Reed, which came either from Mr. Allard, secretary of the Liberal Association, or Messrs. Horton & Redfern, solicitors. Alto- gether he received about a dozen affidavits, bit did not take notice from what particular individual they emanated. The letters that accompanied them were destroyed. He ad- mitted that he had sought from Mr. Schnadhorst informa- tion respecting the riot, but indignantly repudiated the sug- gestion that he incited the procuring of the affidavits. The cross-examination of Mr. Jarvis was resumed, and the case was ultimately adjourned. The whole of Thursday was occupied with the examination of Mr. Jarvis, the Conserva- tive complainant, who WAS in the witness box when the court adjourned.

IN PARLIAMENT, SESSION 1888. RUNCORN GAS. (Additional Capital, Application of Funds, Consolidation of Capital. Additional Lands, Construction of New and Maintenance of 011 Works, Manufacture and Storage of Gas and Residuals on old and new sites, Limits of Sup- ply, Sale of Lands, Breaking up of Streets. Supply of Gas Meters, Stoves, B:c., Price of Gas and Dividends, Sliding Scale. Purity, Quality, and Pressure of Gas, Public Lighting. New Provisions respecting Regulation of Company, Rates, Rents, and Charges, Patent Rights. Incorporation and Amendment of Acts.) NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that application is in- tended to be made to Parliament in the ensuing year. by the Runcorn Gag Company (hereinafter called "the Com- pany"), for leave to bring in a Bill (hereinafter called "the Bill ") for all or some of the following amongst other pur- poses, that is to say, To authorize the Company to raise, for the purposes of the Bill and the general purposes of their undertaking, additional capital by the creation and issue of new ordinary and prefer- ence shares and stock, arad by borrowing and by the creation and issue of debenture stock, or by any of such methods, and to attach to any such shares, stocks, or loans any pre- ference or priority of dividend or interest, and to apply to the purposes aforesaid any capital, funds, or money now belonging to or authorized to be raised or borrowed by the Company, and to consolidate and arrange the shares and stocks of the Company. To authorize the Company to purchase, lease, or otherwise acquire by agreement, and to hold and use for the purposes of their undertaking, and in addition to the lands which they are empowered to purchase and hold by the Runcorn Gas Act. 1847 (hereinafter called "the Act of 1847 "), the following lands (that is to say) : First. A piece of land, containing 4 acres 19 perches or there- abouts, known as Culvert Meadow, situate in the township of Runcorn, in the parish of Runcorn. in the County of Chester, and lying on the south side of and adjoining the Bridgewater Canal, and bounded on the north or north west side thereof by the said canal and property belonging, or reputed to belong, to the Bridgewater Navigation Company, Limited on the west side thereof by property belonging, or reputed to beloog, to the trustees of the Duke of Bridgewater; on the south side thereof by the public highway known as the Halton-road. leading from Runcorn to Warrington ; and on the east side thereof by land belonging, or reputed to belong, to the execu- tors of the late William Henry uckleston. Secondly. A piece of land containing 2 rrods and 12 perches or thereabouts, with the building thereon, known as Highfield House. situate in the said township of Runcorn. and parish of Runcorn, and county of Chester, and lying on the north side of the said Bridgewater Canal; and bounded on the south side thereof by the road adjoining the towing path of the said canal, and leading from Canal-street, Runcorn, to Bates Bridge, Halton ; on the west side thereof by land belonging, or reputed to belong, to the trustees of the Duke of Bridge- water and on the north and east sides thereof by land belong- ing, or reputed to belong, to the trustees of Mrs. Eliza Ann Kirkham. And to authorize the Company on those lands, or part or parts thereof, to erect, construct, make, and maintain and on the lands hereinafter described as the site of the Company's existing gas works, to maintain and continue, and as regards all such lands from time to time extend, enlarge, and improve gas works, and works for the manufacture, distribu- tion, storage, and supply of gas, and for the manufacture, con- version, utilization, storage and distribution of materials used in and about the manufacture of gas and of residual products resulting from such manufacture, and to empower the Com. pany on and from all such lands to manufacture, store, and supply gas, and to manufacture, convert, utilize, distribute, and store such materials and residual products as aforesaid, and to extend and make applicable to, and to enable the Com- pany to exercise, in respect of the before-mentioned lands, and of the supply of gas therefrom all or some of the provi- sions of the Act of 1847 as altered, amended, or enlarged by the Bill. The site of the Company's existing Gas Works consists of the pieces of land hereinafter described, that is to say : Flrst.—A piece of land containing 1,7115 square yards or there- abouts, situate in the said township and parish of Runcorn, in the county of Chester, on the east side of Gas-street, and bounded on the westerly side thereof by that street, on the southerly, or south-easterly side thereof by the towing path of the Bridgewater Canal, on the easterly side thereof by a street known as Stone-street, and on the northerly side thereof by land belonging, or reputed to belong, to the Marquis of Chol- mondeley Secondly.—A piece of land containing 2.609 square yards, or thereabouts, situate in the said township and parish of Run- corn, on the west side of Gas-street, and bounded on the north side thereof by land belonging, or reputed to belong, to the said Marquis of Cholmondeley, on the east side thereof by Gas-street, on the south side thereof by land belonging, or reputed to belong, to the Runoorn Smelting Company, and on the west side thereof in part by Sutherland-street, and on the remaining parts by land belonging, or reputed to belong, to the Trustees of the United Methodist Free Church, and by land belonging, or reputed to belong, to the Trustees of the Duke of Bridgewater respectively. To amend or repeal section 7 of the Act of 1847, and to alter and define the limits within which the Company may supply gas, such limits to include the town of Runcorn, otherwise called Higher and Lower Runcorn, the township of Runcorn, and the townships or hamlets of Halton, Astmore, otherwise A.stmore-with-Halton, Norton, Weston, Weston Point, and Clifton, otherwise Clifton-with Racksavage, in the County of Chester, or such of them, or such parts thereof as may be speci- fied in the Bill. To empower the Company, from time to time, to sell, ex- change, let on lease, or otherwise 1,0 dispose of any lands at the time belonging to them, which they may not require for the purposes of their undertaking. To give power to the Company within their limits of supply to lay down, maintain, use, alter, and renew mains, pipes, ar d other conveniences for the distribution, supply. and disposal of gas and residual products, and to open, break up, and inter- fere with streets, roads, highways, bridges, railways, canals, sewers, drains, and other passages and places, and gas and water, telegraphic, telephonic, and other pipes, wires, and apparatus. To authorize the Company to manufacture, purchase, hire, sell, let, supply, and deal in, and to fix, alter, remove and refix gas meters, fittings, gas engines, stoves, ranges, pipes, and other appliances and apparatus for lighting, he•ting, motive power, ventilating, cooking, and other purposes for which gas may be used, and to empower the Company to supply gas for any such purposes, and to manufacture, buy, sell, and deal in coal, lime, coke, tar, ammoniacal liquor, chensioals, and other materials used in or resulting from the manufacture of gas. and to carry on any business usually carried on by a Gas Company. To regulate the price to be charged by the Company for gas, and the rate of dividends which they may divide, and, if thought fit, to provide for the variation of the mtc of divi- dends according to the price charged for gas, and to make provision for the mahatenanee and formation of insurance and reserve funds to meet deficiencies in divi ends and accidents, strikes or other extraordinary claims and circum- stances. To make provision with respect to the purity, quality, and pressure of gas to be supplied by the Company, and the testing of gas and meters, the supply of gas and lamps for public light- ing, and the erection, cleaning, lighting, extinguishing, and repairing of such lamps. To amend or repeal the provisions of the Act of 1847, with respect to the time of ordinary meetings, the scale of voting by shareholders, the number and quorum of directors, the number of directors to constitute, and the quorum of com- mittees, the holding of proxies, the remuneration of directors, and such other matters relating to the regulation and mannge- ment of the Company as may be dealt with in the Bill ; and to make other and further provisions in respect thereto, and to alter and fix the period of the year up to which the annual ac- counts of the Company shall be made up. To vary and extinguish any rights and privileges connected with any lands, streets, roads, highways, canals, sewers, drains, pipes, wires, and other apparatus and property to be acquired or interfered with by the Company, and any other rights and privileges which „would interfere with the objects and purposes of the Bill, and to confer all such rights and pri- vileges as may be necessary or convenient for effecting sueh objects and purposes. To authorize the Company to demand, levy, and recover rates, rents, and charges for the supply of gas and other mat- ters and things supplied, and services rendered by them, and to alter rates, rents, and charges, and to confer, vary, or ex- tinguish exemptions from the payment of rates, rents, and charges, and to proride for the allowance of discounts. To authorize the Company to purchase, hold, and use patent rights or licenses for the use of inventions, relative to the manufacture and supply of gas, meters, fittings, apparatus, engines, stoves, ranges, pipes, and other apparatus and ap- pliances. To incorpoiate with and apply to the Bill (sa far as may be applicable, and except so far as expresily varied thereby), all or some of the provisions of the Companies Clauses Ornsolida- tion Act, 1845, the Companies Clauses Act, 1863, and the Com- panies Clauses Act, 1869; the Lands CiRMeS Consolidation Acts, 1845, 1880, and 1869, the Gas Works Clauses Act, 1847. and the Gas Works Clauses Act, 1871, with such variations or modifications as may be thought expedient, or may be provided for by the Bill, and to make all or some of the provisions of the last-mentioned Act apply to the existing undertaking of the Company, and to amend, alter, or repeal, solar as may be necessary for the purposes of the Bill, all or Some of the pro- visions of the Act of 1847, and any other Acts relating to the Company, the Runcorn Improvement Act. 1852, and any other Act relatineto the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners, and any other Act affected by the Bill. Printed copies of the Bill will be deposited in the Private Bill Office of the Moose of Commons on or before the Twentieth day of December next Dated this Fourteenth day of November, 1884, ROBERT DAVIEts, SHARP, 8: KIRROONNEL, Market-place, Warrington, Solicitors for the Bill. GRAHAMES, CURREY, & SPENS. 30, Great George-street, Westminster, Parliamentary Agents.
